Senses.Explanation: One shout separates guest and host while illumination and use happen together; six present teachers test the claim with shouts, gestures, and questions. Qianyan Yuanzhang tells the assembly that one shout distinguishes guest and host and brings illumination and use together. He shouts, asks which of those four terms applies, shouts again and momentarily says this is each of them, then shouts again and denies all four labels before asking what it is. He closes by warning against stepping forward for an explanation. The repeated shouts make the paired line a live test of fixed classifications, not a simple one-to-one chart of roles. When a visiting monk arrives, Yun'e Xi raises and strikes his staff and gives a shout before voicing the paired line. He says the shout splits the peach pit and reveals the person within, then asks what further explanation is needed once that person is seen. His following images insist that guest remains guest and host remains host, yet asks how their fit can be spoken. The headword belongs to Yun'e's present welcoming sermon and its staff-and-shout action, not the visitor's speech. After replying to questions from monks about the hall and entry into the Way, Binya Jian strikes the Chan seat and voices the paired line. He follows it with images of white waves on a mountain and red dust beneath the sea and says one who understands it can make noon strike the third watch. He then sets aside understanding and cites an old question about what happens to the vine when the tree falls. The headword is Binya's present pivot from question-and-answer to a verse and further test. At a sermon marking his emergence as abbot and the completion of a Buddha hall, Jie'an Jin speaks of the assembled community's work and asks whether there is still an upward matter. After a pause he shouts and ends with the line that one shout separates guest and host while illumination and use happen together. The phrase is the close of his current institutional occasion and challenge, not a reply by the earlier monks in the sermon or by the next birthday-sermon participants. In a short hall address Zixian Jue first states that one shout distinguishes guest and host while illumination and use proceed together. He then gives a shout and asks the assembly whether it is guest or host; those who can separate them have an opening, while others still have work ahead. The headword is Zixian's own immediate challenge, and the source supplies no recorded successful answer from the assembly. Senses.Note: Linji says one shout can act like the diamond king’s sword, then names other possibilities and asks a monk how he understands them. Tianyin shouts before asking his own assembly which type that shout was. Chuiwan calls the scheme a second breaking of an already fixed account. Sanfeng gives the sword image a new tactical reading. Yuan’an says his present shout is sword, lion, probing pole, and a shout not used as a shout; Liao’an asks why such range can now be allowed. The image names a function, not a permanent class of sound.

After Linji's swordlike shout he adds his own response, 'demons and Buddhas cut down together'; he answers the lion, probing-pole and non-shout types with separate battle images. He then asks whether anyone understands the diamond-king shout as a monk begins to come forward. The headword remains Linji's cited line; Hanyue supplies a new tactical gloss for this occasion. At a memorial talk for attendant Jiyuan You, a monk asks Yuan'an Liao where the deceased goes when the next breath does not come. Yuan'an answers that he is always passing before the questioner's face, strikes after a stock verse, and then shouts during his sermon on life and death. He says this very shout is like the diamond king's sword and also performs the other three traditional shout functions, cutting doubt and showing the original face. Here Yuan'an applies the sword image to his own present shout rather than merely reciting Linji's older question. In an evening talk Liao'an Qingyu shouts and asks the assembly whether they know where that shout lands. He then quotes Linji's first-person fourfold list, starting with the swordlike shout, and describes how grasping saint and ordinary, subject and object, can fall away. He asks why an approach he had just rejected can now be allowed and shouts again. The sword phrase is Linji's cited wording; Liao'an uses it to test the audience's shifting 'can' and 'cannot' rather than to assign a permanent label to his own shout.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來

Senses.PreferredTarget: When the ox enters the grass, pull it back by the nose at once
AlternateTargets: Each time the ox strays into grass, seize its nose and draw it back
SearchAliases: ox enters grass pull nose back Shigong
Senses.Note: Mazu asks Shigong how he herds his ox. Shigong says that whenever it enters the grass he pulls it back by the nose. Baichi develops the image for a disciple, Xiangyan puts it in a preface on ox-herding pictures, Xingkong answers a monk who quotes it, and Beijian asks whether the familiar move is still adequate. The full pair preserves both the straying and the immediate tug.

Occurrences.Kwic: 而不宰其功，歷代祖師於此微中了悟而弗睹其狀，參玄上士於此微中咨究而罔測其蹤，由若然，則子之欲剖微也，又向何處下手耶？今再謬為解曰：世尊拈花，迦葉微笑、馬祖一喝，百丈耳聾，此其善剖微者也；龍潭吹滅紙炬而德山洞徹、臨濟喫黃檗三頓痛棒向大愚肋下還拳，此其善剖微者也；以至須彌山木上座破砂盆、娘生褲、三腳驢子弄蹄行、八角磨盤空裏走并、及五君臣、四賓主、三玄、九帶、十智同真等語如利劍轟雷，莫可紀極皆其善剖微者也。子欲剖微，能就是而學之，則無微而不剖，無剖而非微矣。外此而別求剖微之道，實非予所知也，倘若曰予之所說俱為剖微，錯下註腳耳。阿呵呵，夫復何憾？自牧說自牧說不借人力謂之自，善為調制謂之牧，能卑謙以自牧，則在在無虧，頭頭合轍矣。君亦知牧牛乎？鞭之、勒之、馴之、伏之，毋使犯苗稼，故我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌，至今參學人皆藉此以為口實也。石鞏禪師居馬祖會下，在廚作務，次祖問：「子在此作麼？」鞏云：「牧牛。」祖云：「牛作麼生牧？」鞏云：「一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來。」祖云：「子真牧牛也。」看他古人真實踐履，雖尋常作務之頃未嘗須臾忘此道，豈若近代師僧迷昧自己，向外馳求，無捍禦調護之功，而終其身坐沉黑水乎？上人號自牧，予見夫頭角崢嶸，乃為略申其義，併說偈曰：自牧、牧自，莫分一二，依而行之，更有何事？淨雲說淨雲說卷舒萬變，蔽日排空，世間之雲也，若有一毫未淨，則大地山河尚存點污，起滅不停，妄緣日積，吾心之雲也。若有一毫未淨，則生來死去終屬輪迴，是故知識出興於世，或示語言、或主棒喝，種種方便，總為諸人開迷雲、現慧日，以與天下共見耳。雲開日現即淨雲之說也，吾儕依知識之教亦當思所以淨吾心之雲，吾心之雲既淨，如獲舊物、如歸故家，心戶洞明，性天恢廓，而為雲從雲等語皆歷歷有據矣。禪人號淨雲，予乃說淨雲之義如此。常關說常關說是室坐堯峰法堂後，一座三間，未有額，予為題「常關」二字。問者曰：「據師立意，其亦門雖設常關，效陶公之賦歸去來乎？」曰：「不然也。予所謂常者，常而不常，不常而常也。常而不常，如烏兔麗天，東出西沒而弗變其位；不常而常，如江湖行地，東流西注而弗易其波也。「予所謂關者，關而不關，不關而關也。關而不關，如皇畿帝殿，防衛甚嚴而任人來往；不關而關，如懸巖窮谷，仰瞻甚邇而絕人躋攀也。「今且以虛空為堂奧
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. In a teaching for a disciple called Zimu, Baichi Xingyuan explains self-herding as guiding oneself without borrowing another's force. He quotes the old kitchen exchange in which Mazu asks Shigong Huizang how he herds his ox, and Shigong says that whenever it goes into the grass he suddenly pulls it back by the nose. Mazu approves him as a true herder. Baichi uses the old answer to urge attention during ordinary work, rather than letting the herding image become a stock phrase repeated without practice.

Occurrences.Kwic: 喫蜜相似。然古來自了漢、俱胝打地之流，雖不大興波作浪，而流芳千古者，皆真實中來。因以如意一柄與之，使其於本分中如意行持，不為物礙，管取臘月三十日得自由自在去也。偈曰：即心即佛事無差，會得從教到處誇，如意行持無不是，頭頭物物更何加？珍重。此事不論僧俗男女皆可了悟，以人人本具之佛性靈明廓徹，但為妄想執著各成異見，乃有六道四生之別。故曰：迷即眾生，悟即諸佛。只在一念回機而已。慧燈上座於辛酉歲在普明堂中聞舉即心即佛公案，而得自受用三昧，雖未到大梅田地，其固守自寶藏，不為外物所轉，志可嘉也。但惜闡尼失於參，不能再進竿頭，如啞人作夢而不能道也。然能念念不忘、心心無間，焉知不到末山總持輩境界耶？茲值六旬之誕，道人不應世諦祝慶，因書片語以助竿頭。且如做生日，不識他是阿誰生底？本來父母今在何處？請下一語相稱，是真做生日也。速道！速道！序記跋新元和尚牧牛圖序新元和尚牧牛圖序昔馬祖問石鞏：「汝在此作甚麼？」答曰：「牧牛。」祖曰：「作麼生牧？」答曰：「一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來。」祖曰：「子真善牧牛者。」以致南泉、溈山、懶安、郭功甫輩，皆牧成一頭露地白牛，踏翻香海、踢倒須彌，超然物外，得大自由。及五代時，有普明禪師，老婆心切，起模畫模，作牧牛圖并頌，自未牧初調，以致人牛兩忘，曲盡態度。其頌十首，流傳已久，倡和亦多，獨嚴𨍏轢居士和韻十有餘過。復又中興普明古剎，請我先師聞法，大振鞭策，欲使盡地奔狂，頓成獨照。新元和尚為先師猶子，首座普明則亦橐鞬從事於大牢君者，深獲牧牛之法，卜隱蓮溪，為嘉禾紳衿請住漏澤禪院，意欲耕轉鴛湖之地，以牓四維，可謂有志於大白牛車者矣。曾於丁亥示余牧牛圖一冊，皆近世名公尊宿所書，詩畫相兼，曲入奧妙。今戊午冬，余繼席開戒，和尚枉贊羯磨，說法之暇，出卷索題，展之，則又牧牛圖也。筆法古俏，形體殊絕，曲盡馴梗之狀，云是明州大老黃公之筆，其與趙文敏之用心亦勝矣。所和原韻，辭旨超逸，深得牧牛之法，則又一士大夫李次公之製，可與𨍏轢並轡。展玩再四，不忍釋手，深愧牛性未調，牛力未備，焉能提舉牧牛之旨？然已入此牛欄，或致牽繩挽鼻，於和尚分中亦大費力，只得道個吽吽，和尚亦撫掌呵呵，相忘於人牛之外。若曰題頌，其實未能。敘異記敘異記昔先師翁屬我先師云：「直指西來意，楊岐正脈通。」先師後為臨安邑侯楊琳請住縣
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB424.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangyan. In a preface to monk Xinyuan's ox-herding pictures, Xiangyan recounts Mazu asking Shigong how he herds an ox. Shigong gives the line about pulling it back by the nose when it enters the grass, and Mazu approves. The preface then traces later ox-herding figures and pictures, praises the new collection's poems and images, and admits the writer's own ox is not yet well trained. The headword is Shigong's speech within the old case; Xiangyan is the later preface writer applying it to the pictures.

Occurrences.Kwic: ，師以拄杖打，退歸方丈。示眾。「德山云：『今夜不答話。』未必心頭似口頭。『問話者，三十棒。』瞞神嚇鬼。有僧便禮拜，刺腦入膠盆。山便打，不得放過。僧云：『某甲話也未問，為甚打某甲？』不識好惡。山云：『你是那裡人？』審其來歷，僧云：『新羅人。』一款成招。山云：『未跨船舷，好與三十棒。』可謂踞虎頭、收虎尾。此則公案，據山僧看來，德山雖有偷天換日之手，檢點將來不無滲漏。當時山僧若在，只消咳嗽一聲；他若問：『作麼？』山僧便道：『看破了也。』拂袖便出，直教德山老漢倒疑三十年。且道看破個什麼？」僧便喝，師直打出堂。示眾。舉：「僧問趙州：『如何是不錯路？』州云：『識心見性是不錯路。』」師云：「且道性作麼生見？心又作麼生識？適纔有僧問：『心不在內，不在外，不在中間，畢竟在什麼處？』師垂下一足，云：『會麼？』僧云：『不會。』師云：『向紅爐點雪。』僧禮拜。」師云：「諸仁者！若識得紅爐點雪，便可見得自性；其或未然，莫道不疑好。」示眾。僧問：「古人道：『一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來。』未審點頭在什麼處？」師便打。進云：「只如不落階級又如何履踐？」師於地上一劃，云：「向這裡會取。」進云：「某甲終不與麼。」師云：「汝作麼生？」進云：「但見皇風成一片，不知何處是封疆？」師云：「收。」示眾。「古人道：『一人所在也須到，聞名不如見面；半人所在也須到，見面不如聞名。』還有見面者麼？有疑請問。」僧問：「不與萬法為侶者是什麼人？」師直與攔胸一椎。僧云：「某甲不與麼道。」師云：「作麼生？」僧云：「兩鏡相照，萬象森然。」師云：「闍黎被他換卻眼睛。」僧歸位。師云：「適來這僧未具眼在。何故聻？兩鏡相照，猶有光在；萬象森然，猶有境在。光境未忘，見地不脫，如何了得生死？若是超生脫死真實道流，直須向十字街頭識得天子、百草頭上薦取老僧始得。」示眾。「海底剔金燈，虛空釘木橛，打倒須彌山，石人驚吐舌。此四句中，有縱有奪，有殺有活，若人會得，一生參學事畢。」除夕，示眾。「春臘交加處，寒溫欲解時，山藤驅疫去，野火炤田歸。柳眼藏金線，梅腮吐玉蕊，竹聲催漸曉，幽鳥盡啼枝。」示眾。「諸仁者！選佛這裡結制，無別奇言妙語與汝諸人商量，亦勿論歲月豐儉，只要知時識候，白米八分一斗、乾柴三錢一擔。柴米貴賤且置，秖如雲門乾屎橛、洞山麻三斤、青州七斤衫、南泉二

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB461.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xingkong Zhen. An unnamed monk asks Xingkong Xingzhen where the point of assent lies in the old saying about pulling the ox back by the nose whenever it enters the grass. Xingkong strikes him. The monk asks how to practice without falling into stages; Xingkong draws a line on the ground and tells him to understand there. The monk refuses that answer and offers a verse, which Xingkong stops. The line originates in Shigong's old Mazu case but is voiced here by the questioning monk; Xingkong's blows and drawn line test more than repetition of the inherited image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一場愁。上堂：恰纔冬至過了十日，看看臈月三十日，便在眼前報恩，不是預搔待癢。且道汝等諸人，臈月三十日又作麼生折合？謝莊主，上堂。插鍬叉手，驢前馬後；㘽田愽飯，徐六擔板。開田說大義，彼此相鈍置；開得一片畬，隨手種空花。如斯作略，儘可觀光。若是移山塞海、奪食駈耕，須還我報恩門下始得。且道報恩有甚長處？。臈八，上堂，舉孝宗皇帝問佛照：釋迦佛入山六年，所成何事？佛照對云：將謂陛下忘却。師頌云：六年勤苦竟何如？為問君王記得無？直下雖知難抵諱，到頭終不受塗糊。上堂：三到投子含元殿裏，九上洞山更覔長安。自從夜雪擁鰲山，一度思量一度寒。元宵，上堂。二千年前，靈山會上，青天白日，釋迦老子平白地道：我見燈明佛，本光瑞如此。啞！相似尚如此，何況真箇是？上堂：窮廝煎，餓廝吵，古岸風高，玉壺春曉。便恁麼去，未免偏枯話墮了也。蘇盧！蘇盧！浴佛，上堂：二千年前，朱明屆八，何物老嫗，生此寧馨？九龍飜水九河傾，洗到驢年也只寧。上堂：結夏已十日，水牯牛作麼生？若道一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來，未免傷鋒犯手。不然溪東，不然溪西，但念水草，餘無所知。人牛都不見，正是月明時。上堂：教中道，衲衣在空閑，假名阿練若。誑惑世間人，自謂行真道。汝等諸人總被誑惑了也，便好拽轉，痛與一頓。若無報恩，今日失利。上堂：識得一，萬事畢。了事衲僧，一字不識。直饒恁麼，未稱全提。禹力不到處，河聲流向西。上堂：今日中夏了也，畢竟事作麼生？當陽一機，轉身一步。左右逢原，了無回互。本等牧牛人，何曾頭角露？謝監収，上堂。千年父祖舊田疇，萬寶垂成及早収。無底鉢盂開口笑，聖凡一等飽󳯲󳬕。瑞慶節，上堂：天中天，聖中聖，贊不及，述不盡。四海九州，一印印定。重明以麗乎正。開爐，上堂：今日開爐，報恩隨例。火筯香匙，各有節制。若待豆𪹼冷灰，未免󳯝相鈍置。識火色，辨風旨，曲突徙薪，已落第二。明因立菴至，上堂。若論此事，如兩陣對圓，旗皷相望，來如震霆，去如迅電。若一向繩之以孫吳，大似紲韓盧而責獲。跌宕繩墨，信手方圓，度外出奇，勝中闘劣。或遇明眼人，不滿一笑。從前汗馬無人識，何必重論蓋代功？上堂：一大藏教，總是魔說。日可冷，月可熱。是假易除，是真難滅。雪中，上堂：亂山裹雪玉崔嵬，萬行門庭八字開。惆悵善財歸去後，寥寥不見一人來。臘八，上堂：若謂如來今日成道，則為謗佛；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1365.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Beijian Jujian. Ten days into the summer retreat, Beijian Jujian asks the assembly what has happened to the water buffalo. He says that if one merely repeats the old line about pulling it back by the nose when it enters the grass, one risks cutting one's own hand. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 喫蜜相似。然古來自了漢、俱胝打地之流，雖不大興波作浪，而流芳千古者，皆真實中來。因以如意一柄與之，使其於本分中如意行持，不為物礙，管取臘月三十日得自由自在去也。偈曰：即心即佛事無差，會得從教到處誇，如意行持無不是，頭頭物物更何加？珍重。此事不論僧俗男女皆可了悟，以人人本具之佛性靈明廓徹，但為妄想執著各成異見，乃有六道四生之別。故曰：迷即眾生，悟即諸佛。只在一念回機而已。慧燈上座於辛酉歲在普明堂中聞舉即心即佛公案，而得自受用三昧，雖未到大梅田地，其固守自寶藏，不為外物所轉，志可嘉也。但惜闡尼失於參，不能再進竿頭，如啞人作夢而不能道也。然能念念不忘、心心無間，焉知不到末山總持輩境界耶？茲值六旬之誕，道人不應世諦祝慶，因書片語以助竿頭。且如做生日，不識他是阿誰生底？本來父母今在何處？請下一語相稱，是真做生日也。速道！速道！序記跋新元和尚牧牛圖序新元和尚牧牛圖序昔馬祖問石鞏：「汝在此作甚麼？」答曰：「牧牛。」祖曰：「作麼生牧？」答曰：「一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來。」祖曰：「子真善牧牛者。」以致南泉、溈山、懶安、郭功甫輩，皆牧成一頭露地白牛，踏翻香海、踢倒須彌，超然物外，得大自由。及五代時，有普明禪師，老婆心切，起模畫模，作牧牛圖并頌，自未牧初調，以致人牛兩忘，曲盡態度。其頌十首，流傳已久，倡和亦多，獨嚴𨍏轢居士和韻十有餘過。復又中興普明古剎，請我先師聞法，大振鞭策，欲使盡地奔狂，頓成獨照。新元和尚為先師猶子，首座普明則亦橐鞬從事於大牢君者，深獲牧牛之法，卜隱蓮溪，為嘉禾紳衿請住漏澤禪院，意欲耕轉鴛湖之地，以牓四維，可謂有志於大白牛車者矣。曾於丁亥示余牧牛圖一冊，皆近世名公尊宿所書，詩畫相兼，曲入奧妙。今戊午冬，余繼席開戒，和尚枉贊羯磨，說法之暇，出卷索題，展之，則又牧牛圖也。筆法古俏，形體殊絕，曲盡馴梗之狀，云是明州大老黃公之筆，其與趙文敏之用心亦勝矣。所和原韻，辭旨超逸，深得牧牛之法，則又一士大夫李次公之製，可與𨍏轢並轡。展玩再四，不忍釋手，深愧牛性未調，牛力未備，焉能提舉牧牛之旨？然已入此牛欄，或致牽繩挽鼻，於和尚分中亦大費力，只得道個吽吽，和尚亦撫掌呵呵，相忘於人牛之外。若曰題頌，其實未能。敘異記敘異記昔先師翁屬我先師云：「直指西來意，楊岐正脈通。」先師後為臨安邑侯楊琳請住縣

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 一場愁。上堂：恰纔冬至過了十日，看看臈月三十日，便在眼前報恩，不是預搔待癢。且道汝等諸人，臈月三十日又作麼生折合？謝莊主，上堂。插鍬叉手，驢前馬後；㘽田愽飯，徐六擔板。開田說大義，彼此相鈍置；開得一片畬，隨手種空花。如斯作略，儘可觀光。若是移山塞海、奪食駈耕，須還我報恩門下始得。且道報恩有甚長處？。臈八，上堂，舉孝宗皇帝問佛照：釋迦佛入山六年，所成何事？佛照對云：將謂陛下忘却。師頌云：六年勤苦竟何如？為問君王記得無？直下雖知難抵諱，到頭終不受塗糊。上堂：三到投子含元殿裏，九上洞山更覔長安。自從夜雪擁鰲山，一度思量一度寒。元宵，上堂。二千年前，靈山會上，青天白日，釋迦老子平白地道：我見燈明佛，本光瑞如此。啞！相似尚如此，何況真箇是？上堂：窮廝煎，餓廝吵，古岸風高，玉壺春曉。便恁麼去，未免偏枯話墮了也。蘇盧！蘇盧！浴佛，上堂：二千年前，朱明屆八，何物老嫗，生此寧馨？九龍飜水九河傾，洗到驢年也只寧。上堂：結夏已十日，水牯牛作麼生？若道一回入草去，驀鼻拽將來，未免傷鋒犯手。不然溪東，不然溪西，但念水草，餘無所知。人牛都不見，正是月明時。上堂：教中道，衲衣在空閑，假名阿練若。誑惑世間人，自謂行真道。汝等諸人總被誑惑了也，便好拽轉，痛與一頓。若無報恩，今日失利。上堂：識得一，萬事畢。了事衲僧，一字不識。直饒恁麼，未稱全提。禹力不到處，河聲流向西。上堂：今日中夏了也，畢竟事作麼生？當陽一機，轉身一步。左右逢原，了無回互。本等牧牛人，何曾頭角露？謝監収，上堂。千年父祖舊田疇，萬寶垂成及早収。無底鉢盂開口笑，聖凡一等飽󳯲󳬕。瑞慶節，上堂：天中天，聖中聖，贊不及，述不盡。四海九州，一印印定。重明以麗乎正。開爐，上堂：今日開爐，報恩隨例。火筯香匙，各有節制。若待豆𪹼冷灰，未免󳯝相鈍置。識火色，辨風旨，曲突徙薪，已落第二。明因立菴至，上堂。若論此事，如兩陣對圓，旗皷相望，來如震霆，去如迅電。若一向繩之以孫吳，大似紲韓盧而責獲。跌宕繩墨，信手方圓，度外出奇，勝中闘劣。或遇明眼人，不滿一笑。從前汗馬無人識，何必重論蓋代功？上堂：一大藏教，總是魔說。日可冷，月可熱。是假易除，是真難滅。雪中，上堂：亂山裹雪玉崔嵬，萬行門庭八字開。惆悵善財歸去後，寥寥不見一人來。臘八，上堂：若謂如來今日成道，則為謗佛；

Occurrences.Kwic: 睛眼便花。除却黃龍頭角外，自餘渾是赤斑蛇。法昌小剎，路遠山遙。景物蕭疎，游人罕到。敢謂黃龍禪師曲賜光臨，不唯泉石生輝，亦乃人天欣悅。然雲行雨施，自古自今。其奈爐鞴之所，鈍銕尤多。良醫之門，病者愈甚。瘥病須求靈藥，銷頑必藉金錘。法昌這裏有幾箇垛根阿師，病者病在膏肓，頑者頑入骨隨。若非黃龍老漢到來，總是虗生浪死。拈拄杖，曰：要會麼？打麵還他州土麥，唱歌須是帝鄉人。問：古鏡未磨時如何？師曰：却須磨取。曰：未審如何下手？師曰：鏡在甚麼處？僧遂作一圓相，師便打曰：這漆桶，碌甎也不識。師與感首座歲夜喫湯次，座曰：昔日北禪師分歲，曾烹露地白牛。和尚今分歲，有何施設？師曰：臘雪連山白，春風透戶寒。座曰：大眾喫箇甚麼？師曰：莫嫌冷淡無滋味，一飽能消萬劫饑。座曰：未審是甚麼人置辦？師曰：無慙愧漢，來處也不知。英、勝二首座到山相訪，英曰：和尚尋常愛點檢諸方，今日因甚麼却來古廟裏作活計？師曰：打草祇要蛇驚。英曰：莫塗糊人好。師曰：你又刺頭入膠盆作甚麼？英曰：古人道，我見兩箇泥牛鬬入海，所以住此山。

Senses.Explanation: One sitting-cloth’s area of ground is a small plot conceived through the space occupied by a monastic sitting cloth. In the Huineng land story, Huineng asks Chen Yaxian for 一坐具地 and displays his cloth when Chen asks how broad it is. Later speakers stretch that compact measure rhetorically. Qingxi says that Bodhidharma’s one patch was occupied at once after Shenguang’s three bows; Yingshan and Zijian identify monastery precincts as this one sitting-cloth ground; Boshan locates it amid the sense fields; and an unnamed monk claims that the whole earth is his sitting-cloth ground, beyond even a buddha’s encroachment. The scale can expand from a requested plot to the whole earth, but the cloth-based image remains the measure. The headword is the cloth-based land measure; ordinary references to land without the sitting cloth do not establish this unit.

Senses.Explanation: To bury people or their competing positions together in one pit is to reject them in a single disposal verdict. Huitong Qingdan gives this answer when his teacher contrasts the two Baizhang cause-and-effect responses. Yunju Zhuang applies it to Huisi and Zhigong; Wuzhun Shifan applies it when a monk brings Zhaozhou and Xuansha into his questions; Dahui Zonggao uses it to appraise Pang and his daughter Lingzhao together. The image does not require an actual burial: it refuses to preserve either side as the successful answer. In the retained Chinese Zen cases, one-pit burial is a shared-disposal verdict. Huitong Qingdan directly answers a wild-fox challenge with it; other masters direct it at different pairs. The two X66 files repeat one old Yunju comment, so only the fuller X66n1296 copy remains.

Miaoyun Zhenxiong recounts visiting his elder Muyun, who forbids him to answer by raising a fist or shouting and asks for one honest phrase. Miaoyun offers the quiet-hall couplet. Muyun immediately asks how he would respond to the old injunction not to stay where there is Buddha and to hurry past where there is none; Miaoyun answers that this is where he stakes his life, and Muyun strikes him. The couplet is Miaoyun's remembered reply in a live teacher-student test, not a final verdict accepted without further probing.

Linquan Conglun has been discussing sayings about the Buddha in a jeweled hall and the fire-flame teachings of Xuefeng and Yunmen. He says these startling images share a line of force, asks the assembly whether they understand, and closes with the quiet-hall couplet. The phrase is Linquan's present conclusion to a sequence of old statements; the earlier Buddha, Xuefeng, and Yunmen are figures he cites, not speakers of this final line.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the old exchange in which Emperor Suzong asks National Teacher Zhong what teaching he received at Caoxi, and Zhong answers by asking whether the emperor sees a cloud in the sky. Tianyin praises Zhong's answer but asks what the emperor could have said to turn the exchange around. After a long pause Tianyin supplies the quiet-hall couplet. The line is Tianyin's own proposed turning word for this cited emperor-teacher encounter, not a reply uttered by Zhong or Suzong in the old case.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan. At the closing of a retreat Yinyuan Longqi speaks of opening the gates, driving out idle ghosts, and leaving the hall empty, quiet, and awake. He voices the quiet-hall couplet for this inner-hall matter, then asks what word will serve monks traveling east or west. An attendant raises a fist; Yinyuan smiles and answers with an image of a slight misstep on the road. The couplet describes the cleared teaching space, while the subsequent exchange tests what can be carried beyond it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J35/J35nB343.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyin of Shengjue Monastery, Guangfu Mountain. Miyin Zhenchuan has just answered a monk's question about clear seeing and hearing with a sharp warning. In his ensuing address he speaks of hearing the river and seeing clear light, then warns against looking for the Way in famous teachers or in words. He asks how to say one clear, undimmed phrase and answers with the quiet-hall couplet. The line is Miyin's current answer to his own question about clarity, not a quotation from the next old case raised in the following sermon.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB387.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gusuzun. At a hall sermon requested by lay donor Wen Yunsheng, a monk asks Gusu Zun how humans and devas meet and see one another. Gusu answers directly with the quiet-hall couplet. The monk then asks separately about Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the donor's benefit; Gusu gives different replies and strikes when the monk tries to continue. The couplet belongs to the first question in this current exchange, not to all of the later questions or to the donor's blessing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Holding the fly-whisk, Tian'an Sheng asks what shape the wind has and rejects guesses that it is round, square, flat or long. He then says speaking, listening, and investigating are each like the wind, asking whether he himself is speaking and whether the assembly is hearing. He closes that present address with the cool-hall couplet. The line gathers his argument that the matter is clear through those activities without being captured by any one shape or verbal description.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB191.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangtian Jinian. At the opening of a retreat Jinian Jingxian raises his fly-whisk, puts it down, and asks what remains when the devices used to catch fish or rabbits and the words used to reach meaning are forgotten. He questions whether seeing mind or nature in familiar formulas is enough, then asks what counts as a monk's real hold on the matter. He answers with the cool-hall couplet. This is Jinian's current conclusion to a series of live gestures and questions, not a phrase spoken by Bodhidharma in the saying he discusses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB206.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Xiaotang. At a hall address accepting the abbacy of Sanju Hermitage, a lay visitor asks Xiaotang what is happening as the new master ascends the seat, setting aside the hall's usual style. Xiaotang gives the cool-hall couplet. The visitor replies with moon and wind images; Xiaotang dismisses them as surplus talk and says silence would be better. The couplet is Xiaotang's direct answer to this visitor, and his follow-up prevents the visitor's decorative verse from being treated as an agreed interpretation.

Zhiyan Xiu recalls a conversation with Yulin, who asks where Zhiyan's former teacher Tiantong can now be seen. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB220.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Faxiyin. On entering Qinghua Monastery, Faxi Yin moves through its buildings with brief remarks and offerings. At the ancestral hall he voices the cool-hall couplet, asks what exactly is clear, pauses, and gives a terse exclamation. He then moves to the abbot's quarters and uses his staff in a separate set of host-and-guest gestures. The couplet belongs to Faxi's present ancestral-hall address and its open question, not to those later gestures.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB365.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shipuzhi. After a monk has asked about sweeping an old teacher's stupa, Shipu Chaozhi strikes his staff and allows the assembly to look. The monk asks what word is available at an unexpected meeting; Shipu answers with the cool-hall couplet. When the monk adds a decorative image of a phoenix and unicorn, Shipu strikes him and warns him not to see wrongly. The couplet is Shipu's direct reply in this stupa exchange, and the blow marks his refusal to let the monk's embellishment stand as its explanation.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB415.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miaoyun of Dabei. Miaoyun Zhenxiong recounts visiting his elder Muyun, who forbids him to answer by raising a fist or shouting and asks for one honest phrase. Miaoyun offers the quiet-hall couplet. Muyun immediately asks how he would respond to the old injunction not to stay where there is Buddha and to hurry past where there is none; Miaoyun answers that this is where he stakes his life, and Muyun strikes him. The couplet is Miaoyun's remembered reply in a live teacher-student test, not a final verdict accepted without further probing.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the old exchange in which Emperor Suzong asks National Teacher Zhong what teaching he received at Caoxi, and Zhong answers by asking whether the emperor sees a cloud in the sky. Tianyin praises Zhong's answer but asks what the emperor could have said to turn the exchange around. After a long pause Tianyin supplies the quiet-hall couplet. The line is Tianyin's own proposed turning word for this cited emperor-teacher encounter, not a reply uttered by Zhong or Suzong in the old case.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan. At the closing of a retreat Yinyuan Longqi speaks of opening the gates, driving out idle ghosts, and leaving the hall empty, quiet, and awake. He voices the quiet-hall couplet for this inner-hall matter, then asks what word will serve monks traveling east or west. An attendant raises a fist; Yinyuan smiles and answers with an image of a slight misstep on the road. The couplet describes the cleared teaching space, while the subsequent exchange tests what can be carried beyond it.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J35/J35nB343.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyin of Shengjue Monastery, Guangfu Mountain. Miyin Zhenchuan has just answered a monk's question about clear seeing and hearing with a sharp warning. In his ensuing address he speaks of hearing the river and seeing clear light, then warns against looking for the Way in famous teachers or in words. He asks how to say one clear, undimmed phrase and answers with the quiet-hall couplet. The line is Miyin's current answer to his own question about clarity, not a quotation from the next old case raised in the following sermon.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB387.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gusuzun. At a hall sermon requested by lay donor Wen Yunsheng, a monk asks Gusu Zun how humans and devas meet and see one another. Gusu answers directly with the quiet-hall couplet. The monk then asks separately about Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the donor's benefit; Gusu gives different replies and strikes when the monk tries to continue. The couplet belongs to the first question in this current exchange, not to all of the later questions or to the donor's blessing.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng. Holding the fly-whisk, Tian'an Sheng asks what shape the wind has and rejects guesses that it is round, square, flat or long. He then says speaking, listening, and investigating are each like the wind, asking whether he himself is speaking and whether the assembly is hearing. He closes that present address with the cool-hall couplet. The line gathers his argument that the matter is clear through those activities without being captured by any one shape or verbal description.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB191.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangtian Jinian. At the opening of a retreat Jinian Jingxian raises his fly-whisk, puts it down, and asks what remains when the devices used to catch fish or rabbits and the words used to reach meaning are forgotten. He questions whether seeing mind or nature in familiar formulas is enough, then asks what counts as a monk's real hold on the matter. He answers with the cool-hall couplet. This is Jinian's current conclusion to a series of live gestures and questions, not a phrase spoken by Bodhidharma in the saying he discusses.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB206.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Xiaotang. At a hall address accepting the abbacy of Sanju Hermitage, a lay visitor asks Xiaotang what is happening as the new master ascends the seat, setting aside the hall's usual style. Xiaotang gives the cool-hall couplet. The visitor replies with moon and wind images; Xiaotang dismisses them as surplus talk and says silence would be better. Senses.Explanation: A cool, spare hall and a clear old meaning form one lexical couplet in two graphic spellings across twelve distinct present contexts. Miaoyun Zhenxiong recounts visiting his elder Muyun, who forbids him to answer by raising a fist or shouting and asks for one honest phrase. Miaoyun offers the quiet-hall couplet. Muyun immediately asks how he would respond to the old injunction not to stay where there is Buddha and to hurry past where there is none; Miaoyun answers that this is where he stakes his life, and Muyun strikes him. The couplet is Miaoyun's remembered reply in a live teacher-student test, not a final verdict accepted without further probing. Linquan Conglun has been discussing sayings about the Buddha in a jeweled hall and the fire-flame teachings of Xuefeng and Yunmen. He says these startling images share a line of force, asks the assembly whether they understand, and closes with the quiet-hall couplet. The phrase is Linquan's present conclusion to a sequence of old statements; the earlier Buddha, Xuefeng, and Yunmen are figures he cites, not speakers of this final line. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the old exchange in which Emperor Suzong asks National Teacher Zhong what teaching he received at Caoxi, and Zhong answers by asking whether the emperor sees a cloud in the sky. Tianyin praises Zhong's answer but asks what the emperor could have said to turn the exchange around. After a long pause Tianyin supplies the quiet-hall couplet. The line is Tianyin's own proposed turning word for this cited emperor-teacher encounter, not a reply uttered by Zhong or Suzong in the old case. At the closing of a retreat Yinyuan Longqi speaks of opening the gates, driving out idle ghosts, and leaving the hall empty, quiet, and awake. He voices the quiet-hall couplet for this inner-hall matter, then asks what word will serve monks traveling east or west. An attendant raises a fist; Yinyuan smiles and answers with an image of a slight misstep on the road. The couplet describes the cleared teaching space, while the subsequent exchange tests what can be carried beyond it. Miyin Zhenchuan has just answered a monk's question about clear seeing and hearing with a sharp warning. In his ensuing address he speaks of hearing the river and seeing clear light, then warns against looking for the Way in famous teachers or in words. He asks how to say one clear, undimmed phrase and answers with the quiet-hall couplet. The line is Miyin's current answer to his own question about clarity, not a quotation from the next old case raised in the following sermon. At a hall sermon requested by lay donor Wen Yunsheng, a monk asks Gusu Zun how humans and devas meet and see one another. Gusu answers directly with the quiet-hall couplet. The monk then asks separately about Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and the donor's benefit; Gusu gives different replies and strikes when the monk tries to continue. The couplet belongs to the first question in this current exchange, not to all of the later questions or to the donor's blessing. Holding the fly-whisk, Tian'an Sheng asks what shape the wind has and rejects guesses that it is round, square, flat or long. He then says speaking, listening, and investigating are each like the wind, asking whether he himself is speaking and whether the assembly is hearing. He closes that present address with the cool-hall couplet. The line gathers his argument that the matter is clear through those activities without being captured by any one shape or verbal description. At the opening of a retreat Jinian Jingxian raises his fly-whisk, puts it down, and asks what remains when the devices used to catch fish or rabbits and the words used to reach meaning are forgotten. He questions whether seeing mind or nature in familiar formulas is enough, then asks what counts as a monk's real hold on the matter. He answers with the cool-hall couplet. This is Jinian's current conclusion to a series of live gestures and questions, not a phrase spoken by Bodhidharma in the saying he discusses. At a hall address accepting the abbacy of Sanju Hermitage, a lay visitor asks Xiaotang what is happening as the new master ascends the seat, setting aside the hall's usual style. Xiaotang gives the cool-hall couplet. The visitor replies with moon and wind images; Xiaotang dismisses them as surplus talk and says silence would be better. The couplet is Xiaotang's direct answer to this visitor, and his follow-up prevents the visitor's decorative verse from being treated as an agreed interpretation. Occurrences.Kwic: 過去是現在弟子，實有此理。天童悟云：我若作阿難，待世尊云是我弟子，但問佛是甚麼人弟子，擬開口便作禮休去。蓮柎䇿云：阿難當時見道是吾弟子，何不便禮三拜，管教黃面老子置身無地。世尊坐次，見二人舁豬過，乃問：者個是甚麼？曰：佛具一切智，豬子也不識。世尊曰：也須問過。太陽玄云：不因世尊問，幾乎忘却。地藏恩云：老漢也是無端節目上更生節目，忽被二人呵呵大笑，舁豬便行，一場懡㦬。壽昌經云：君子有成人之美。萬峯藏云：舁向前過，世尊早墮了也。資福侶云：利動君子。綠雨蕉云：世尊大似勾賊破家，設使二人待問，便打豬一棒，云何不抵對？世尊又如何折合？捨筏懷兼濟，逢耕更問津却將未歸意，說與欲行人。世尊！因異學問：諸法是常耶？世尊！不。對曰：諸法是無常耶？世尊！亦不。對曰：世尊！具一切智何不對我？世尊曰：汝之所問皆為戲論。高峯妙云：異學有言：若啞世尊，無語如雷。

Occurrences.Kwic: 和尚當頭道。師曰：河北驢鳴，河南犬吠。問：如何是佛？師咄曰：這驢漢。問：盡大地是一隻眼底人來時如何？師曰：堦下漢。問：諸佛不到處，是甚麼人行履？師曰：聃耳鬅頭。曰：何人通得彼中信？師曰：驢面獸腮。問：隨緣認得時如何？師曰：錯。問：如何是西來意？師曰：一人傳虗，萬人傳實。問：不落干將手，如何是太阿？師曰：七星光彩耀，六國罷煙塵。問：鶴立枯松時如何？師曰：地下底一場懡㦬。問：會昌沙汰時，護法善神向甚麼處去？師曰：三門前兩箇一場懡㦬。問：滴水滴凍時如何？師曰：日出後一場懡㦬。洛京靈泉歸仁禪師洛京靈泉歸仁禪師初問疎山：枯木生花，始與他合。是這邊句，是那邊句？山曰：亦是這邊句。師曰：如何是那邊句？山曰：石牛吐出三春霧，靈󳭋不棲無影林。住後，僧問：如何是靈泉家風？師曰：十日作活九日病。曰：此病如何？師曰：回避不得。曰：還療得也無？

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以道。當時便與推倒。若便向至白無白處。認著正是墮在無色界中。雪竇所以別指出一條活路。向推倒處。却教扶起。佛眼云。若向這裏扶持起來。甚生次第事。萬松道。若是他宗異派。不道不得。更須知有洞上宗風正倒時便起。正起時便倒底時節。然後起倒同時。起倒不立。更買草鞋。行脚三十年不見。佛覺頌云。一色無過指示人。白銀世界裏頻申。超然推倒還扶起。爭似東風煦日新。萬松道。日出後一場懡㦬。一等學人。見雲門推倒雪竇扶起。便作機鋒轉換。大用無方會。見向一色邊不得色邊會。以為宗旨血脈。已有佛覺為證。如或不信。更問天童。頌云。一倒一起雪庭師子慎於犯而懷仁。勇於為而見義清光照眼似迷家明白轉身還墮位衲僧家了無寄同死同生何此何彼暖信破梅兮春到寒枝涼飈脫葉兮秋澄潦水師云。雲門一倒。雪竇一起。仰山指師子。要過此色。三箇鼎足闕一不可。三玄三要盡在於茲。仰山恐人

Senses.Explanation: Not establishing a single speck of dust is an absolute clearing claim that masters use, test in interviews, and explicitly refuse to treat as arrival. Konggu Daocheng pairs it with every scene empty. Yizhong Zhiji answers a minister's room-capacity question with it, then lifts the curtain when challenged. Tianyin Yuanxiu says it is still halfway; Ruibai Mingxue assigns it while asking what the close examination is. Questioners also present it as an accomplished state. Hanyue Fazang answers one such formulation, while Gulin Qingmao responds to an unnamed questioner's inference from crossed swords by congratulating him on peace under heaven—a public check rather than an interpretive definition.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB186.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Linyexi. At a tonsure and novice-ordination sermon, Linye Tongqi says that when one speck enters right reception, complete command arises in all specks. He follows this with the release of every speck from entanglement and tells the new practitioners that grasping this would repay both parents and Buddha. If they cannot, he urges them to shave, wear robes, enter the community, and seek senior teachers; he then asks what to do after entering. The line starts a practical exhortation on training rather than describing an isolated supernatural event.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1350.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baoning Renyong. Baoning Renyong gives the one-speck line and immediately reverses it: all specks enter right reception and complete command arises in one speck. Senses.Explanation: One speck enters right reception; complete command arises in all specks. Five present teachers work with this relation of one and many. At a tonsure and novice-ordination sermon, Linye Tongqi says that when one speck enters right reception, complete command arises in all specks. He follows this with the release of every speck from entanglement and tells the new practitioners that grasping this would repay both parents and Buddha. If they cannot, he urges them to shave, wear robes, enter the community, and seek senior teachers; he then asks what to do after entering. The line starts a practical exhortation on training rather than describing an isolated supernatural event. Sanyi Mingyu raises his fly-whisk and says that the beings of the whole earth are addressed through one speck entering right reception, while complete command arises in all specks. He immediately adds images of daylilies easing grief, birds understanding speech, and creatures sensing weather. The paired one-and-many line is Sanyi's present declaration with the whisk, placing ordinary natural responses beside it; the surrounding old case and later memorial sermon are separate occasions. In a requested hall sermon Zhe'an Jingfan says the Buddhas' treasury is open to beings according to their capacities and then applies the one-speck and all-specks line to the work of a monk. He moves from it to speech as sharp as metal, rapid responsiveness, dogs and cocks voicing the teaching, and the danger of drawing rigid boundaries around experience. He says he has been pressed to speak by the patrons and invites everyone to enter the same open gate, before sending them to the meal. The line is Zhe'an's current call to respond without fixed divisions. Baofu says a thief has a guilty conscience, Changqing says they have grown, and Yunmen says 'barrier.' Hongzhi follows with his own verse weighing the four old speakers and warning against smoothing away their turns. The headword is Cuiyan's challenge inside the inherited case; Hongzhi's verse is a later response, not another summer-end utterance by Cuiyan. Qianyan Yuanzhang introduces Cuiyan Lingcan's summer-end eyebrow question, followed by Baofu's guilty-thief reply, Changqing's 'grown' reply and Yunmen's 'barrier.' Qianyan then gives a new verse picturing Cuiyan losing his brows and the people in the house noticing, with further painful blows to follow. The headword is Cuiyan's old question as quoted here; Qianyan's verse comments on the cost and force of the exchange without becoming a fifth reply inside it. Yuejiang Zhengyin raises Cuiyan's old summer-end eyebrow challenge and the three replies from Baofu, Changqing and Yunmen. He then composes a verse that names the four and pictures people in one boat treating one another as opponents, with eyebrows lost and regrown. The headword remains Cuiyan's speech in the cited old case; Yuejiang's present act is to recast the interplay among the four figures in verse. Wuyi Yuanlai quotes the same exchange: Cuiyan asks the assembly whether his brows remain after a summer of speaking, and Baofu, Changqing and Yunmen give their compact responses. Wuyi comments that each old master has shown a hand, then asks what their replies really accomplished and warns the listeners to cherish their own eyebrows. The headword is Cuiyan's old question; Wuyi's later question tests the value of all four moves rather than reporting a new Cuiyan sermon.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB463.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gumeilie of Weishan. At the close of the winter practice period, a monk asks Gumei Dinglie about binding and releasing. Gumei answers with a sealed door and a door opened wide. Asked what instruction to take away at release, he gives the traveler's hat, bundle and staff carrying clear wind and bright moon. If someone ahead demands an account of the winter at Guishan, he replies that the weather is warm and there is no need to approach the fire. When the monk bows and says he will go spread the word, Gumei strikes him and warns against false reports. He then asks for a sentence of release, strikes his staff and gives the falling-blossom couplet. That open, spreading image is immediately checked: staying here for winter and going elsewhere for summer can both be mere secondhand echoes with one's heels off the ground. Asked how someone firmly grounded travels, he finally repeats staying here for winter and going there for summer. The couplet is Gumei's own release sentence, but neither the beautiful scene nor outward travel alone certifies the monk's footing.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. The anthology's inline section explicitly names Xuedou Zhijian and records a brief hall address: the World-Honored One has an intimate saying, and Kasyapa does not conceal it. Xuedou then gives the night of falling flowers and the fragrance of flowing water throughout the city. The natural image is his present continuation of the inherited saying, not an additional sentence attributed directly to the Buddha or Kasyapa. It puts the tension between intimacy and nonconcealment into something diffusely perceptible: fragrance travels with the water. The unit supplies no monk's question, explanation of a secret content, staff gesture or further reply. The preceding accounts of a woman providing baths and other named teachers belong to separate inline sections and must not be assigned to this speaker. Nor should the nearby, different heading for Xuedou Chi be conflated with the explicitly named Zhijian section.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1350.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baoning Renyong. Baoning Renyong declares that it is raised at all times and spoken everywhere, with no prohibitions or interruption. Holding his staff horizontally, he asks whether the assembly understands and gives the falling-blossom couplet. He then strikes the staff once and leaves the seat. The phrase is his own completion of the address, not an answer to a recorded monk's question. Its fragrance spreading through the city gives a concrete image for the preceding unrestricted raising and speaking, while his held and struck staff makes the presentation an action before the listeners as well as words. He suddenly takes up his staff, draws a line or sweeping mark with it, and says the falling-blossom couplet. Both the strange horn contrasts and the flower-and-water close belong to his present turn. The couplet moves from contradictory-looking classifications to a spreading sensory scene after a staff gesture; the source does not identify each animal with a particular doctrinal position or state that flowers are mind and water is knowing. No monk's question, reply of approval or further action is recorded in this unit. The preceding imperial scripture ceremony and the following Buddha-bathing address are separate occasions, so their political and ritual purposes should not be imported as the immediate occasion of this couplet.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB463.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gumeilie of Weishan. At the close of the winter practice period, a monk asks Gumei Dinglie about binding and releasing. Gumei answers with a sealed door and a door opened wide. Asked what instruction to take away at release, he gives the traveler's hat, bundle and staff carrying clear wind and bright moon. If someone ahead demands an account of the winter at Guishan, he replies that the weather is warm and there is no need to approach the fire. When the monk bows and says he will go spread the word, Gumei strikes him and warns against false reports. He then asks for a sentence of release, strikes his staff and gives the falling-blossom couplet. That open, spreading image is immediately checked: staying here for winter and going elsewhere for summer can both be mere secondhand echoes with one's heels off the ground. Asked how someone firmly grounded travels, he finally repeats staying here for winter and going there for summer. The couplet is Gumei's own release sentence, but neither the beautiful scene nor outward travel alone certifies the monk's footing.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 斷人舌頭底句，直下如大火聚，近之則燎却面門。道舊至，上堂。青山白雲裏，客來無可迎。草藥帶煙掘，野茶和露烹。磐陀石上坐，長嘯時一聲。擊拂子，下座。朝廷看藏經滿散，上堂：毗盧藏中有大經卷，量等三千大千世界，書寫三千大千世界中事悉盡無餘。今上皇帝以清淨天眼觀此大經卷在一微塵中，敦遣使臣頒降御香，命天下僧員破此一塵、出此經卷，普使法界有情知一一塵中有如是經卷，一一經卷有如是章句，一一章句有如是妙義，一一妙義有如是奇特、如是殊勝、如是廣大、如是自在。今朝滿散之次，仍命山僧升于此座，舉揚無上般若，表懺上項功德，所有種種法門智慧海、種種因果德相海、種種進修行願海、種種教導方便海、種種依正究竟海、種種互融攝入海、不可說不可說種種功德光明海，普用回向真如實際，莊嚴無上佛果菩提，四方銷兵革之憂，萬民樂畊桑之業。正與麼時，八表來朝、萬󳬛入貢一句作麼生道？但見皇風成一片，不知何處是封疆。上堂。心不是佛，兔馬有角；智不是道，牛羊無角。驀拈拄杖畫一畫，云：一夜落華雨，滿城流水香。浴佛，上堂。指天指地稱第一，胞胎曾出向今朝，雲門打殺與狗喫，翔鳳山僧惡水澆。示眾：兄弟，此箇夢幻㲉子，一呼吸間便歸無常，向此娑婆界上覓箇甚麼物作依倚憑仗？有什麼佛法禪道可學？有甚麼玄解義路可求？設有求得學得底，試拈出一絲頭看。直饒𡎺得一肚皮，口裏說得一堆一擔，也只虗頭詐偽、妄想記憶中來，臘月三十日一點也用不著。何如直下無事，向自己衣單下密密體會取好？豈不見古人云：參須實參，悟須實悟。閻羅大王，不怕多語。結夏，上堂。二千二百五十年前，光明藏中金口親曾付囑。二千二百五十年後，比丘行端其當顯示。護生須是殺，殺盡始安居。會得箇中意，鐵船水上浮。上堂，舉：僧問風穴：如何是佛？穴云：丈林山下竹筋鞭。師頌云：丈林山下竹筋鞭，疑殺禪和萬萬千，唯有首山提得起，新婦騎驢阿家牽。上堂，謝夏齋秉拂。雪峯和尚云：演一句，則千句萬句流通，拈向一邊；飲一味，則千味百味具足，置之一壁。雪峯低頭歸庵。巖頭聞云：雪峯與我同條生，不與我同條死，且作麼生臨朕碪？井底種林禽，今年桃李貴，一顆直千金。為別谷和尚入祖堂。白雲作叢林紀綱，以達磨居中，開山居左，百丈居右，天下依而行之，絲毫無有紊亂。別谷和尚在茲山為二十六代，涓以此日居于此堂，晨香夕燈，其永無替。為此上座下

The couplet moves from contradictory-looking classifications to a spreading sensory scene after a staff gesture; the source does not identify each animal with a particular doctrinal position or state that flowers are mind and water is knowing. ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 一夜落華雨，滿城流水香

Senses.Explanation: A night of falling blossoms becomes fragrance carried through the city by running water. The image gives a sensuous close to different teaching turns: release from a practice period, an answer to hiddenness, unrestricted expression, and a challenge to fixed claims about mind and knowing. Its local force depends on those turns rather than a single decoded meaning for flowers or water. At the close of the winter practice period, a monk asks Gumei Dinglie about binding and releasing. Gumei answers with a sealed door and a door opened wide. Asked what instruction to take away at release, he gives the traveler's hat, bundle and staff carrying clear wind and bright moon. If someone ahead demands an account of the winter at Guishan, he replies that the weather is warm and there is no need to approach the fire. When the monk bows and says he will go spread the word, Gumei strikes him and warns against false reports. He then asks for a sentence of release, strikes his staff and gives the falling-blossom couplet. That open, spreading image is immediately checked: staying here for winter and going elsewhere for summer can both be mere secondhand echoes with one's heels off the ground. Asked how someone firmly grounded travels, he finally repeats staying here for winter and going there for summer. The couplet is Gumei's own release sentence, but neither the beautiful scene nor outward travel alone certifies the monk's footing. The anthology's inline section explicitly names Xuedou Zhijian and records a brief hall address: the World-Honored One has an intimate saying, and Kasyapa does not conceal it. Xuedou then gives the night of falling flowers and the fragrance of flowing water throughout the city. The natural image is his present continuation of the inherited saying, not an additional sentence attributed directly to the Buddha or Kasyapa. It puts the tension between intimacy and nonconcealment into something diffusely perceptible: fragrance travels with the water. The unit supplies no monk's question, explanation of a secret content, staff gesture or further reply. The preceding accounts of a woman providing baths and other named teachers belong to separate inline sections and must not be assigned to this speaker. Nor should the nearby, different heading for Xuedou Chi be conflated with the explicitly named Zhijian section. Baoning Renyong declares that it is raised at all times and spoken everywhere, with no prohibitions or interruption. Holding his staff horizontally, he asks whether the assembly understands and gives the falling-blossom couplet. He then strikes the staff once and leaves the seat. The phrase is his own completion of the address, not an answer to a recorded monk's question. Its fragrance spreading through the city gives a concrete image for the preceding unrestricted raising and speaking, while his held and struck staff makes the presentation an action before the listeners as well as words. The surrounding collection contains separate discussions of knowing, language and changing seasons; those should not be fused into one continuous dialogue or treated as a stated explanation of each blossom. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 。法眼因僧問：「如何是曹源一滴水？」師曰：「曹源一滴水。」答處仍將問處酬，從來直道懶綢繆，茆庵一個源頭上，那管飛花逐水流？天台韶國師因聞前語即得開悟萬山堆裏碧崔嵬，占斷春風消息稀，無意反聞聞底事，曹源一滴絕流機。宋太祖問：「臥龍深處不朝天，來此何事？」雪竇云：「難逃至化。」白雲巖下不貪閒，直欲敲開金鎖關，不是無心逃至化，大都有意面堯顏。宋太祖托缽問王隨：「大庾嶺頭提不起，今日因何在朕手裏？」丞相無語。不忘付囑作家君，治化淵源迥不群，托起缽盂輕借問，智臣應得諳斯文。僧問投子：「一大藏教，還有奇特事也無？」師曰：「演出一大藏教。」嘗言一字值千金，寫盡黃庭一卷經，世上所傳皆膺本，徒然留得換鵝名。五祖戒禪師因僧問：「如何是佛？」曰：「踏著秤錘硬似鐵。」秤錘踏著硬紏紏，拾得歸來便好休，只個己靈仍不重，阿誰更向佛邊求？太陽玄禪師曰：「道即不辭，恐上紙筆在。」驀會觀音吳道畫，始知處處得逢渠，道即不辭恐上紙，斯言鐫石又何如？清涼燈禪師問：「如何是西來意？」僧曰：「不東不西。」師不肯，僧即躡前問，師曰：「不東不西。」殺活從來作者機，莫將心識妄思齊，鳳凰鳴在青霄上，爭比山雞胡亂啼？慈炤圓禪

Senses.Explanation: The entire Buddhist canon cannot explain it is Yuanwu's polemical appraisal of the canon's inability to reach the matter. Yuanwu places the line in a four-part parallel: the buddhas only know it themselves, the patriarchs cannot present it, the canon cannot explain it, and clear-eyed patch-robed monks cannot save themselves. The source leaves the object contextual, so the translation does not invent one.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB192.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daxiu Zhu. Daxiu Zhu stresses how difficult it is to obtain human life, become a monk, practice seriously and awaken. He says monastery rules and discipline work on a person’s habitual conduct, then warns that anger can lead to a beast’s condition. He raises an account in which Buddha points out ants that have remained ants through the time of seven Buddhas. Daxiu draws his own conclusion: once human birth is lost, it is not regained for countless ages. The exact pair is his current warning after that story, not a continuation of Buddha’s quoted words. He applies it to present anger, harmful schemes and the responsibility of influencing others. His claim supplies urgency for conduct and serious practice; it should not be turned into an independently established chronology of rebirth.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. Guxue Zhenzhe first raises his whisk and asks the assembly about seeing, then strikes it and asks about hearing. He tells the monks that genuinely understanding birth and death is different from merely learning explanations. As death approaches, borrowed understanding may still leave them frantic, just as talking about food cannot fill a stomach. He therefore urges real inquiry and actual realization and warns against wasting a life: once human birth is lost, it is not regained for countless ages. He follows with Yuanwu’s illness exposing the limits of his cleverness and Dahui’s refusal to be satisfied with premature approval. Guxue is the present speaker of the pair. The warning turns the sensory demonstration toward the need to test understanding in one’s own life, rather than treating correct talk about seeing and hearing as sufficient.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1318.xml). Continued Essentials from the Sayings of Ancient Worthies. In the X68 record of Yunmen Wenyan’s speech, Yunmen urges listeners with something genuine to investigate to remain with it for ten or twenty years rather than wander from region to region for pleasant scenery, meals and clothing. He asks how they can repay the support of donors and teachers and what they will rely upon when dying, when empty boasts will no longer help. He then warns them not to let time pass idly: once human birth is lost, it is not regained for countless ages. He closes by urging effort and invoking the worldly saying that one may die in the evening after hearing the way in the morning. The exact pair belongs to Yunmen’s recorded admonition, not the monk questions that follow it. Here it focuses a travelling practitioner’s responsibility and use of time; it is not a separate new case each time the same speech is copied into a lamp.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1376.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chijue Daochong. Chijue Daochong turns the warning around in an instruction to the officer Shaoming. He says Bodhidharma brought poison from the west and that Shenguang alone was struck by it, losing human birth beyond recovery; the poison then spread through the generations. He describes Linji as poisoned at Huangbo and later venting it through shouts, and Xinghua as passing it on through blows and expulsion. Chijue asks who among the present teachers and travelling monks has truly taken this poison and can use it well. Thus Chijue is the current speaker, while Shenguang, Linji and Xinghua are figures in his provocative account. Unlike the other retained warnings, this use deliberately gives irreversible loss a valued role in transmission. It should not be flattened into a literal claim that those patriarchs became animals or into ordinary advice merely to avoid danger.

He says monastery rules and discipline work on a person’s habitual conduct, then warns that anger can lead to a beast’s condition. He raises an account in which Buddha points out ants that have remained ants through the time of seven Buddhas. Daxiu draws his own conclusion: once human birth is lost, it is not regained for countless ages. The exact pair is his current warning after that story, not a continuation of Buddha’s quoted words. He applies it to present anger, harmful schemes and the responsibility of influencing others. His claim supplies urgency for conduct and serious practice; it should not be turned into an independently established chronology of rebirth. Guxue Zhenzhe first raises his whisk and asks the assembly about seeing, then strikes it and asks about hearing. He tells the monks that genuinely understanding birth and death is different from merely learning explanations. As death approaches, borrowed understanding may still leave them frantic, just as talking about food cannot fill a stomach. He therefore urges real inquiry and actual realization and warns against wasting a life: once human birth is lost, it is not regained for countless ages. He follows with Yuanwu’s illness exposing the limits of his cleverness and Dahui’s refusal to be satisfied with premature approval. Guxue is the present speaker of the pair. The warning turns the sensory demonstration toward the need to test understanding in one’s own life, rather than treating correct talk about seeing and hearing as sufficient. In the X68 record of Yunmen Wenyan’s speech, Yunmen urges listeners with something genuine to investigate to remain with it for ten or twenty years rather than wander from region to region for pleasant scenery, meals and clothing. He asks how they can repay the support of donors and teachers and what they will rely upon when dying, when empty boasts will no longer help. He then warns them not to let time pass idly: once human birth is lost, it is not regained for countless ages. He closes by urging effort and invoking the worldly saying that one may die in the evening after hearing the way in the morning. The exact pair belongs to Yunmen’s recorded admonition, not the monk questions that follow it. Here it focuses a travelling practitioner’s responsibility and use of time; it is not a separate new case each time the same speech is copied into a lamp. Chijue Daochong turns the warning around in an instruction to the officer Shaoming. He says Bodhidharma brought poison from the west and that Shenguang alone was struck by it, losing human birth beyond recovery; the poison then spread through the generations. He describes Linji as poisoned at Huangbo and later venting it through shouts, and Xinghua as passing it on through blows and expulsion. Chijue asks who among the present teachers and travelling monks has truly taken this poison and can use it well. Thus Chijue is the current speaker, while Shenguang, Linji and Xinghua are figures in his provocative account. Unlike the other retained warnings, this use deliberately gives irreversible loss a valued role in transmission. It should not be flattened into a literal claim that those patriarchs became animals or into ordinary advice merely to avoid danger.

Senses.PreferredTarget: When one child leaves home as a monk, nine degrees of kin rise to heaven
AlternateTargets: One child’s ordination brings the extended family to heaven
SearchAliases: one child becomes monk nine degrees kin heaven
one son leaves home nine clans ascend heaven
Senses.Note: This familiar saying claims that one person’s ordination benefits a wide span of family. Masters cite it while speaking of parental gratitude, memorial rites, or the benefit of entering religious life. The line is a received claim in these sources; some monk questions challenge how it fits cases of relatives still suffering.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. Monk Ligen asks Miyun Yuanwu for a verse to commend deceased relatives. Miyun says one must first know how to benefit oneself before benefiting others, because the living and departed share the same present matter. He then cites the old saying that one child leaving home brings heavenly benefit to nine kin groups. The line is Miyun's present quotation in a short memorial verse request; its earlier author is not named, and the surrounding claim concerns effective practice rather than a recorded ascent to heaven.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB185.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushi. At the placement of the remains of temple officer Guyu's father, mother and elder sister in a stupa, Fushi Tongxian recites the maxim that one child leaving home raises nine kin groups to heaven. He immediately calls it an old saying that is not empty, lifts the remains, and asks the assembly whether they understand before adding a pathfinding image. The speaker here is Fushi conducting a family memorial act; the source does not identify the maxim's first author or report that the relatives visibly ascended.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB192.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daxiu Zhu. Writing to his nephew Wulun, Daxiu Zhu recalls the deaths of his mother and brother and says he has stayed away, lost sleep, completed his religious work and carried on the ancestral teaching to repay care from earlier generations. He applies the line about one child leaving home benefiting nine kin groups to his own course, then asks the nephew to encourage two younger relatives and take care of family matters. The phrase is Daxiu's present claim in a family letter, not a command that Wulun himself must take robes.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi Xingyuan addresses the monk Rixiu before he goes to see his living mother. Baichi rejects the idea that a monastic may simply abandon parents, remembers his own inability to care for his mother directly, and says his present work can still repay parental kindness. He cites the old maxim about one child leaving home and nine kin groups reaching heaven, then gives Rixiu a verse about visiting his mother. The saying is a received claim used to argue for filial responsibility; Baichi is its current citer, not a named original author.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB395.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Qizhencheng of Neihuguo Monastery, Jingnan. In a personal account of his parents, Qizhen Cheng recalls losing his father, fleeing conflict with his mother and later losing her too. He says he took robes to repay them, then cites the community's teaching that one child leaving home benefits nine kin groups in heaven. He treats the saying as trustworthy and writes a birthday verse for his deceased mother about seeking benefit through worship. This is Qizhen's filial memoir and devotional application of a cited maxim, not a report of a witnessed heavenly event.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. Monk Ligen asks Miyun Yuanwu for a verse to commend deceased relatives. Miyun says one must first know how to benefit oneself before benefiting others, because the living and departed share the same present matter. He then cites the old saying that one child leaving home brings heavenly benefit to nine kin groups. The line is Miyun's present quotation in a short memorial verse request; its earlier author is not named, and the surrounding claim concerns effective practice rather than a recorded ascent to heaven.

At the placement of the remains of temple officer Guyu's father, mother and elder sister in a stupa, Fushi Tongxian recites the maxim that one child leaving home raises nine kin groups to heaven. He immediately calls it an old saying that is not empty, lifts the remains, and asks the assembly whether they understand before adding a pathfinding image. The speaker here is Fushi conducting a family memorial act; the source does not identify the maxim's first author or report that the relatives visibly ascended.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB192.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daxiu Zhu. Writing to his nephew Wulun, Daxiu Zhu recalls the deaths of his mother and brother and says he has stayed away, lost sleep, completed his religious work and carried on the ancestral teaching to repay care from earlier generations. He applies the line about one child leaving home benefiting nine kin groups to his own course, then asks the nephew to encourage two younger relatives and take care of family matters. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB395.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Qizhencheng of Neihuguo Monastery, Jingnan. In a personal account of his parents, Qizhen Cheng recalls losing his father, fleeing conflict with his mother and later losing her too. He says he took robes to repay them, then cites the community's teaching that one child leaving home benefits nine kin groups in heaven. He treats the saying as trustworthy and writes a birthday verse for his deceased mother about seeking benefit through worship. This is Qizhen's filial memoir and devotional application of a cited maxim, not a report of a witnessed heavenly event.

Senses.Explanation: A received saying links one child leaving home for monastic life with benefit to nine kin groups; five current speakers apply it to filial duties or memorial acts. Monk Ligen asks Miyun Yuanwu for a verse to commend deceased relatives. Miyun says one must first know how to benefit oneself before benefiting others, because the living and departed share the same present matter. He then cites the old saying that one child leaving home brings heavenly benefit to nine kin groups. The line is Miyun's present quotation in a short memorial verse request; its earlier author is not named, and the surrounding claim concerns effective practice rather than a recorded ascent to heaven. At the placement of the remains of temple officer Guyu's father, mother and elder sister in a stupa, Fushi Tongxian recites the maxim that one child leaving home raises nine kin groups to heaven. He immediately calls it an old saying that is not empty, lifts the remains, and asks the assembly whether they understand before adding a pathfinding image. The speaker here is Fushi conducting a family memorial act; the source does not identify the maxim's first author or report that the relatives visibly ascended. Writing to his nephew Wulun, Daxiu Zhu recalls the deaths of his mother and brother and says he has stayed away, lost sleep, completed his religious work and carried on the ancestral teaching to repay care from earlier generations. He applies the line about one child leaving home benefiting nine kin groups to his own course, then asks the nephew to encourage two younger relatives and take care of family matters. The phrase is Daxiu's present claim in a family letter, not a command that Wulun himself must take robes. Baichi Xingyuan addresses the monk Rixiu before he goes to see his living mother. Baichi rejects the idea that a monastic may simply abandon parents, remembers his own inability to care for his mother directly, and says his present work can still repay parental kindness. He cites the old maxim about one child leaving home and nine kin groups reaching heaven, then gives Rixiu a verse about visiting his mother. The saying is a received claim used to argue for filial responsibility; Baichi is its current citer, not a named original author. Senses.Explanation: Once one word enters the official gate, even nine oxen cannot pull it back warns that a public commitment is hard to reverse. Four speakers adapt the legal image to a monastery deed, a vow, an earlier exchange, and a portrait praise. Pufu Zhuo holds up an old document concerning the monastery's land and calls it the ancestors' deed of self-sale. He says he cannot state a fifth wish, because even nine oxen cannot drag back a word once it enters the official gate. The proverb explains his comic refusal to add another public pledge. Sanyi Mingyu recounts an older encounter in which a master promises to answer a monk about the ancestral meaning when Rufu nods. Sanyi inserts the official-gate proverb immediately after that promise, marking how a spoken condition can bind the speaker before the old exchange continues. In a praise of Bodhidharma's portrait, Jieweizhou Xingzhou recalls the meeting with the Liang emperor, the move to Shaolin, and later people trying to recover Bodhidharma's face from an image. He closes with the official-gate proverb, making the public trace of that story difficult to take back or resolve.

Senses.Explanation: Once a word enters the government office, nine oxen cannot drag it out: the saying describes words that cannot be taken back. Ruibai Mingxue uses it after warning that the ancestral seal must be protected. Liao’an Qingyu and Tianyin Yuanxiu quote Ying'an Tanhua's wording before commenting or supplying parallel sayings. Xieyun Jiji and Wenmu Nian turn the same irretrievability toward their own words.

Senses.PreferredTarget: One stroke hangs down at both ends
SearchAliases: one stroke hangs down at both ends
Senses.Note: Muchen gives this as an answer to the paired formulas “the three realms are only mind” and “the myriad things are only consciousness.” Wanru says it when a monk asks whether an ancient ascent and the present teaching are the same or different, then challenges the monk’s conclusion. Yi’an uses it when a bamboo strip must neither be named nor left unnamed. Mixing and Qibai answer comparisons between an earlier figure and a present one. The one-mark, two-end image holds the terms together without choosing either simple identity or simple separation.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB182.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wanru. A monk asks Wanru Tongwei whether the Buddha's old ascent to teach and Wanru's hall address today are the same or different. Wanru replies with the one-character, two-ends image. When the monk says today's event is thus the old one, Wanru asks where the ancient figure is; the monk shouts and Wanru strikes him. The phrase is Wanru's first answer in an active old-versus-present exchange, and the blow prevents the monk's easy identification from settling it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB394.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yi’an. A monk presents Yi'an Shanzan with a bamboo-strip challenge: naming it touches it, refusing the name turns away, so what can it be called without either error? Yi'an answers with the one-character, two-ends image. The monk bows and Yi'an adds that the original cannot be marked by strokes. Entries.SourceTerm: 一字是一字，一句是一句

Senses.PreferredTarget: One character is one character; one sentence is one sentence.
AlternateTargets: A word stays a word, and a sentence stays a sentence
Senses.Note: Two independent named-master hall poems use this exact paired line for different turns: Wuzu Fayan amid returning home and ordinary steps, Hanyue Fazang (Sanfeng Zang) amid not misquoting a Chan instruction. Five other exact source files recopy one of those poems; the two-family depth exception is provisional and scoped.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1318.xml). Continued Essentials from the Sayings of Ancient Worthies. In the Wuzu Fayan section of this recorded collection, Wuzu's hall verse says that realizing and not realizing return along the old road home. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB299.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Sanfeng Zang. In a separate hall sermon Hanyue Fazang, called Sanfeng Zang in this record, cites the older warning not to remain where there is a Buddha, not to linger where there is none, and not to report the instruction wrongly when meeting someone far away. He then insists that one character is one character and one sentence is one sentence, immediately turns with 'then do not go', and continues into a flower-plucking verse about disturbing body and mind. The selected line is Hanyue's present insistence on the exact words and turn of an instruction, rather than a copy of Wuzu's homecoming poem.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase means “one room has six windows” in Zhongyi Hong'en's comparison offered to Yangshan Huiji. Five distinct records preserve the headword inside the full Zhongyi–Yangshan case: Yangshan asks about seeing Buddha-nature, Zhongyi describes the six-window room and its answering macaque, Yangshan asks about the sleeping macaque, and Zhongyi descends, takes his hand, and dances. The fuller recensions continue with the tiny jiaoming insect on a mosquito's eyelash, while later records explicitly connect the six apertures with mutual functioning at the six sense-root gates and also test or criticize Zhongyi's comparison.

Recorded Sayings of Baichi, Buddha-birthday and entombment address: Baichi Xingyuan imagines peace before the Buddha's birth and Bodhidharma's arrival, then describes the stir caused by their appearances with one ape calling and many answering, and one household's affair making a hundred busy. Senses.Explanation: One household's affair keeps a hundred households busy: a single event draws many others into its repercussions. Foyin Liaoyuan uses the proverb to appraise Mahakasyapa's attempt to expel Manjusri; several anthologies repeat that one comment. Shoushan Xingnian gives it as an answer to a monk's question about seeing, while Chushi Fanqi uses it to react to Yunmen's words and staff gesture. Miyun's record quotes Dahui summing up appraisals of Lingyun with the proverb, then shows Miyun challenging it. Baichi Xingyuan applies the spreading bustle to the history of teaching before returning to the day's communal duties. The proverb marks repercussions that mobilize many beyond the household directly involved.

Senses.Explanation: The once-each-year of the Chan records: the ritual calendar's single yearly round — counted at the solstice, handed as incense, laughed over the tea, and priced as an annual disaster by turns. Zhufeng Zhenxu raises the whisk and rules Old Gautama's day a once-each-year disaster for his descendants, while he, the seat-follower Xu, rises and falls along with him, each at his own convenience, before the donor feast where pearl and jade are all flung away and the Vulture-peak assembly seems never to have dispersed, Yezhu Fuhui, wild monk of the mountain, after the meal strongly brewing the East Court tea, sends word to the way-attainers everywhere — once each year laughing at cloud-mists — and asked what the laugh is, holds a long silence: the wall bursts, the lamp flies at the trees, the rafter slips, the moon leaks through the robe, Lianfeng Su counts one heat each year and one cold each year at the solstice — the massed yin stripped away, one yang reborn, great houses and village elders congratulating each other while the man of the groves sees only leaf-fall at the treetops and frost heaped at the roof-corner, dozing hooded in his patched blanket, and Shanyi Ruchun, at the founder's memorial, weighs the hundred-thousand-li sea crossing, the loss at the emperor's court, the uprooting before the peak, the tricked arm-cutting that killed the heroic spirits' laughter for a thousand years — why then once each year one burning of incense, the five tones and six pitches each finding their key? Shaweng Huihai on his own annual day is ashamed the way-work lies fallow while once each year he draws the crowd busy — mounting the hall, standing in for the drum, saying nothing, borrowing tortoise-hair to spread it, until seeing and hearing open wide in a laughing face, Zizhou Chuan, reciting the seventeenth generation's Ying'an Hua at the grand memorial, concedes the old teacher's whole career — every trick failing to close, twenty years on the curving chair, sheep's heads hung and dog meat sold — proof-less, and yet the incense burns once each year while a thousand years' regret cuts deeper, Feiyin Tongrong at the old teacher's memorial day asks what the season is — the deedless body shown, the stilling teaching spoken, neither eye-seen nor ear-heard — and answers: the once-each-year incense day, the whole realm manifest with nothing hidden, and Poshan Haiming on the enlightenment day lets his mouth flap once each year — all the sweet melons and the bitter melons told out together, while the crowd that cannot offer them gets the comet-star and sand in the eye.

Senses.Note: The formula gathers a full year into one count. Speakers use it especially when the old year ends, asking what has been done or what the turning of the year reveals. The number functions as the wording of the source formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歸未合，遠山無限碧層層。上堂：一冬二冬，你儂我儂。暗中偷笑，當面脫空。雖是尋常茶飯，誰知米裏有虫。豈不見南泉道，夜來好風，吹折門前一枝松。上堂：開口即錯，閉口即喪。不開不合，十萬八千。到這裏如何通信？監院昨日設齋，若僧若行俱飽，燈籠露柱亦飽。一飽忘百飢，人人盡展眉。太平無事日，唱箇囉囉哩。好大哥！上堂：一年三百六十日，臘月盡是歲除夜。夜來臘月已盡，舊歲當去，今日新歲到來。及至天曉，大開門戶，祇候新歲，竟不見來。躊躇良久，正沒理會處，忽然撞著箇聦明大王出來道：長老，長老，好把曆日子細看，更有一箇閏月在。山僧被佗點破，不覺呵呵大笑：過去已過去，未來亦未來，即今名現在，現在安在哉？三段不同，收歸上科。卓拄杖一下。上堂：若論
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1382.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wuzhun Shifan. In a hall address at the turn of the year, Wuzhun Shifan says that the year's 360 days have reached New Year's Eve. He imagines opening the doors at dawn to welcome the new year, then finding it absent, until a clever visitor points out an intercalary month on the calendar. Wuzhun laughs and turns the calendar joke into a question about where the present moment is. The year count sets up that shift; the visitor voices the leap-month objection, not the headword.

Occurrences.Kwic: 昨夜飄梧葉，地北天南又早秋。師一日入園，見典座割瓜，師問：刈得幾个祖師頭？座云：三十個。師云：那個皮下有血？座云：和尚何得重重相戲？師云：好心不得好報。八月旦，開堂，請監收并謝雨，上堂。今朝八月初一，天外雲收日出。夜來灌門龍王見大神變降注大雨，盡大地草木叢林、稻禾菽粟皆得霑濟。隆教寺裏普請監收，個個得人。一年三百六十日，管取粥足飯足，江南兩浙春寒秋熱。下座。育王石堂和尚遺書至，并入祖堂。上堂：五十三年，弄巧成拙。踏破虗空赤脚行，萬象森羅咲不徹。大眾，個是育王石室和尚末後為人底句子。明如杲日，寬若太虗。權實照用俱備，擒縱殺活皆全。可以津濟四生，可以梯航九有。蚊子上鐵牛，無你插觜處。卓拄杖：這裏見得，無一處不睹慈容，無一時
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1421.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yu’an Zhiji. At the first-day-of-the-eighth-month hall gathering, Yu'an Zhiji thanks for rain and addresses the monastery's overseers and workers. He says the rain has helped grasses, trees and crops, and that the workers at Longjiao Temple are capable. Yu'an then promises that through the year's 360 days they will have enough gruel and rice. The headword measures the coming span of communal provision, rather than marking New Year's Eve in this case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 在語默上。我且問渠：不在語默上，畢竟在甚麼處？畢竟如何是離語默底事？有等噇酒糟漢，便來擎拳竪指，下喝行棒，此輩正好分付在東園裏運糞。若真寂禪，未夢見在。咦！賣扇老婆手遮日，笑殺匋街趙七郎。除夜普說。四時八節循環過，挨到今宵歲已窮。簡點一年成底事，却如夢幻一場空。諸仁者，當此臘月三十日到來，試各自簡點看。此一年三百六十日中，不耕而食，不織而衣，享檀信之膏脂，飲行人之汗血，畢竟作麼生消受？又一年三百六十日中，親師取友，問道參禪，探諸佛之教言，窮祖師之命脉，畢竟有何進益？又一年三百六十日中，歲變月遷，時移刻減，光陰迅速，剎那不住，既無駐顏妙藥，又無換骨靈丹，畢竟作麼生得不蹉跎光陰去？此事且置，祇如大限到來，四大分離，識神無
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian. In a New Year's Eve general talk, Yongjue Yuanxian asks the assembled practitioners to examine what they accomplished during the year. He first asks how they can rightly consume the food and clothing supplied by donors and workers; he then asks what progress came from visiting teachers, seeking companions and studying teaching; finally he asks how not to squander swiftly passing time. The repeated 360-day count makes each question cover their whole year, and Yongjue presses them to account for it.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. In a New Year's Eve small gathering, Miyun Yuanwu says that all 360 days have collided with this night, when the matter is fully exposed. He turns at once to the ancient image of the moment of death, when the light of each sense organ falls away and ordinary seeing and knowing cease. The year count opens his direct address to the listeners; the later death passage is presented as an old comparison, not a separate speaker of the headword.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. In a New Year's Eve small gathering, Baichi Xingyuan says the year's 360 days are nearly spent. He pictures firecrackers in one village, paper offerings in another, and people running to collect debts, then asks why the audience has come to demand something of him when he owes them nothing. After a pause he says it is better to go home and greet the new year tomorrow. The headword launches Baichi's year-end challenge about what the audience seeks from him.

Occurrences.Kwic: ：蘇嚧蘇嚧。也是折錐探地。明眼漢到者裏，若作佛法商量，正是平地死人；不作佛法商量，坐在荊棘林裏，三千里賣却布單，特為此事而來，何曾夢見十方聚會？選佛場開，長期百二十日，諸人若善參詳，明取生佛未具已前透頂透底，便是沒量漢也。阿呵呵，也大奇，搖扇取涼，伸脚打睡，三萬六千日，自倒還自起。咄！咄！咄！除夜，小參。一年三百六十日，今夜方始到頭，是汝諸人於自己分上事，亦須知有到頭時節，若未得到頭，直須向前決擇。豈不見？大隨和尚參七十餘員善知識，具大眼目者只有一二。且如何是具大眼目者？五祖老人海上參尋十數員尊宿，洎至浮山圓鑑會中，直是開口不得，後到白雲，咬破一箇鐵餕餡，方得百味具足。遂云：花發雞冠媚早秋，誰人能染紫絲頭？有時風動頻
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. At a New Year's Eve small gathering, Gulin Qingmao tells his listeners that the year's 360 days end tonight and asks whether their own matter has likewise reached an end. If it has not, he urges further discernment. He then recalls Dasui's visits to many teachers and Wuzu's search that led through Fushan to Baiyun, using these earlier examples to press the current audience. Gulin speaks the headword; the older masters appear in his following illustration.

Occurrences.Kwic: ：胡漢俱隱。師云：古人可謂隱顯無礙，去來自由。山僧即不然，忽遇明鏡來時如何？只向他道：禮拜了退。且道與他古人相去多少？若也道得，自然不坐在明鏡裡；若道不得，且向胡漢邊著到。久立。臘八，上堂。毛頭星現出山來，此日平生眼豁開，大地眾生總成佛，與誰携手上高臺？除夜，小參。如來無禪，祖師無意，明眼衲僧討甚巴鼻？一年三百六十日、七十二候、二十四氣一時過了，明朝依舊孟春猶寒，即今夜靜更深，諸人正好休去、歇去。若真箇休歇得去，佛也不奈你何、祖也不奈你何，更說什麼生魔、死魔、煩惱魔、五陰魔、天魔、鬼魔？便好出三界、破魔網，與他眾魔同一手，作諸勞侶。外道六師是汝之師，汝師所墮，汝亦隨墮，毀於佛、謗於法，不入眾數。阿呵呵！會也麼？自從舞得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. In a New Year's Eve small gathering, Liao'an Qingyu says the year's 360 days, seventy-two seasonal periods and twenty-four solar terms have all passed, while tomorrow still brings the cold of early spring. He tells the listeners that this late night is a good time to rest completely, and says that such rest would leave even Buddhas, patriarchs and demons no hold on them. The headword measures the completed annual cycle before Liao'an turns to the present night's practical injunction.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ：蘇嚧蘇嚧。也是折錐探地。明眼漢到者裏，若作佛法商量，正是平地死人；不作佛法商量，坐在荊棘林裏，三千里賣却布單，特為此事而來，何曾夢見十方聚會？選佛場開，長期百二十日，諸人若善參詳，明取生佛未具已前透頂透底，便是沒量漢也。阿呵呵，也大奇，搖扇取涼，伸脚打睡，三萬六千日，自倒還自起。咄！咄！咄！除夜，小參。一年三百六十日，今夜方始到頭，是汝諸人於自己分上事，亦須知有到頭時節，若未得到頭，直須向前決擇。豈不見？大隨和尚參七十餘員善知識，具大眼目者只有一二。且如何是具大眼目者？五祖老人海上參尋十數員尊宿，洎至浮山圓鑑會中，直是開口不得，後到白雲，咬破一箇鐵餕餡，方得百味具足。遂云：花發雞冠媚早秋，誰人能染紫絲頭？有時風動頻

At a New Year's Eve small gathering, Gulin Qingmao tells his listeners that the year's 360 days end tonight and asks whether their own matter has likewise reached an end.
