ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 一年三百六十日，今夜方始到頭

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ：胡漢俱隱。師云：古人可謂隱顯無礙，去來自由。山僧即不然，忽遇明鏡來時如何？只向他道：禮拜了退。且道與他古人相去多少？若也道得，自然不坐在明鏡裡；若道不得，且向胡漢邊著到。久立。臘八，上堂。毛頭星現出山來，此日平生眼豁開，大地眾生總成佛，與誰携手上高臺？除夜，小參。如來無禪，祖師無意，明眼衲僧討甚巴鼻？一年三百六十日、七十二候、二十四氣一時過了，明朝依舊孟春猶寒，即今夜靜更深，諸人正好休去、歇去。若真箇休歇得去，佛也不奈你何、祖也不奈你何，更說什麼生魔、死魔、煩惱魔、五陰魔、天魔、鬼魔？便好出三界、破魔網，與他眾魔同一手，作諸勞侶。外道六師是汝之師，汝師所墮，汝亦隨墮，毀於佛、謗於法，不入眾數。阿呵呵！會也麼？自從舞得
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. In a New Year's Eve small gathering, Liao'an Qingyu says the year's 360 days, seventy-two seasonal periods and twenty-four solar terms have all passed, while tomorrow still brings the cold of early spring. He tells the listeners that this late night is a good time to rest completely, and says that such rest would leave even Buddhas, patriarchs and demons no hold on them. The headword measures the completed annual cycle before Liao'an turns to the present night's practical injunction.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 一年三百六十日、七十二候、二十四氣一時過了

Senses.Explanation: The year's three hundred sixty days names the complete annual round, which these teachers use to test what has happened or what must be done at a particular moment. In a hall address at the turn of the year, Wuzhun Shifan says that the year's 360 days have reached New Year's Eve. He imagines opening the doors at dawn to welcome the new year, then finding it absent, until a clever visitor points out an intercalary month on the calendar. Wuzhun laughs and turns the calendar joke into a question about where the present moment is. The year count sets up that shift; the visitor voices the leap-month objection, not the headword. At the first-day-of-the-eighth-month hall gathering, Yu'an Zhiji thanks for rain and addresses the monastery's overseers and workers. He says the rain has helped grasses, trees and crops, and that the workers at Longjiao Temple are capable. Yu'an then promises that through the year's 360 days they will have enough gruel and rice. The headword measures the coming span of communal provision, rather than marking New Year's Eve in this case. In a New Year's Eve general talk, Yongjue Yuanxian asks the assembled practitioners to examine what they accomplished during the year. He first asks how they can rightly consume the food and clothing supplied by donors and workers; he then asks what progress came from visiting teachers, seeking companions and studying teaching; finally he asks how not to squander swiftly passing time. The repeated 360-day count makes each question cover their whole year, and Yongjue presses them to account for it. In a New Year's Eve small gathering, Miyun Yuanwu says that all 360 days have collided with this night, when the matter is fully exposed. He turns at once to the ancient image of the moment of death, when the light of each sense organ falls away and ordinary seeing and knowing cease. The year count opens his direct address to the listeners; the later death passage is presented as an old comparison, not a separate speaker of the headword. In a New Year's Eve small gathering, Baichi Xingyuan says the year's 360 days are nearly spent. He pictures firecrackers in one village, paper offerings in another, and people running to collect debts, then asks why the audience has come to demand something of him when he owes them nothing. After a pause he says it is better to go home and greet the new year tomorrow. The headword launches Baichi's year-end challenge about what the audience seeks from him. If it has not, he urges further discernment. Senses.PreferredTarget: The year is nearly gone tonight, and the traveller ten thousand miles away has not come home
SearchAliases: the year is nearly gone tonight, and the traveller ten thousand miles away has not come home
Senses.Note: The year is ending, yet a traveller far away has not returned. Guxue speaks the line while saying that the news of home is already present; Luyan asks how someone who has reached home would hear it. Yuejian presses the assembly to identify the unreturned one, and Gulin answers with the possibility of someone never outside in the first place. The old homesickness image becomes a test of what “home” and “return” mean in the listener’s own situation.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. In a New Year's Eve address, Guxue Zhenzhe first answers a monk's questions about place, person and higher teaching, finally striking when the monk presses that last question. Guxue then says that year, month, day and hour have ended, yet people fail to trust the news of getting home. He recites the image of a traveller still far from home and asks the assembled monks whether their knots of doubt are exhausted. His further description of release depends on that answer; the headword is Guxue's present poetic challenge, not the earlier monk's reply.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB452.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lüyan He. In a New Year's Eve address to the community, Luyan He recites the year-ending night and the distant traveller who has not returned. He says that one who has arrived home could handle every move intimately, then asks for a phrase that shows arrival home. If the listeners can answer, they may sit together and speak of nonarising; otherwise, he asks how someone still unable to return to the rich homeland could travel in fine clothes at night. The traveller image sets up Luyan's test of recognition, not a report about an actual journey.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：大小歸宗，大似騎賊馬殺賊，未為好手。有問薦福：如何是佛？拈棒便打。至日，上堂。竪拂子，云：過去佛，現在佛，未來佛，只今在東湖拂子頭上聚首同觀。東方金色光明雲，西方銀色光明雲，中央黃色光明雲，無端露明柱子出來。彈指一聲，呵呵大笑。且道笑箇什麼？俗氣不除。佛成道日，上堂。打圓相，云：這一星兒，二千二百年前臘月八夜，輝天鑑地，放大光明。釋迦老子與一切眾生同一眼見，同證無上正等正覺，惟有薦福主丈子不曾將眼󳬇著。何故？鄉自用鄉法。除夜，小參。一年將盡夜，萬里未歸人。師召眾，云：且道誰是未歸者？三世諸佛止宿草菴、歷代祖師坐在半途、天下老和尚正買草鞋行脚，我此現前一眾不慕諸聖、不重己靈，飢來喫飯、困則噇眠，石爛松枯，誰管你一年將盡不盡？似這般底，正是純鋼打就、生銕鑄成。雖然，畢竟如何是到家句？只今歸去便歸去，欲覔了時無了時。元日上堂：新年頭佛法鏡清，道有智門道無。行盡江南江北路，家家門首釘桃符。元宵，上堂，謝兩斑：治國者，元首明，股肱良，則庶事康。薦福：股肱良，法道昌，萬炬蓮開優鉢香。上堂：漁舟一箇
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1392.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuejian. At a New Year's Eve small gathering, Yuejian recites the year-ending traveller line, calls to the assembly and asks who the unreturned person is. He contrasts Buddhas lodging in a grass hut, patriarchs halted halfway and teachers still buying travel sandals with his present community, which simply eats when hungry and sleeps when tired. He then asks for a phrase of getting home and answers that one may return now without seeking a final time of completion. Yuejian voices the headword and probes the image; the Buddhas and patriarchs are figures in his comparison.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1412.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gulin Qingmao. At a New Year's Eve small gathering, Gulin Qingmao recites the distant traveller line and asks the assembly who has not returned. He imagines someone replying that the person has never gone in or out, then recalls Linji's two people: one always on the road without leaving home, the other always home without leaving the road. Gulin asks who deserves offerings and strikes his staff before giving his own verse about finding the way and sparing one's worn feet. The headword is Gulin's present question; Linji supplies a later cited comparison, not the present utterance.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 云：大小歸宗，大似騎賊馬殺賊，未為好手。有問薦福：如何是佛？拈棒便打。至日，上堂。竪拂子，云：過去佛，現在佛，未來佛，只今在東湖拂子頭上聚首同觀。東方金色光明雲，西方銀色光明雲，中央黃色光明雲，無端露明柱子出來。彈指一聲，呵呵大笑。且道笑箇什麼？俗氣不除。佛成道日，上堂。打圓相，云：這一星兒，二千二百年前臘月八夜，輝天鑑地，放大光明。釋迦老子與一切眾生同一眼見，同證無上正等正覺，惟有薦福主丈子不曾將眼󳬇著。何故？鄉自用鄉法。除夜，小參。一年將盡夜，萬里未歸人。師召眾，云：且道誰是未歸者？三世諸佛止宿草菴、歷代祖師坐在半途、天下老和尚正買草鞋行脚，我此現前一眾不慕諸聖、不重己靈，飢來喫飯、困則噇眠，石爛松枯，誰管你一年將盡不盡？似這般底，正是純鋼打就、生銕鑄成。雖然，畢竟如何是到家句？只今歸去便歸去，欲覔了時無了時。元日上堂：新年頭佛法鏡清，道有智門道無。行盡江南江北路，家家門首釘桃符。元宵，上堂，謝兩斑：治國者，元首明，股肱良，則庶事康。薦福：股肱良，法道昌，萬炬蓮開優鉢香。上堂：漁舟一箇

He contrasts Buddhas lodging in a grass hut, patriarchs halted halfway and teachers still buying travel sandals with his present community, which simply eats when hungry and sleeps when tired. At a New Year's Eve small gathering, Gulin Qingmao recites the distant traveller line and asks the assembly who has not returned. He imagines someone replying that the person has never gone in or out, then recalls Linji's two people: one always on the road without leaving home, the other always home without leaving the road. Gulin asks who deserves offerings and strikes his staff before giving his own verse about finding the way and sparing one's worn feet. The headword is Gulin's present question; Linji supplies a later cited comparison, not the present utterance.

Senses.Explanation: The year is ending, yet the traveller remains far from home: four teachers use the line to test the audience's understanding of arrival. In a New Year's Eve address, Guxue Zhenzhe first answers a monk's questions about place, person and higher teaching, finally striking when the monk presses that last question. Guxue then says that year, month, day and hour have ended, yet people fail to trust the news of getting home. He recites the image of a traveller still far from home and asks the assembled monks whether their knots of doubt are exhausted. His further description of release depends on that answer; the headword is Guxue's present poetic challenge, not the earlier monk's reply. In a New Year's Eve address to the community, Luyan He recites the year-ending night and the distant traveller who has not returned. He says that one who has arrived home could handle every move intimately, then asks for a phrase that shows arrival home. If the listeners can answer, they may sit together and speak of nonarising; otherwise, he asks how someone still unable to return to the rich homeland could travel in fine clothes at night. The traveller image sets up Luyan's test of recognition, not a report about an actual journey. Senses.Explanation: Once bitten by a snake, one fears even a broken well rope. The proverb names caution that persists after a sharp encounter. The first two source owners discuss an older use; the third uses it as a present reply. Additional distinct current uses: Chijue Daochong in X70n1376, Gulin Qingmao in X71n1412.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不施功，萬里秋天西北風，無孔鐵鎚成隊走，苦哉滅却少林宗。佛忌，上堂：教中道：一切無涅槃，無有涅槃佛，無有佛涅槃，遠離覺所覺。今朝是二月十五，鳥啼花笑，水綠山青。歲旦，上堂：舊年說話，新年說話。一法從萬法生，萬法無一法實。月影有若干，真月無若干。諸源水有若干，水性無若干。森羅萬象有若干，虗空無若干。結夏，小參。護生須是殺，恁麼那殺盡始安居？老僧有分會得箇中意，箇中意會不得，鐵船水上浮，有時乘好月，特地過滄洲。文殊、普賢起佛見、法見，貶向二鐵圍山。東山五祖道：今後更敢也無？又道：一度被蛇傷，怕見斷貫索。以拄杖劃一劃，云：你諸人總在鐵圍山裏。上堂。金陵報慈遂禪師問僧：從什麼處來？僧云：撫州曹山來。師云：幾程到此？僧云：七程。問云：行却許多山林溪㵎，何者是你自己？僧云：總是。師云：眾生顛倒，認物為己。僧云：如何是學人自己？答云：總是。師云：一等道箇，總是有認物為己，有不認物為己。退院，上堂。各各未出母胎，夙緣已是無差。老僧來住此山首尾六年，仰荷諸耆舊作成四海五湖兄弟同聚，擊碎今時窠窟，喚回二三百年前舊話，俾知有臨濟一宗未曾斷絕，況瓦礫堆中復成梵宇？此日辭退，深慰卑懷。大眾珍重
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1411.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hengchuan Xinggong. In a summer-retreat small session Hengchuan Rugong describes treating Manjushri and Samantabhadra as if they were sent to iron mountains for fixed views. He then quotes Wuzu of Dongshan asking whether they would dare again and the selected snakebite-and-rope proverb, draws a line with his staff, and tells the assembly they are all inside those mountains. The proverb is the older Wuzu's quoted line; Hengchuan applies it to his present warning.

Occurrences.Kwic: 云：長期進道：西天以蠟人為驗。未審此間以何為驗？慶云：鐵彈子。僧云：意旨如何？慶云：大底大，小底小。師拈云：長慶與麼答話，也是貪觀雲裏鴈，失却渡頭船。我此一眾，箇箇自謂握靈蛇之珠、抱荊山之璞，且山僧如此批判，還有不甘者麼？良久：儗心湊泊終難會，達者應須暗裏驚。次日，上堂，僧問云：道藉言傳，傳由文字，非文字不足紀言，非言焉能顯道？和尚為什麼戒人不要看讀文字？師云：咬人屎橛是甚好狗！僧云：恁麼則五千四十餘卷皆成剩語。師云：我亦不知。僧云：和尚既不知，為什麼戒人不要看讀文字？師云：一度被蛇傷，怕見斷貫索。師復舉：開山彥禪師到夾山，山問云：何處來？師云：臥龍。山云：來時龍還起也未？師近前，以目顧視。山云：灸瘡瘢上更著艾焦。師云：和尚又何苦如此？山休去。師拈云：二尊宿一挨一拶，如善舞太阿，不傷其手，然也有到處，也有不到處。上堂。未有無心境，曾無無境心，心境兩俱忘，未是到家句。東弗于逮打鼓，西瞿耶尼說禪，且道是什麼人分上事？狗䑛熱油鐺。上堂，舉：保福在病，問僧云：我與你相識年深，有何名方妙藥相救？僧云：藥方甚有，聞說和尚不解忌口。師拈云：者僧也不易得，爭奈保福心且未甘，當時只好輕
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1416.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shuzhong Wuyun. A monk challenges Shuzhong Wuyun for warning people away from reading written texts, arguing that words are needed to convey the teaching. After Shuzhong replies sharply and says he does not know whether the canon is surplus talk, the monk presses him again. Shuzhong answers directly with the snakebite-and-rope proverb, warning how a prior injury can distort one's response to texts; the selected words are his current reply.

Senses.Explanation: One showing, two gains is a compact appraisal of an act or exchange that brings two things together. Zixian Jue uses it when a question juxtaposes his old and new abbacy; an unnamed monk gives it after Yinyuan Longqi compares his address with seeing the morning star. Xueqiao Yuanxin applies it to naming one image as both Maitreya and Budai. Xueyan Zuqin says it after Tieniu Chiding makes an overturning gesture in response to his test. Dahui Zonggao caps a closing-retreat address with it after lifting his whisk and striking the seat. These uses supply the appraisal's force without assigning it a single fixed pair of gains. Entries.SourceTerm: 一得無心便道情，六門休歇不勞形

Senses.PreferredTarget: Once no-mind is gained, the feeling of the Way comes; the six gates rest without straining the body.
AlternateTargets: With no-mind, the Way is felt and the six senses come to rest without bodily effort.
SearchAliases: no-mind six gates rest without strain
Senses.Note: Longya Judun's verse links no-mind with rest at the six sense gates; Kongyin Daodu later quotes it to caution students against making another object of mental observation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若文字之狀矣。且曰：魯仲尼與溫伯雪子揚眉瞬目示其道，而何妨言語哉？乃為之序云耳。偈頌凡九十五首。夫人學道莫貪求，萬事無心道合頭。無心體得無心道，體得無心道也休。學道先須且學貧，學貧貧後道方親。一朝體得成貧道，道用還如貧底人。學道蒙師指却閑，無中有路隱人間。直饒講得千經論，一句臨機下口難。學道先須立自身，直教行處不生塵。僧真不假居巖室，到處無心即在人。學道先須有悟由，還如曾鬬快龍舟。雖然舊閣閑田地，一度贏來方始休。學道先須息萬機，將機學道轉生疑。此門廣大無遮障，學者雖多達者稀。一得無心便道情，六門休歇不勞形。有緣不是余朋友，無用雙眉却弟兄。一得無心便豁空，祇因先聖祖門通。箇中若向三乘學，萬劫無因得遇逢。自體如如任運常，因茲行歇住三湘。雙眉無用是毫相，說處無分舌廣長。自小從師學祖宗，閑花猶似纏人蜂。僧真不假栖雲外，得後無心色亦空。得聖超凡不作聲，臥龍長怖碧潭清。人生若得長如此，大地那能留一名。得道還同未得人，心無勝負自安神。從前古德稱貧道，向此門中能幾人。心空不及道空安，道與心空狀一般。參玄不是道空士，一乍相逢不易看。此生不息息何時，息在今生共要知。心息祇因無妄想，妄空心息是休時
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1298.xml). Gāthās and Verses of the Chan Gate’s Patriarchs. Under the section explicitly headed as Longya's verses and preface, Longya Judun gives short teachings on practicing without grasping. This selected couplet says that no-mind brings the Way close and lets the six sense gates rest without bodily strain. Its following lines distinguish true companions from merely useful gestures; this is Longya's own authored verse, not a generic anthology narrator's words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 却非心，打除煩惱破。憎愛不關心，長伸兩脚臥。六祖大師恁麼語話，雖則平白，其實正是向上人底行履，不似今人掠虗道理上簇花簇錦，有什麼難？尋常憎愛是非底心，容易消遣不得。達磨初祖云：外息諸緣，內心無喘。心如牆壁，方可入道。二祖安心之後，纔對他說：豈更別有？祇是圖箇實落。于今勿論內心無喘，祇如外息諸緣一句作麼生？目前山河大地、明暗色空，外既有境，則內必有心。心境相對，動輙傷鋒。須是知有底人，方纔在者裏平帖帖地，不犯絲毫頭手脚。若未到者田地，也勉強不得。待你覺照將來，早是錯過了也。咦！一得無心便道情，六門休歇不勞形。有緣不是予朋友，無用雙眉却弟兄。良久，云：已過不可得，常思於後。念念圓明者，都為他得底人，方解與麼話。不然，纔有所重，便成窠臼。須是轉轆轆地始得。示眾，僧問：心地無非自性戒，如何是自性戒？師云：今日有居士從泊頭來。進云：戒光從口出，如何是戒光？師云：好大雨。進云：破戒之人為甚不墮地獄？師云：無孔鐵鎚。進云：恁麼則泥牛吼破天邊月，木馬騰空過北關。師便喝，進云：好一喝。師云：且退。僧禮拜，起云：啞人唱罷無生曲，黑月堂前拍掌遊。師云：敗闕不少。又一僧纔出，師便喝，僧擬進，師云：背
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1443.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zongbao Daodu. In a recorded exhortation Kongyin Daodu warns that opposing outer scenes to inner mind makes every move hazardous, while trying to inspect that state can itself miss it. After an exclamation he voices the no-mind and resting-six-gates couplet, pauses, and warns against grasping an achieved condition as another fixed perch. This local passage does not name Longya: its wording matches Longya's earlier verse in X66, but Kongyin is the present exact speaker and uses the line to redirect his students' practice.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一從事却潘郎後，也解人前不識羞

Senses.PreferredTarget: Since marrying Pan Lang, she even knows how to appear before others without shame.
AlternateTargets: Once she has married Pan Lang, she no longer blushes to show herself before people.
SearchAliases: since marrying pan lang, she even knows how to appear before others without shame.
once she has married pan lang, she no longer blushes to show herself before people.
Senses.Note: Baoning’s old verse on Jianyuan’s search for his teacher’s remains first depicts a woman waiting and checking a mirror, then gives this Pan Lang couplet. Dachuan raises Caoshan’s answer about before and after a Buddha appears, asks how to recognize Caoshan, and answers with Baoning’s Pan Lang couplet. The Pan Lang figure is a literary allusion, not a Chan speaker. Two independent contexts survive, so this reading is provisional.

Occurrences.Kwic: 保寧勇云：終日挨門復倚樓，幾回明鏡照梳頭。一從事却潘郎後，也解人前不識羞。

Senses.PreferredTarget: one mind
Senses.Note: The single mind can be the common ground of appearances or the field in which conflicting commitments arise. Preface authors and biographical narration must be distinguished from direct master speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 指歸妙源。所謂舉一心為宗。照萬法為鑑
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2016.xml). Zongjing Record, Yang Jie's preface: Yang praises Yongming Yanshou's compilation as taking one mind as its guiding principle and illuminating the many phenomena as its mirror. He then compares buddhas and living beings as reflections and connects the differing good and bad paths to the same source. The phrase describes the book's organizing principle in Yang's signed introductory prose; this is not a direct statement by Yanshou.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The preface opens with an explicit author line naming Yang Jie. Its headword claim praises Yanshou in third person; it is outside Yanshou’s own text.

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸佛共一皮袋子，一心、一智慧、力、無
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1435.xml). Expanded Record of Wuyi Yuanlai, Boshan addresses: Wuyi tells the gathering that thick ice, rising water and accomplished conduct do not arise in a day. He asks what today's affair is, saying that to understand it is to share one skin-bag with Shakyamuni and the countless buddhas, one mind and one wisdom. He immediately warns against merely declaring ordinary and holy alike. One mind states the unity he is testing, within an address that resists an easy verbal claim to it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 棗。如此等人日用一心中。常有二主互相
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (B/B25/B25n0145.xml). Extensive Record of Zhongfeng, addresses to the assembly: Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes students who turn earlier sayings into plausible explanations. In their one mind during everyday life, he says, two rulers continually replace one another: attention to wisdom excludes worldly affairs, and attention to worldly affairs excludes wisdom. He contrasts this divided conduct with another group's indiscriminate flattening of differences. One mind is the single field in which the conflicting commitments arise; it belongs to Zhongfeng's criticism, not the compiler's biography of him.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門人智顗代講，至一心具萬行，有疑請決
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X83/X83n1578.xml). Record Pointing at the Moon, Nanyue Huisi biography: the compiler reports that Huisi explained the Prajna and Lotus texts and then had his disciple Zhiyi lecture in his place. On reaching the topic that one mind includes the myriad practices, Zhiyi became doubtful and asked for a decision. Huisi's answer begins only afterward and distinguishes the two teachings. The phrase here is the narrator's label for the topic that prompts Zhiyi's question, not a recorded utterance by Huisi.

ActorAttribution.ActorLabel: the compiler narrating the Huisi biography
ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The clause says Zhiyi lectures up to the topic and asks for a decision. The narrator introduces this before Huisi’s separate reply, explicitly marked as master speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 具足淵源。三才一心之故，自少遍窮，行布本圓，五地五明，至頤象宜，直鹽醬也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB311.xml). Complete Record of Juelang of Tianjie, Xu Fang's preface: Xu praises the scope of Juelang Daosheng's responses and conduct, linking the three powers of heaven, earth and humanity with one mind and saying this was something Juelang investigated from youth. The phrase occurs in the preface author's appraisal of the master. The closing signature names Xu Fang; it is neither an anonymous compiler's remark nor Juelang's own quoted speech.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The initial preface ends with Xu Fang’s signature; its headword sentence praises the master’s scope and learning, preceding the next separate preface.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖並不論別事唯論一心亦云一乘所以十方
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C077/C077n1710.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Masters, Huangbo's Wanling Record: in reply to a question about whether one must still cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices, Huangbo Xiyun distinguishes means of receiving and helping people from buddha-mind itself. He says that from buddhas to ancestors the discussion concerns only one mind, also called one vehicle. The phrase names the concern of the transmission within his answer, rather than an additional practice alongside the others.

Occurrences.Kwic: 虗幻不實，皆不出一心之所變現。但今人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1437.xml). Expanded Record of Yongjue Yuanxian, instruction to layman Wang Xinzai: Yongjue calls mountains, earth and boundless space the many phenomena, then says their bubble-like appearances do not go beyond what one mind manifests. He immediately challenges the layman to locate that mind: inside, outside and between are all rejected, as are unstable passing thoughts. One mind introduces the inquiry he requires Wang to pursue; the speaker is Yongjue, not Wuyi Yuanlai.

Senses.Explanation: One mind names the single mind under discussion when speakers contrast it with many phenomena, practices, or divided commitments. Huangbo Xiyun says the buddhas and ancestors discuss only one mind; Yongjue Yuanxian starts from the claim that phenomena are its manifestations and then challenges his recipient to locate it. Wuyi Yuanlai speaks of sharing one mind with the buddhas while warning against easy claims that ordinary and holy are alike. Zhongfeng Mingben describes two competing rulers arising within one mind in everyday conduct. The retained prefaces and biographical narration use the wording in their own framing and are distinct from those masters’ direct speech. The single mind can be the common ground of appearances or the field in which conflicting commitments arise. Preface authors and biographical narration must be distinguished from direct master speech.

Senses.PreferredTarget: single-mindedly
Senses.Note: The adverbial use belongs to the recitation instruction in Yulin’s afterword. Its Pure Land setting must remain visible rather than being generalized into every occurrence of one mind.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂執持名號，一心不亂，決定往生，此先自利而後利人者之所為也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperial Selections, Selected Sayings of State Preceptor Yulin, afterword on a Medicine Buddha daily office: Yulin Tongxiu distinguishes practices suited to different commitments. Those firmly resolved to leave the three realms should rely on the Amitabha text, holding the name single-mindedly without distraction; he calls this first helping oneself and then others. He then contrasts people still attached to worldly advantages and recommends the Medicine Buddha's vows for their situation. One mind functions adverbially as undivided attention within the inherited recitation instruction. The section belongs to Yulin, not Yongjue Yuanxian.

Senses.Explanation: Single-mindedly describes undivided attention in the instruction to hold the name without distraction. In his afterword on a Medicine Buddha daily office, Yulin Tongxiu uses the wording for those firmly resolved on rebirth through the Amitabha practice, then contrasts their situation with people who still seek worldly benefits. Here one mind modifies how the name is held; it does not name a separate mind or add another practice. The adverbial use belongs to the recitation instruction in Yulin’s afterword. Its Pure Land setting must remain visible rather than being generalized into every occurrence of one mind.

Senses.PreferredTarget: When the one mind does not arise, the myriad things are without fault.
SearchAliases: When the one mind does not arise, the myriad things are without fault
Senses.Note: The Xinxin Ming line is applied to the way grasping mind creates fault in things. It does not say that ethical harm becomes harmless.

Senses.Explanation: When the one mind does not arise, the myriad things are without fault. The Xinxin Ming line is applied to the way grasping mind creates fault in things. Selected current deployments: Poshan Haiming in J26nB177, Linji Yixuan in J23nB134, Daxiu Zhu in J27nB192, Yinyuan Longqi in J27nB193. The full paired wording is the entry unit. It does not say that ethical harm becomes harmless.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase “not one thought arises.” The phrase is quoted in Zhang Zhuo's verse, “not a single thought arises—the whole body appears; the six faculties barely move and clouds cover it.” Yuanwu places it beside resting, not falling into sense-objects, and not dwelling in conceptual imagining. Yongjue gives an explicit explanation: “this mind functions yet is constantly still, is still yet constantly functions,” and says one's thoughts remain apart from encountered objects. The records also subject the phrase to public testing. The recorded questioner asks Yunmen whether not a single thought arising still has a fault; Yunmen answers “Mount Sumeru.” Xuedou later asks Zhimen why it has a fault and is struck when he comes forward.

Senses.PreferredTarget: No single thought arises; the bounds of before and after are cut off
AlternateTargets: Not a thought comes up, and the divide between past and future falls away
SearchAliases: no single thought arises the bounds of before and after are cut off
Senses.Note: The line pairs the absence of a newly arising thought with a break in the sense of before and after. Chan teachers use it to point to a moment no longer organized by calculation: Guxue links it to the ending of self-centered conflict, Yuanwu to direct insight, and Gaofeng to sustained doubt. Zhulang and Zhanran use it while warning that the phrase itself must not become a fixed state to hold.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. After contrasting an emperor's song about returning home with the Buddha's vow on leaving family life, Guxue Zhenzhe asks his assembly whether the worldly ruler and the Dharma ruler are the same or different. He rejects a simple identification because their actions differ, yet also says both are moved to help the world. Guxue urges the listeners to wake from ambition and empty out self-versus-other thinking; at that point he says no thought arises and before and after are cut off. The phrase is his proposed way through the comparison, before his later citation of Yongjia.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1357.xml). Essentials of the Mind by Chan Master Foguо Keqin. In an instruction addressed to the official Zhang, Yuanwu Keqin describes realizing the ancestral teaching without becoming caught in objects, language or conceptual explanation. He places the no-thought and severed-before-and-after line among signs of that direct clarity, then tells the story of Qinglin's reply about a fire child seeking fire and Fayan's correction of a monk who explained it only as a word puzzle. The headword is Yuanwu's advice to Zhang; the Qinglin and Fayan exchange is a following example of why mere verbal interpretation misses his point.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1400.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gaofeng Yuanmiao. In a hall address, Gaofeng Yuanmiao says a practitioner needs an urgent concern: when that concern gives rise to real doubt, ordinary distractions cease, no thought arises, and the bounds of before and after are cut off. He says this makes a breakthrough possible, whereas wearing out countless sitting mats without such doubt will not do it. Gaofeng voices the phrase as a consequence of pressing inquiry, not as an instruction merely to suppress thought by sitting.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB427.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhulangsheng of Qingcheng. In a small gathering, Zhulang Chesheng first says that someone who cannot reach the matter through mind and ideas must let go of mind, intention and consciousness. He then gives the no-thought and severed-before-and-after line, paired with stillness and movement having one source. Yet he immediately adds that the Linji school also moves freely through public streets and forceful encounters, and asks whether such a person is present in the hall tonight. The phrase marks one step in Zhulang's address, which he refuses to leave as a static achievement.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1444.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhanran Yuancheng. An unnamed monk asks Zhanran Yuancheng why he cannot get free of mind, intention and consciousness, quoting an older instruction about leaving them behind. Zhanran questions what shape these supposed enemies have and where the monk would send them. When the monk swings toward saying they do not exist, Zhanran explains that the three names distinguish functions of one unborn body. He then says that if no thought arises and before and after are cut off, even 'one' no longer names it, much less three. The headword is Zhanran's present response to the monk's conceptual trap; the earlier quoted saying is background.

Senses.PreferredTarget: When no thought arises, the whole is revealed
SearchAliases: when no thought arises, the whole is revealed
Senses.Note: The line says that when a thought does not arise, the whole is revealed. Tianyin opens a verse on Yunmen with it and asks his audience to examine the case. Poshan gives it to a patron who has turned back to look. Shiqi answers a question about discriminating wisdom with the line, then strikes when the monk tries to stand outside both sides. Banshui speaks it after striking his staff at a memorial, reversing the order of the familiar old couplet. Dabo ends a sermon with it after warning that an artificial pose is only a display. These uses press the difference between disclosure and rehearsing a description of stillness.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB177.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan. In a short instruction to the lay patron Xiao Taiyu, Poshan Haiming compares study to climbing a very high mountain one step at a time. Once the summit is reached, he says, the view shows that the matter never left one's own heels. He then adds that if the patron understands this, no thought arises, the whole is revealed, and there is no place in the ten directions without Vairocana. The headword is Poshan's direct instruction to Xiao, not a quotation from another master.

Senses.Explanation: Without a thought arising, the whole is present; as the six sense faculties stir, a cloud covers it. The pair contrasts immediate disclosure and obscuration. Shiqi gives the line as a direct answer to a question about discriminating wisdom and strikes when the monk claims to avoid both sides. Dafang puts it in a patron verse, then raises a fist and asks after the light. Konggu uses the inherited pair but warns against dead sitting and presses a live question. Dabo sets it beside an unstruck bell and a mirror. These are current deployments of Zhangzhuo verse wording, not independent origins of the verse.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一念嗔心起，百萬障門開

Senses.PreferredTarget: One angry thought arises; a million gates of obstruction open.
Senses.Note: The million gates intensify the warning; the passages do not enumerate a million particular obstacles. Accounts of lost eyebrows and future rebirth are the sources teaching claims, not independently established consequences.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1303.xml). Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Master Touzi Qing’s Verses on Ancient Cases: Empty Valley Collection. Linquan Conglun recounts Danxia burning a wooden Buddha during severe cold at Huilin. The abbot scolds him; Danxia says he is burning it for relics. When the abbot denies that a wooden Buddha has relics, Danxia asks to burn two more. The account says that the abbot's eyebrows and beard later fell away. Linquan then brings in the saying that when mind arises, things arise, and when mind ceases, things cease. Applying it to the abbot's anger, he gives the warning that a single angry thought opens a million gates of obstruction and asks whom the abbot could blame for his lost hair. He follows with the contrast of the whole appearing when no thought arises and clouds veiling it when the senses stir. The headword here is Linquan's present application within his telling of the case, not words spoken by the angry abbot. It directs attention to the abbot's reaction without establishing the account's bodily result as a general physical law.

Occurrences.Kwic: 目。彼亦不來，此亦不去。不來故，彼城非無。不去故，此想非有。以非有非無故，各住一際。各住一際故，一人想則城現一人想中。若千人萬人想，則城現千人萬人想中。曾無定體，不因一人想而城為之一，不因多人想而城為之多。故曰：非如非異，非實非虗。非如故非一，非異故非多，非虗故隨想成辦，非實故想處不真。子如一念不生，山河大地當下泯絕，何處更有山河大地來？是知一切皆隨想念建立。故云：三界惟心，萬法惟識。豈虗語哉？有新戒欲募緣造寺謁師，師誡之曰：大抵出家人要以生死為本，福緣次之也。昔者楊岐老人親總十年院事，及住楊岐，屋頹壁敗，門人欲修飾之，老人誡却之。葢老人親從此中過來，艱辛備歷，乃有此語，可謂曾為浪子偏憐客矣。今之人不聞如是之訓，纔出家來，把個脚跟未穩話丟向一邊，祇欲幹辦緣事，以消歲月。倘因果一差，失脚三途，經劫罔返。此事且置，祇如因正果正，福享人天，何曾不云迷中倍人。何也？大凡人都被善惡二種因果輪迴六道，自己佛性終成迷背。故曰：作善則善現，作惡則惡現，真心則隱沒。豈不見梁武帝問達磨云：弟子造寺度僧有功德否？磨云：實無功德。功德在自性中求，豈外求耶？如此則我出家人不以生死為念，向自性中求可乎？曰：然。福德亦不可少耳。如某某修營寺宇，嗔怒無當，人不為過，豈非福力所持耶？師曰：實非福力，乃魔持耳。棗柏曰：一念嗔心起，百萬障門開。修菩薩行者，慎勿起嗔。苟有一毫嗔念，則有一分嗔怒，魔增其勢力。捨命之後，繼有福德，報為大力鬼王，并修羅夜叉之類。福消報盡，還墮三途。曰：起嗔如是，未審修道還有加勢力也無？師曰：有。華嚴經十住、十行、十向、十地菩薩，各有如來威力加被，說當位法門，是其義也。曰：若然者，佛與魔果何物耶？而能與人勢力若是？師曰：本非外物，皆自心之力，法爾如然故也。譬如世人，燔燒屋宅亦用火，蒸煑飯食亦用火，燒煉丹藥亦用火。凡用火之時，各有一分自然風力，與之俱發，成熟其事。燔屋，邪也；煑飯，正也；煉丹，道也。風火皆無分別，而能隨事得失。亦猶佛魔無有分別，而能隨心是非。藉風發火，因心成事，皆不得而異也。良繇真如不守自性，隨緣成熟。今人不了自心，甞隨境轉，魔得其便，牽入惡道。皆繇未明佛性，自無作主，使之然也。豈魔佛云乎哉？如此，則子所言福德，亦不可少。其可信諸？不可信諸？有客游禹陵過訪，問曰：彼中有窆石甚異焉。師曰：何謂也？曰：始吾於無心之際推之則動，其後著意推之則不動，其故何也？師曰：破色心論云：佛說心力最大，水無香故動作勝地，火無香味故動作勝水，風無色香味故動作勝於三大，心非四大故動作勝於諸大。是知無心之力無有限量，其量能轉天為地、轉地為天，大中現小、小中現大，一為無量、無量為一，故淨名以不思議目之。夫不思議
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1444.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhanran Yuancheng. In Zhanran Yuancheng's question-and-answer record, a questioner asks whether a temple builder who becomes excessively angry yet receives no reproach is being sustained by the power of merit. Zhanran answers that this is demonic support, not merit, then explicitly quotes Zaobai: one angry thought arises and a million gates of obstruction open. He warns someone undertaking the compassionate path not to arouse anger and describes anger gaining force, followed by powerful ghostly rebirth and further painful consequences after blessings are exhausted. The next question asks whether cultivating the path also brings added strength; Zhanran says it does, and later explains both kinds of support through the powers of one's own mind, comparing destructive and useful applications of fire. The warning remains Zaobai's locally attributed quoted voice, while Zhanran supplies the present answer about anger amid apparently successful religious work. No doctrinal original is counted as another witness, and the named older source is not assigned a Zen-master identity on the strength of this quotation alone.

Senses.Explanation: One angry thought arises; a million gates of obstruction open. Linquan Conglun recounts Danxia burning a wooden Buddha during severe cold at Huilin. The abbot scolds him; Danxia says he is burning it for relics. When the abbot denies that a wooden Buddha has relics, Danxia asks to burn two more. The account says that the abbot's eyebrows and beard later fell away. Linquan then brings in the saying that when mind arises, things arise, and when mind ceases, things cease. Applying it to the abbot's anger, he gives the warning that a single angry thought opens a million gates of obstruction and asks whom the abbot could blame for his lost hair. He follows with the contrast of the whole appearing when no thought arises and clouds veiling it when the senses stir. The headword here is Linquan's present application within his telling of the case, not words spoken by the angry abbot. It directs attention to the abbot's reaction without establishing the account's bodily result as a general physical law. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. At a hall address requested by lay patrons while Miyun Yuanwu travels to take up the Huangbo invitation, he says the matter was never hidden and divisions of monk or lay, noble or low arise from failing to recognize it. One thought turning the light back lets the matter stand exposed, he says, with no fixed distinction of birth and death or of rank. He then asks for a phrase about quietly serving the country, lifts his staff and cites dedicating a deep mind to all lands. Miyun speaks the headword as the turning point of this present address.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB203.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yune Xi. Yun'e Xi describes an original, ample capacity that is present in every movement and cannot be taken away even by the appearance of Buddhas. He urges the audience to turn the light back in one thought and personally confirm the Vairocana storehouse, then asks whose grace makes this possible and answers with a line about an empty mind and walking on lotus flowers. The headword is Yun'e's present exhortation within a hall address, not a claim that a named earlier master has just spoken.

In a verse responding to layman Lin Shili, Yinyuan Longqi sketches a recluse among mountains and clouds, surrounded by fantastical figures who make claims of spiritual power. At the end, the walker reaches the limit of the mountains, turns the light back in one thought, and finds all things complete. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB223.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shanhui. In an address to the assembly, Shanhui Huan urges practitioners to examine who wears clothes and eats, looking while walking, sitting and lying down, day after day. He warns them not to relax on hearing that sustained inquiry can lead to the realm of Buddhas and patriarchs. A capable person, he says, can reach the crucial point by turning the light back in one thought; his long-term advice is for those who cannot yet manage that. The headword qualifies Shanhui's preceding instructions rather than cancelling them.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1442.xml). Drafts from Chan Master Weilin’s Traveling Hermitage. In a birthday text for a monk called Yuan, Weilin Daopei says true life is without a fixed form or limited duration, though beings share it without recognizing it in daily use. One thought turning the light back, he writes, yields a lasting realization, and he offers that understanding to Yuan before recounting Yuan's earlier training and service. Weilin is the author of this present prose tribute; Yuan is its recipient and subject, not the utterer of the headword.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1443.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zongbao Daodu. At an opening hall address, Kongyin Daodu compares the Buddha's flower held up before Kashyapa with his own raised whisk before the current assembly and asks whether the two events are the same or different. He warns listeners against calculating the answer and says that if they turn the light back in one thought and lay down their tricks, nothing remains to chase. He then criticizes mistaking blank unseeing for the point and cites the Sixth Patriarch on not clinging to form or emptiness. Kongyin speaks the headword to his current listeners; the earlier flower scene is the comparison he introduces.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1444.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhanran Yuancheng. Zhanran Yuancheng addresses lay supporters who have supplied the monastery, contrasting their useful generosity with the old layman Pang's famous throwing away of wealth. He says they still lack Pang's freedom from being a companion to all phenomena. If they cannot trust this directly, he tells them to hold before themselves the question of where birth comes from and death goes, morning and evening; a thought turning the light back may let them meet Pang across the ages. The headword is Zhanran's conditional advice to these patrons, not a line spoken by Pang.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 丈夫真。贈恒默二兄進關贈恒、默二兄進關一聲哮吼震千山，兩個泥牛鬥入關，跛鱉盲龜傍努目，人天龍象正開顏。不萌枝上聯芳秀，無影堂中竟日閒，氣息盡時消息盡，不堪攀處卻堪攀。次士禮林居士次士禮林居士卓立千峰別洞天，剪雲綴衲度殘年，猿修野供丹崖上，鳥獻名花古樹前。玉女攢眉賣俊俏，石徒點首弄機權，悠悠行到山窮處，一念回光萬法全。佛誕日贈居士林恬生佛誕日贈居士林恬生突出蓮胎亙古今，曇花門外雨沉沉，洗清曩劫娘生垢，獨露渾身紫磨金。炤世眼睛奔電掣，撩天鼻孔吼雷音，堪憐稚子隨高下，潦倒傍觀忍不禁。執中林居士求偈薦室執中林居士求偈薦室大道本無男女相，歸根豈有去來身？紅爐菡菡因該果，鐵樹菩提果具因。半偈未宣超法界，一言聊舉等冤親。

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 。大眾！趁此色力強健，看者皮袋子原從甚處得來？又看者穿衣喫飯底是箇甚麼物件？行也看，坐也看，臥也看，除非瞌睡時方休。倘一覺來，便又看今日也如此，明日也如此，今歲也如此，明歲也如此，今生也如此，來生也如此，今劫也如此，來劫也如此，如此做去，自然到得佛祖田地。大眾！又不可聞此說便放鬆了，靈利漢又那在多少時？但一念回光便是極處，祇恐不能生死，乃如此勸喻耳。珍重。」生日，小參。「仝聲相應，仝气相求，水流溼，火就燥，雲從龍，風從虎，聖人作，萬物睹。」拈拄杖，驀豎起，云：「聖人作也，且作麼生睹？者裏見得，便知古聖、後聖亦只如此，化民正俗、接物利生。不特此也，乃至人物、艸木、山川、谿谷一切皆然，所謂一物一陰陽、一物一太極者也。

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 齋禪者為求福，十方檀越仰遮蓋。諸禪德！勤精進，莫懈怠，當下徹明了辦去，免勞拖欠一身債。」舉拂示眾，云：「會麼？若向者裏會得，鏵頭本是生鐵瀉，泥餅原來是土塊；者裏不會，分明慧日光常暉，卻被癡雲來覆蓋。有禪速去參禪，無戒出班受戒。」依文傳衣竟，下座。上堂。云：「者段真風不用猜，尋常勿外動中乖，百謀千算渠先識，一念回光萬物諧。雖然如是，東廊不打鼓，西舍怎知音？堂中纔擊磬，彌陀十萬聲。生鐵不經爐錘，難作農家器；頑石不琢磨，何為鎮國寶？蝵蟺悟蛟龍而飛騰，驚天動地；人有真參實悟，焉不成佛？作祖成佛且置，今朝是我德進居士發最上心而求無上菩提者麼？呵呵！擬求菩提尤更遠，若得無心心自明，忽覺翻身枕子墮，滿床自獲現珠珍。」上堂。云：

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 、薛代聖、羅以佐、陳興津、薛興棟等，僉具書請余文為公壽。余曰：公之美德茂行，余所宜壽，惡俟請為？然既重以諸公之請，曷可緩乎？因竊試論之曰：夫真身無相，真壽無量，剎那本自無生，起滅當處湛寂。所以劫火燒空，而徹體清凉；大浸稽天，而通身不溼。世相常住，法住法位，以具如是真身，故有如是真壽。羣生同有，日用不知，一念回光，一得永得。源公其達此者，故敢以是進之。公三山人，出於何氏，族多名士。而公不樂世氛，幼入緇門，禮智光師，落󳻍納戒於博山無異老人。年三十餘，上鼓山歸，先師座下一見，許其參堂，與余單次相隣，日夕磨礪。時叢林方興，百務蝟集，眾舉公執勞辦事，公弗獲已，乃就職。先師既掩化，權余忝補處，凡所以為佛、為法、為僧及山門所未

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1443.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zongbao Daodu. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 。以山僧公論，則老龐佛法有餘，世法不足，爭似此間眾友入山供眾，非惟眾僧安心行道，其種福德於劫劫生生，乃至成佛莫可窮盡，較他擲於無用江水又何如耶？你諸友則世法有餘，佛法不足。何也？未能如老龐這漢不與萬法為侶，若能直下自信，我也許你吸盡西江去。若未得如是，且把個生從何來、死從何往的話頭頓在面前，朝暮提持，倘得一念回光，必然與老龐把手，千古之上如不相委，不免葛藤自收去也。良久，云：啼得血流無用處，不如緘口過殘春。上堂。春夏秋冬四季分，爾今一分往前過，禪和日用事如何？今日不了何劫悟？大眾！纔說進堂，又是兩月矣。若已透關，不在限內；如未透關的，也須著些精彩始得，不可只麼度時便當參禪也。葢此事不屬文言，不因工夫，在活路上觸著

Senses.Note: In his hall sermon, Zhangxue Tongzui cites an unnamed earlier master, then challenges the assembly to set aside its anxious calculations; the quoted pair equates turning attention back with what is already attained. In a New Year hall sermon, Yezhu Fuhui imagines the Eastern Emperor telling his messenger that one turn of attention is already equal to original attainment; the scene tests who can turn the Dharma wheel. In a memorial small talk, Baiyu Jingsi cites an unnamed earlier saying after describing nature as open space; the full pair supports his challenge to waiting for a later means of becoming Buddha. Three independent recorded teaching contexts survive; this reading is provisional.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB192.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Daxiu Zhu. In his general address settling the community at Nanhua, Daxiu Zhu describes the difficulty of sustaining the ancestral monastery and explains why he has come south. He insists on preserving the rules, praises those who maintained the buildings and asks for a broad outlook that welcomes people seeking the way. He says that if the many determined practitioners at Caoxi turn around in a single thought and accord with what was originally theirs, there need be no fear that the teaching will fail to spread. Daxiu himself voices the pair as part of this present institutional exhortation. He then tells the officers to understand his intention, leave the monastery open to those who come and go, and avoid discriminating by wealth, status or cleverness. The formula connects personal recognition with responsibility for an actual community; it is not merely another copy of Bodhidharma’s farewell speech.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB448.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lingji. Lingji Xingguan asks the student Boru what benefit he gained during a seven-day practice period at Jinsu. Boru says that everything is already present. Lingji stretches out a hand and asks him to bring out what is present; Boru cannot answer. Boru then says the exact turning-and-original-possession pair. Lingji asks for his own original word, and Boru raises a fist. The teacher presses him about death and burning the body; Boru rises and circles three times. Lingji rejects the circling, asks him to speak further and tests his answer about the nostrils. When Boru hesitates, Lingji splashes tea in his face. Boru, not Lingji, is the exact speaker of the formula. The encounter makes the gap between asserting original possession and answering the teacher’s concrete demands its point; it does not report that Boru’s first assurance was accepted.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB449.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zuliangqi. At Dezang’s assembly for the day commemorating Buddha’s awakening, Zuliang Chaoqi first answers monks’ questions with his fist, words and blows. He then begins his own address with the exact pair: turn around in a single thought and accord with what was yours from the start. Opening both eyes, he says, there is clear daylight—what is delusion and what is awakening? He calls the account of seeing the morning star a blemish in the eye, raises the claim that beings possess awakened wisdom but fail to realize it, and gives a loud shout. He says such a shout long ago could have cut off the ensuing verbal entanglements, then asks the present assembly where it lands. Zuliang is the current speaker; the cited Buddha account is an object of his challenge rather than the speaker of the pair. The assurance is immediately put to a present test, not offered as a substitute for one.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X68/X68n1319.xml). Imperially Selected Recorded Sayings. In the historical Bodhidharma section, Bodhidharma instructs Huike about transmitting the teaching and using the robe as a sign of confidence. He distinguishes explaining principle from carrying it through and urges Huike to make the teaching known without slighting those who have not awakened. He then gives the exact pair about turning in one thought and according with original possession, before announcing his verse about coming to this land and a flower opening into five petals. Bodhidharma is the locally attributed speaker, Huike the recipient, and the later collection the transmitter of that narrative. This useful historical witness gives the formula a transmission setting against which the independent current uses can be read. Parallel versions of the same instruction do not become additional occasions, and the attribution does not verify every prediction embedded in the surrounding narrative.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一念普觀無量劫，無去無來亦無住

Senses.PreferredTarget: In one thought, survey countless ages; neither going nor coming, nor abiding
AlternateTargets: A single thought sees through measureless aeons without departure, arrival, or dwelling
SearchAliases: one thought sees countless ages no coming going
measureless aeons neither going nor coming
Senses.Note: The line comes from a verse in the Flower Garland scripture: one thought ranges across countless ages without going, coming, or settling. Later masters put that immense temporal image into concrete sermons. Ruibai raises a whisk; Wuyi compares a monastery site three centuries apart; Guting cautions students against stopping at grand images of Buddhahood.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chushi Fanqi. In a hall address connected with laywoman Miaolian's gift of a precious canopy, Chushi Fanqi imagines the lands of the ten directions gathered on a needlepoint. From a cloud of light on that point appears a lotus canopy containing hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. In Chushi's narrated vision those Buddhas speak the Flower Garland verse with one voice, saying that one thought surveys immeasurable ages without coming, going or abiding; they then disappear into the needlepoint. Chushi narrates the scene and owns the record, while the exact verse is assigned inside his story to the collective imagined Buddhas, whose individual names are not supplied.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB188.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Rujiu Ruibai. Ruibai Mingxue opens a hall address by reciting the Flower Garland line about seeing countless ages in one thought without coming, going or abiding. He lifts his whisk and says the Buddhas, patriarchs and worlds all appear and teach at its tip, then asks whether listeners understand that ancient and present time do not leave this thought. The address was requested for the tenth anniversary of layman Chen's deceased father, with a meal and a wish for the father's future liberation. Ruibai is the present reciter of the inherited verse; its scriptural origin remains distinct from the memorial occasion.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. At a Buddha-bathing day hall address, Liao'an Qingyu recites the full Flower Garland stanza about surveying countless ages in one thought and understanding events in the three times. He asks how to voice a blessing for the meal and answers by reciting the Flower Garland stanza about one thought surveying boundless ages without coming, going or abiding. He then laughs at counting dust-like aeons. Tian'an is the current reciter; the verse serves his response to the donor's occasion, while its earlier scriptural source is not a separate person in this assembly.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 一念普觀無量劫，無去無來亦無住

Senses.Explanation: This Flower Garland verse sees immeasurable ages within one thought; the six current passages place its inherited words in visions, memorials and questions about time. In a hall address connected with laywoman Miaolian's gift of a precious canopy, Chushi Fanqi imagines the lands of the ten directions gathered on a needlepoint. From a cloud of light on that point appears a lotus canopy containing hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. In Chushi's narrated vision those Buddhas speak the Flower Garland verse with one voice, saying that one thought surveys immeasurable ages without coming, going or abiding; they then disappear into the needlepoint. Chushi narrates the scene and owns the record, while the exact verse is assigned inside his story to the collective imagined Buddhas, whose individual names are not supplied. Ruibai Mingxue opens a hall address by reciting the Flower Garland line about seeing countless ages in one thought without coming, going or abiding. He lifts his whisk and says the Buddhas, patriarchs and worlds all appear and teach at its tip, then asks whether listeners understand that ancient and present time do not leave this thought. The address was requested for the tenth anniversary of layman Chen's deceased father, with a meal and a wish for the father's future liberation. Ruibai is the present reciter of the inherited verse; its scriptural origin remains distinct from the memorial occasion. At a Buddha-bathing day hall address, Liao'an Qingyu recites the full Flower Garland stanza about surveying countless ages in one thought and understanding events in the three times. He calls that scope a circle from which even Shakyamuni's descent, departure, awakening, many assemblies and final flower gesture cannot escape; he says the same of the listeners whether they believe or understand. Liao'an voices the verse here and uses it to encompass the Buddha's whole career, rather than reporting a new event in which the scripture speaker appears. At the opening of a retreat, Wuyi Yuanlai observes that earlier teachers spoke on this monastery ground three hundred years ago and that he speaks on the same ground now. He asks the assembly to see that earlier and present time do not stand apart, then cites the Flower Garland verse about one thought and immeasurable ages. He says that is still the scriptural side and asks for the Chan side, striking his staff before a verse about cold clouds and flowers. Wuyi is the present citer; the staff action marks his next question, not a separate source for the inherited verse. Guting Shanjian challenges students who keep placing Buddhas, scriptures, purity and defilement into fixed conceptual categories. He asks what the Buddhas of past, present and future have accomplished and where all their works could be located, then reproaches students for failing to consider the line that in one thought one surveys immeasurable ages without coming, going or abiding. He urges them to cut through even dazzling Buddha forms rather than make the verse a new object of speculation. Guting cites the inherited line in his present admonition. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB190.xml). Dharma Platform of Chan Master Shiyu. In his first-person preface to Nanming's recorded sayings, Shiyu Mingfang recalls entering the community at Longju, where Nanming guided him. Shiyu suddenly asks how one moment's dependent arising can be unborn and surpass the provisional study of the three vehicles, and whose arising could then be born. Nanming gives a thunderous shout. Shiyu says he was bewildered, then sat for the time it takes several sticks of incense and realized that there was work to do. The headword is Shiyu's question; Nanming's shout is the reply, and the preface does not present the question itself as an attained realization.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. At a hall teaching requested for the birthday celebration offered by layman Lu of Haiyan, Feiyin Tongrong first says that planting beans yields beans on the ordinary plane of cause and effect. He then urges the hearer to recognize that one moment's dependent arising is unborn and thereby go beyond the provisional understanding of the three vehicles. He compares this freedom in changing circumstances to a bell sounding when struck and a moon reflected in stirred water, taps the incense table, and asks where the point can be seen before answering with mountain flowers and stream water. Feiyin voices the line in his own present sermon.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1440.xml). Chan Master Weilin Daopei’s Return to the Mountains Record. Weilin Daopei addresses the assembly about the entrenched habits of mind and consciousness. After citing Shakyamuni, Yongjia and the teaching that past, present and future mind cannot be obtained, he quotes an unnamed author he calls the Huayan treatise author: one moment's dependent arising is unborn and surpasses provisional study. Weilin immediately asks whether the present gathering is not itself dependent arising and how its nonarising could be spoken, pauses, and answers that as soon as arising occurs it cannot be found. The exact line is the author's quoted voice; Weilin's questioning makes it an active Chan sermon use, without making the doctrinal treatise itself a retained witness.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB233.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Jie’an Jin. In a present instruction Jie'an Jin raises the old meeting in which Shiyu Mingfang asks Nanming how one moment's dependent arising can be unborn and who could then have born arising. Nanming shouts, leaving Shiyu bewildered until later seated practice opens a way forward. Jie'an says that Shiyu later told this honestly in the preface to Nanming's sayings, and he adds a verse praising the force and compassion of the shout. The headword remains Shiyu's quoted question; Jie'an is the current commentator, and this appraisal is a new use of the encounter rather than a second original questioning.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一念翛然無異色，任從滄海變桑田

Senses.PreferredTarget: With one free, untroubled thought, its color stays unchanged, though seas turn into mulberry fields.
AlternateTargets: One moment of freedom does not change its color, even as ocean becomes mulberry fields.
SearchAliases: with one free, untroubled thought, its color stays unchanged, though seas turn into mulberry fields.
one moment of freedom does not change its color, even as ocean becomes mulberry fields.
Senses.Note: In his recorded verses, Danxia Zichun comments on the Caoshan heat-and-cauldron exchange: a moment of untroubled freedom stays unchanged though seas become mulberry fields. Linquan Conglun quotes Danxia’s complete verse on the same case, then explains that a free moment is untroubled amid heat and change and that the inner center remains steady. Danxia remains the exact verse speaker when Linquan quotes and interprets it. Two independent contexts survive, so the reading is provisional.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一息不來，向何處安身立命

Senses.PreferredTarget: If the next breath does not come, where will you settle body and life?

Senses.Note: Duanya Liaoyi posed this as a room question about where a practitioner can stand when the next breath does not come. Jifei's recorded answer set later repeats it and replies 'at the tips of the grasses'; the individual answer line is unlabelled but its placement is clear. Three other lamps merely repeat Duanya's biography.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 為眾舉揚曰：盡大地有一人發真歸源。從一皆知之。後歸德清，偕母入武康結茅。越五載還山，峯曰：大有人道你拖泥帶水。師曰：兩眼對兩眼。遂求薙落，更名曰了義。暨峯委席本雍，二公亦相繼而化，師乃勉狥眾請。甞示眾曰：若要超凡入聖，永脫塵勞，直須去皮換骨，絕後再甦，如寒灰發燄，枯木重榮，豈可作容易想？我在老和尚處多年，每被大棒打徹骨髓，不曾有一念遠離心，直至今日，纔觸著痛處，不覺泪流，豈似汝歡喜踴躍，咬著些子苦味，便乃掉頭不顧？殊不知苦味能除百病。或示眾曰：除却語默動靜，道將一句來。又曰：一息不來，向何處安身立命？師說法應機，頗多觕言穢語，人所不堪。元統元年除夕，謂眾曰：有一件事天來大，你還委悉麼？良久曰：明日是年朝。越六日，與僧夜談，乃曰：老僧明日天台去也。僧曰：某甲隨去。師曰：你走馬也趂我不及。翌午，跏趺而寂，壽七十二，臘四十九。初，中峯示寂，會葬齋次，師笑謂眾曰：後十二年更為老僧一會。至是十二年矣，全身藏於獅子岩，賜號佛慧圓明正覺普度大師。杭州天目山大覺寺布衲祖雍禪師杭州天目山大覺寺布衲祖雍禪師明州寧海人。得旨於高峯，躬舂㸑樵。貌甚瘠黑，戇而少文。甞和永明山居偈曰：我要心灰即便

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB371.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Foyuan. Foyuan Chegang welcomes fellow teachers who have come to support his teaching seat, raises his whisk and asks whether those present trust the ancestral charge it represents. He then explicitly quotes a hall poem attributed locally to Longmen Yuan at Jiangshan, beginning with one hand unable to clap alone and two hands sounding together. The old poet, not Foyuan, speaks that exact opening pair. Foyuan compares the old occasion with the support offered by the visiting teachers and gives his own new verse: one hand does not sound, two hands clap; the responsive opening is beyond the sages’ measurement. He also changes the older poem’s jewel image and makes a flute-playing gesture with his whisk. The quotation and current reworking support the present meeting without being counted as two exact occurrences. Longmen Yuan’s source-local name is retained without forcing a personal identification beyond the passage.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB410.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lianfeng. At a small gathering for installing chief officers at Baoen, Lianfeng Su speaks of the transmission between teachers and the participation of those who carry it. He praises response without having to be summoned and work that requires no repeated command, saying that this both makes the occasion successful and sustains the school’s manner. He asks who bears the heavy responsibility, laughs and answers with the exact one-hand and two-hand pair, adding that a son who can maintain the household has the work of a mature person. Lianfeng himself is the current speaker. The proverb gives the officers a shared task rather than attributing the monastery’s functioning to the teacher alone. The following address appointing two ranks of officers is a separate turn and should not be merged into this occurrence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人不信，却自迷頭認影，奔逐狂途，致使竛竮流浪生死。諸禪德，若能一念回光返照到自己脚跟下，褫剝究竟將來，可謂洞門豁開，樓閣重重，十方普現，海會齊彰。便乃凡聖賢愚、山河大地，以海印三昧一印印定，更無纖毫透漏。山僧如是舉唱，若是眾中有本色衲僧聞之，實謂掩耳而回，笑破他口。大眾，且道本色衲僧門下一句作麼生道？良久曰：天際雪埋千尺石，洞門凍折數株松。上堂：釋迦老子當時一手指天，一手指地，曰：天上天下，唯我獨尊。釋迦老子旁若無人，當時若遇個明眼衲僧，直教他上天無路，入地無門。然雖如是，也須是銅沙鑼裏滿盛油始得。上堂，顧視大眾曰：青山重疊疊，綠水響潺潺。遂拈拄杖曰：未到懸崖處，擡頭子細看。卓一下。上堂：寶峰高士罕會到，巖前雪壓枯松倒。嶺前嶺後野猨啼，一條古路清風掃。禪德，雖然如是，且道山僧拄杖長多少？遂拈起曰：長者隨長使，短者隨短用。卓一下。

Occurrences.Kwic: 哉？體之則神。我尋常示汝，何不向衣鉢下坐地，直下參取。須要上來討箇甚麼？既上來，我即事不獲已，便舉古德少許方便，抖擻些子龜毛兔角，解落向汝。諸上座欲得省要，僧堂裏、三門下、寮舍裏參取好。還有會處也未？若有會處，試說看，與上座證明。僧問：如何是棲賢境？師曰：棲賢有甚麼境？問：古人拈椎竪拂，還當宗乘中事也無？師曰：古人道了也。問：學人乍入叢林，乞和尚指示。師曰：一手指天，一手指地。後江南國主請居章義道場。上堂：總來這裏立作甚麼？善知識如河沙數，常與汝為伴。行住坐外，不相捨離。但長連牀上穩坐地，十方善知識自來參。上座何不信取，作得如許多難易？他古聖嗟見今時人不奈何，乃曰：傷夫人情之惑久矣。目對真而不覺，此乃嗟汝諸人看却不知。且道看却甚麼不知？何不體察古人方便，祇為信之不及，致得如此。諸上座但於佛法中留心，無不得者。無事體道去。便下座。

Occurrences.Kwic: 開福道寧禪師浴佛，上堂：未離兜率，已降王宮；未出母胎，度人已畢。諸禪德！日日日從東畔出，朝朝鷄向五更啼。雖然不是桃花洞，春至桃花亦滿溪。又道：毗籃園內，右脇降生，七步周行，四方目顧，天上天下，唯我獨尊。大似貪觀天上月，失却手中珠。還知落處麼？若知落處，方為孝子順孫；苟或未然，不免重下註脚。良久，云：曰：天生伎倆能奇恠，末上輸他弄一場。圓悟勤禪師浴佛，上堂。一手指天，一手指地，末上一機，衲僧巴鼻。步步蓮華，金盆澡洗，西天東土共流傳，至今處處澆香水。良久，云：車不橫推，理無曲斷。下座。雲峯悅禪師四月八日上堂：教中道：四月八是佛生之日，放大光明，照耀十方。地涌金蓮華，自然棒雙足。東西及南北，各行於七步。分手指天地，作獅子吼聲。上下及四維，無能尊我者。後來雲門大師舉了，云：老僧當時若見，一棒打殺與狗子喫却，且圖天下太平。師云：奇恠，諸禪德！

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (P/P155/P155n1519.xml). Essential Compendium of the Zen School, Yantou section: Yantou asks Deshan whether he is ordinary or holy, receives a shout, and bows. When Dongshan praises him, Yantou says the old man has assigned the wrong name and describes his own act as one hand raising while the other grips. Subsequent named masters add their reactions. This recension preserves Yantou's same inherited declaration; the later comments are separate voices.

Senses.Explanation: One hand raises while the other grips: a paired image for handling an encounter in more than one direction at once. Yantou Quanhuo uses it to describe his own response after Deshan shouts and he bows, rejecting Dongshan’s praise as a mistaken label. Yuanwu Keqin later asks where those two movements occur and uses the same wording for Xuedou’s handling of another case. His Blue Cliff pointer places the paired hands within a teacher’s work, while saying this still falls short of the fundamental matter. The gestures supply an image of responsive handling rather than two prescribed physical actions. Senses.Explanation: The willow strands and mist image closes a teaching turn when a direct definition would miss the point. Four recorded speakers use it after questions, a memorial offering, or a raised whisk or staff. Linye Xi answers a monk asking for the phrase beyond the people and setting already discussed. After dismissing the monk's verse as idle words, he asks how to speak without clinging to delusion or awakening, raises his staff, and gives the willow and mist image as his answer. At a hall address for placing Liuru's memorial tablet in the ancestral hall, Sanyi Yu jokes about hiding dangerous medicine in the food and offering Liuru's Yunmen cakes. He draws a circle with his whisk and ends with the willow line, turning the memorial offering into an image that cannot be gathered up. In a New Year hall address, Zixian Jue says each festive sight discloses the Dharma. He asks what the upright body is, pauses, and answers with the willow strands trailing mist over a railing. The image closes his question without defining that body. Chaozong rejects both mind-is-Buddha and not-mind-not-Buddha as fixed answers. He raises his whisk and asks whether it is mind, Buddha, wisdom, the Way, or none of these; then he throws down the whisk and voices the willow line to end the exchange.

Senses.Note: Willow strands escape a single grasp and hang in mist over a jade railing. Feiyin gives the image as a seasonal answer. Shaweng includes it in a sermon verse; Xiangya uses it after challenging Su Dongpo’s poem, and Hengxiulin and Lianfeng make it the visible closing turn of their own comments. The scene offers something plainly there while frustrating the attempt to collect it into one fixed answer.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. At a hall address Feiyin Tongrong compares the Buddha's robe kept at Mount Jizu with his own teacher Miyun's robe housed in a pagoda and asks whether they are the same or different. He says their historical circumstances differ while the underlying matter is one, then asks for a phrase suited to this very occasion. His answer is the willow strands trailing with mist over a jade railing. Feiyin voices the couplet as the seasonal close to his present comparison; the Buddha and Miyun are subjects of the question, not its current speakers.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB308.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangya Ting. Xiangya Xingting recites Su Dongpo's verse identifying stream sound with a teaching voice and mountain color with a pure body, then faults the verse for burying the Buddhas in sights and sounds. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1418.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dai’an Puzhuang. Dai'an Puzhuang retells a case in which Xuansha draws a circle, Gushan says no one can get out of it, and the two dispute who can say so. Dai'an judges both old teachers still lacking insight, then cites Xuedou's warning that fascination with the waves can lose the oar. He suddenly draws with his staff and answers with the willow strands crossing the railing. Dai'an voices the final couplet as his appraisal of this earlier case; Xuansha, Gushan and Xuedou are quoted or discussed figures.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1422.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu. At a hall address for the Buddha's nirvana, Nanshi Wenxiu says there is no nirvana Buddha to grasp and no separate Buddha nirvana. He draws a line with his staff and immediately gives the willow strands trailing with mist across the jade railing. The couplet is Nanshi's own closing response to the nirvana theme, grounded in the recorded staff action; the Buddha is the subject of the occasion, not its speaker.

Yun'e Xi recounts an older exchange in which a visiting doctrinal teacher first takes Chan and scriptural teaching to be the same, then changes his view after hearing another elder's reply. Yun'e asks the present assembly whether the two old answers are the same or different, lifts his whisk, and gives the willow strands across the railing. The couplet is Yun'e's current response to his comparison; the older disputants speak only within the story he has raised.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB185.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushi. Fushi Tongxian raises the old tea-picking exchange between Guishan and Yangshan: shaking the tree, remaining silent, and the final allowance of twenty blows all turn on function and substance. Fushi comments that without those final blows the exchange would not have been settled, and then gives the willow strands that refuse gathering and drape the jade railing. The couplet is Fushi's present appraisal after the cited case; neither Guishan nor Yangshan speaks it in that earlier exchange.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB220.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Faxiyin. At the end of a retreat, Faxi Yin says the ninety days have been held and are now released. He points to bright sun, spring wind, green pines and young willows, asks what the listeners actually see and hear, strikes his staff, then asks who knows the point of his action. After a pause he gives the willow strands on the misty railing, throws down the whisk and leaves the seat. Faxi voices the couplet as his present closing challenge, not as a botanical observation detached from the question.

Buhui Fatong raises the story of Nezha returning flesh to his mother and bones to his father before appearing in another body to teach them. Buhui grants the old story a point yet says it still cannot fully settle the matter, then gives the willow strands across the railing and continues with his own freer verse. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB288.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hanyu Xian. Hanyu Hongxian says the ancestral matter is exposed amid busy streets and sights and sounds. After a monk's earlier exchange and a blow, Hanyu asks why the true body could disappear if it is plainly present, pauses and gives the willow strands over the railing. The headword is Hanyu's present answer to his own question; the monk's earlier poetic replies belong to the preceding exchange, not this couplet.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. At a hall address Feiyin Tongrong compares the Buddha's robe kept at Mount Jizu with his own teacher Miyun's robe housed in a pagoda and asks whether they are the same or different. He says their historical circumstances differ while the underlying matter is one, then asks for a phrase suited to this very occasion. His answer is the willow strands trailing with mist over a jade railing. Feiyin voices the couplet as the seasonal close to his present comparison; the Buddha and Miyun are subjects of the question, not its current speakers.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 堂。僧問：「衣線下大事即不問，請法薦亡事如何？」師曰：「大地無寸土，鑊湯無冷處。」僧喝一喝，曰：「亡靈向者裏承當去也。」師曰：「看者漢今日死中得活。」乃揮拂子，曰：「昨夜霜天皎更清，今朝杲日照分明，靈光獨露常然顯，會取原來無死生。地獄哀兮豈可懼？天堂樂也不稱情，翛然撒手無為事，來往隨分任縱橫。為伊薦拔了也。」復豎拂子，曰：「看，看！陳氏眾等靈魂俱來山僧拂子頭上，同聲而說偈曰：『久在幽冥意未傾，辛酸受盡暗悲聲，今朝幸得無生法，生死出來一夢驚。』看看去也，且道向甚麼處去？樂邦留不住，遍界任騰騰。」春日，上堂。「東風乍起倍精神，柳眼梅腮笑轉新。無限風光藏不住，數聲幽鳥出煙塵。日蕩蕩兮雲漠漠，西來祖意絕疏親。金圈栗棘閒拋出，吞跳莫教鈍置人。所以男兒須蹋上頭關，豈甘苦海受沉淪？」舉拂子，曰：「等閒識取龜毛拂，萬紫千紅不是春。」上堂。「竹戶曉開山色靜，柴床午夢覺身輕。家風一種無人會，添得黃鸝三五聲。」上堂。「如來藏裏說不著，祖師機下亦顢頇。一把柳絲收不得，和煙搭在玉闌干。」水鑑海和尚六會錄卷一水鑑海和尚六會錄卷二嗣法門人原上等編住荊州天王禪寺語錄荊州天王禪寺語錄順治辛丑五月，重開天王寺。斬艸。「蔓艸荒煙幾百春，葛藤那復累諸人？今朝斬斷疑根盡，獻餅天王話轉新。」建佛殿，上堂。拈香。「此一瓣香，千二百年灰冷，而今忽爾光生，奉為本寺開山二宗之祖、一代之師道悟和尚，并及本寺剃度獻餅崇信禪師。此一瓣香已在鐵佛拈出，天下共見共聞，今日重新舉起，再令炙地熏天，奉為臨濟三十二世漢陽棲賢獨冠敬和尚。」僧問：「荊棘林、艸木丘，一朝忽起崔嵬殿閣，為復是神通？為復是玅用？」師曰：「玅用神通掌握中。」乃曰：「千年祖席埋雲冷，一旦中興氣象新，虎穴狐窩俱掀卻，石頭瓦磈盡翻身。拈華老衲從今現，微笑頭陀再悟真，自此一番功業立，普天匝地盡回春。汝等還見回春氣象麼？寶殿凌空法界迥，散華天女繞雲行。」建梵天閣，上堂。「高閣巍巍插梵天，盡塵沙界唯一望。自然瀟灑絕諸塵，誰不心空得高曠？匪獨此時法門興，況乃當來作榜樣。作榜樣，須是諸人登一回，方能物物無遮障。」建東西禪堂，上堂。「達磨不來東土，二祖不往西天。人人鼻孔撩天，箇箇眉毛拖地。碞居穴處，無為而樂。不知有玄路可尋、奇特可慕。及至有馬祖禪堂、百丈清規之後，負笈擔囊，參詢南北，高堂廣
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB230.xml). Six-Session Record of Monk Shuijianhai of Tianwang. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 皇帝祝嚴聖壽萬歲萬歲萬萬歲，此瓣香奉為邑侯鄭公在位尊官，此瓣香昔年酬價龍蟠，不敢被蓋囊藏，如今海眾要知，未免重新舉揚，奉為現住萬峰山太平禪院破山大和尚，用酬法乳。」斂衣趺坐，上首白椎云：「法筵龍象眾，當觀第一義。」問：「拈香祝聖即不問，波羅山點頭時如何？」師云：「有眼莫鑒。」僧喝，師便打，乃云：「靈機迥峻，在處舉揚。智寶圓明，隨方顯露。」拈拄杖云：「大眾會麼？世尊不說說，迦葉不聞聞，天曉起來門正啟，誰家灶裏火無煙？雪峰道：『盡十方世界如粟米粒大；拋向面前，漆桶不快。』神光三拜而得髓，趙州八十猶行腳；所謂若論箇中事，須是箇中人；若是箇中人，不愁箇中事。我此現前四眾，箇箇鼻孔遼天；人人腳跟點地，向上一著，無勞指似。」復舉東坡居士偈云：「谿聲盡是廣長舌，山色無非清淨身；夜來八萬四千偈，他日如何舉似人？」師云：「東坡此偈，古今獨唱，可謂陽春白雪，爭奈把三世諸佛埋沒在聲色堆裏，至今無人救得。山僧恁麼品論，莫有與東坡出氣者麼？」卓拄杖云：「一把柳絲收不得，和煙搭在玉闌干。」開爐，上堂。「法無邊際，緣會而彰；心無彼此，投機而應。其把住也，黃金掩耀；其放行也，瓦礫生輝。若向者裏會得，聚寶峰微笑、波羅山點頭；脫或未然，不免旁通一線去也。」舉：「百丈與溈山圍爐次，百丈命溈山撥火，山撥之無火，丈躬起自撥得一星火，語溈云：『你道無，者箇聻？』溈從此悟去。」師云：「溈山不得百丈，幾乎凍殺；百丈不得溈山，勞而無功。雖然，父子名邁古今，總被者一星火燒卻。」以拄杖吹一吹，云：「大眾會麼？照顧眉毛。」頌曰：「雪壓隆冬品類枯，寒來父子偶圍爐；火星迸出通身煖，勝喫曹山酒一壺。」孝臣龔居士請上堂。「昔日龐居士，逃禪入翠微；西江一口吸，透徹祖師機。且如何是祖師機？莫是揚眉瞬目是祖師機麼？料掉沒交涉。莫是拈拳豎指是祖師機麼？料掉沒交涉。莫是擎叉輥毬是祖師機麼？料掉沒交涉。莫是雀噪鴉鳴是祖師機麼？料掉沒交涉。莫是翠竹黃華是祖師機麼？料掉沒交涉。既都盧沒交涉，畢竟如何是祖師機？」良久，拈拄杖喝一喝，云：「祇園屈曲泉流急，鷲嶺巍峨月上遲。」陞寰李居士請上堂。「父母未生前，鼻孔遼天；父母既生後，腳跟點地。大丈夫漢㘞地一聲，直得南贍部洲種樹、北俱盧洲結果、東勝神洲撞鐘、西牛賀洲擊鼓；不是神通妙用，亦非法爾如然。直下會去，猶較些子；
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB308.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xiangya Ting. Xiangya Xingting recites Su Dongpo's verse identifying stream sound with a teaching voice and mountain color with a pure body, then faults the verse for burying the Buddhas in sights and sounds. He asks whether anyone will defend Dongpo, strikes his staff and answers with the willow strands drifting across the railing. Xiangya voices the couplet as his own answer after criticizing an earlier poet; Dongpo did not speak this willow line in the present record.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB355.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hengxiulin of Lülüo. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ；有問無荅，泥牛海底藏頭角；不問而自荅，獨腳仙人吹尺八。衝風破浪底聞之，突出雲霄；尋香逐臭底聞之，未免被蜘蛛絲絆殺。烈烈轟轟，豁豁達達，德山棒、臨濟喝，也是將鹹止渴。」喝一喝。化主石󵐽領六通禪人請上堂。僧問：「一佛出世，千佛讚揚；千佛出世，阿誰讚揚？」師云：「杲日當空照。」進云：「萬派朝宗歸法海，千峰列勢拱蘆山。」師云：「寒風撲面來。」乃云：「多子塔前事，普天絕漏洩，特借所生口，徹底為君說。」以拂子敲左邊，云：「不是釋迦文。」敲右邊，云：「亦非維摩詰。不二門豁開，穀城山崱屴。」復舉：「傅大士云：『夜夜抱佛眠，朝朝還共起，起坐鎮相隨，語默同居止。欲識佛去處，秪這語聲是。』大小傅大士迷頭認影，抱橋柱洗澡，有甚麼受用處？又云：『空手把鋤頭，步行騎水牛，人從橋上過，橋流水不流。』擬將黑豆換卻天下人眼睛，殊不知自己眼睛已自換了也。是汝諸人還識伊麼？若也不識，山僧為伊重干注腳去也。橫身宇宙，獨少長安，推倒鐵壁，扶起銀山，驢頭向北，馬頭向南，一把柳絲收不得，和煙搭在玉闌干。」下座。臘八，鳳山、南山、梅峰偕林滋謙等請上堂。僧問：「昔日萬乘尊榮，棄如敝屣；六年雪嶺，貌若枯柴。還是不守本分？還是力量過人？」師云：「千古罕聞。」進云：「老瞿曇夜半睹星，悟個甚麼？」師云：「突出眼睛看。」進云：「佛祖位中留不住，堂堂何物受牢籠？」師云：「愁殺人。」僧云：「何人識得渠？」師打退，云：「看破了也。」乃云：「愛閒不打龍華鼓，策杖來探得度師，業債些須償未了，半肩犁杷復何辭？所以，皮毛不惜，筋骨任勞，耕破劫外乾坤，翻轉祖翁田地，直得鳳凰展翅，寶塔放光，孤峰湧月，萬派朝宗。秪如感應道交，則固是祖翁田地，人人還踏著也未？若向諸佛未成道處一踏，到底始救得一半；倘向明星出現處薦取，豈不落七落八？阿剌剌，阿剌剌，將此深心奉塵剎。」下座。諸山禪師至，上堂。「天寒地寒，山凍水凍，十里穀城，梅花遍放。處其中者，無限風光；遊其中者，十分放曠。青鳥一聲兩聲，羅浮似夢非夢，動人春色不須多，聊折一枝平奉送。或有人云：『人人各有一枝，要和尚底作麼？』山僧向伊道：『豈不聞芭蕉道底？』」遂擲拄杖，下座。歲旦，上堂。云：「祥麟瑞鳳兩相親，送去迎來沒二人，海底金輪纔湧曉，世間萬事又翻新。世事既新，佛法亦新，發新條，行新令，風雨調和，人物興盛，草長
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB410.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lianfeng. Lianfeng Su recalls two verses of the lay teacher Fu Dashi, one about sleeping beside the Buddha and another about carrying a hoe with empty hands. Lianfeng criticizes those verses as trapping readers in appearances, asks whether his listeners recognize Fu, and offers a new poetic gloss that ends with the willow strands spread over the railing. Lianfeng voices the willow couplet as his own closing gloss; Fu Dashi is the object of his critique, not the current utterer of that line.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 舞，忉利居日月之上，四禪無風火之灾。且道帝釋宮中所說何法？一牛飲水，五馬不嘶。斷江和尚至，上堂：天平山上白雲泉，雲自無心水自閑。何必奔衝下山去，又添波浪向人間。大眾，圓鑑和尚來也，曇花易見，知識難逢。斷絃須是鸞膠續，佛祖齊教立下風。上堂，僧問：牛頭未見四祖，因甚百鳥㗸花獻？師云：世情偏向有錢家。進云：見後因甚不㗸花？師云：人義盡從貧處斷。師乃云：凡夫色礙，二乘空礙，菩薩色空無礙。嘉州大像騎個蹇驢兒走入陝府，鐵牛鼻孔裏拜白安居，撞見寒山、拾得，跳出來撫掌呵呵大笑，云：佛法不是者個道理。畢竟是什麼道理？任從滄海變，終不為君通。上堂：日裏僧駄像，夜裏像駄僧。黃昏候日出，天曉打三更。新都寺撒骨。如何是佛？新婦騎驢阿家牽。如何是佛？三脚驢子弄蹄行。撞破生死牢關，踏著通天活路。地歸地，水歸水，火歸火，風歸風。橫身三界外，何處覓行蹤？上堂。夜來撾鼓升堂，喚作小參；今日陞堂撾鼓，謂之示眾。示眾、小參，初無二說；夜來、今日，豈有兩般？拍禪牀，云：一把柳絲收不得，和烟搭在玉闌干。喝一喝。䨥林和尚至，上堂。夫善知識者，如優曇花時一現耳；善知識者，如天甘露時一降爾；善知識者，如塗毒鼓時一聞爾。撾塗毒鼓，聞者皆喪；洒天甘露，飲者清涼；開優曇花，見者欣悅。大眾！傅大士道：空手把鋤頭，步行騎水牛，人從橋上過，橋流水不流。作麼生會？若也會得，許你親見明極和尚。開爐上堂，舉雪峯示眾云：世界闊一丈，古鏡濶一丈。玄沙指火爐云：火爐濶多少？峯云：如古鏡濶。沙云：者老漢脚跟未點地在。師云：雪峯、玄沙兩父子摻閩音，直是難會。澱山輙為頌出：世界古鏡火爐，門上休釘桃符，洞賓失却寶劍，果老踏碎葫蘆。古鏡火爐世界，一段風光沒賽，盧公逴得衣盂，佛法依然不會。火爐世界古鏡，知佗是凡是聖？丹霞煖氣烘烘，院主眉鬚落盡。小參小參結制。妙湛總持不動尊，首楞嚴王世希有，銷我億劫顛倒想，不歷僧祗獲法身。山僧威音王已前出家，威音王已前行脚，行脚則與諸人同行脚，出家則與諸人同出家，不知過了多多少少、長期短期？諸人瞞山僧一點不得，山僧亦瞞諸人一點不得。傅大士云：夜夜抱佛眠，朝朝還共起，起坐鎮相隨，語默同居止。若也會得，許你參學事畢；其或未然，大事替汝不得，小事各自抵當。解夏。一拽石，二搬土，發機須是千鈞弩。然則千鈞之弩，不為鼷鼠而發機。百丈再參馬祖，

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 布衫穿。進云：與麼則感恩有分。師云：八花毬子上，不用綉紅旗。僧禮拜，師乃云：罷訪諸方知識，來歸古鄮城中。土面灰頭，養問四壁，其奈宿緣難避，來主江干。蕞爾禪林，水遶千村，槎橫斷港，數聲柔櫓，一曲漁歌，煩佗真正舉揚，直是超情絕謂。無端擊動法鼓，緇素駢臻，更欲山僧為蛇𦘕足。法昌對泥像說法，事急計生，風穴單丁七年，巧盡拙出。汾陽弄西河獅子，神頭鬼面；楊岐㘽田博飯喫，鐵心石膓。者一隊老古錐，熏天富貴，裝出徹骨貧窮。新延慶則不然，竪拂子，天上有星皆拱北，人間無水不朝東。復舉：趙州因僧問：狗子還有佛性也無？州云：無。師云：趙州狗子無佛性，古今多少錯商量？自從六國平來后，蕩蕩無為化日長。上首白椎，云：諦觀法王法，法王法如是。上堂。風不鳴條，雨不破塊。洞山於金剛嶺上栽松，溈山到國清寺裏受戒。東海烏鰂，南山筀筍，總是自家買賣。更問：如何漆桶不快？拍禪床，下座。上堂：建法幢，立宗旨，明明佛敕。曹溪是永嘉大師，雖□□竪降旗，大似偷鈴掩耳。以拂子畫一畫，一把柳絲收不得，和烟搭在玉闌干。開爐，上堂：衲僧活計無多子，放下諸緣緩作程；品字柴頭煨正暖，不知紅日又東昇。上堂，舉汾陽和尚示眾云：識得主丈子，行脚事畢。三角云：識得主丈子，入地獄如箭射。師云：二尊宿總被主丈子穿却。延慶則不然，拈主丈：冬不寒，臘后看。除夜，小參。僧問：一年將盡夜，萬里未歸人。如何是未歸人？師云：眼似鼓椎。進云：誰知遠烟浪，別有好思量？師云：碧落󳬴，無贗木。進云：一言截斷千江口，萬仞峰頭始得玄。師云：錯認定盤星。乃云：纔見冬至，又逢歲除，兩曜奔忙，萬物代謝，浮生若此，榮枯得失徒自紛紜。我沙門釋子無饑寒之迫、無征役之勞，二六時中合作麼生支？準求玄妙，枉費精神，無事無為，又成莽鹵。臨濟大師道：有一無位真人，常在汝等諸人面門出入，未證據者看看。恁麼說話，也是萬里崖州。良久：明年更有新條在，惱亂春風卒未休。復舉投子因僧問：如何是十身調御？投子下禪牀立。又問：凡聖相去幾何？投子下禪牀立。師云：大小投子，將官路，當人情，傷鹽傷醋，過犯彌天。上堂：雞銜燈琖走，鼈吹釣魚竿，寶劒當空擲，神光照膽寒。以拂子畫一畫：波斯嚼碎三斤錢，莫向金剛腦后看。元宵，上堂。叢林中纔見說燈籠與露柱交參，便作奇特商量。及乎尋常說話，是對面蹉過。以拂子畫一畫：今朝正月十五，今夜處

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: ，未免翻成戲論。驀拈拄杖卓一下，云：青山不鎻長飛勢，滄海合知來處高。上堂。今朝五月初一，箇事為君指出，堦下流水潺湲，門外新篁蓊󳬂，非惟歷歷明明，抑且綿綿密密，老僧更無傳持，大眾何有得失？回顧侍者，云：忽若有个無面目漢到來相看，只向他道：不必，不必。便下座。解夏，上堂。諸法從本來，常自寂滅相。若無諸佛住持首楞嚴定，眾生隨順無明業識，然迷悟在人而不在法。徑山一夏與諸人同出同入，要且不離一相三昧。今當自恣之辰，西天蠟人氷、東土銕彈子即不問。拈拄杖，云：拄杖子穿過釋迦老子鼻孔，因甚諸人罔知痛覺？靠拄杖，云：大海若無山隔斷，天光直與水相連。上堂。玄沙因皷山至，畵一圓相，山云：人人出這箇不得。沙云：誠知你向驢胎馬腹作活計。山云：和尚又作麼生？沙云：人人出這個不得。山云：和尚為什麼道得，某甲道不得？沙云：我得你不得。師云：玄沙與皷山，難兄亦難弟，若要出得這個，總欠悟在。雪竇云：只知貪觀白浪，不知失却手橈。師云：緇素眼何在？驀拈拄杖畫一畫，云：一把柳絲收不得，和烟搭在玉闌干。上堂。明明向汝道，開口不在舌頭上。擊石火，閃電光，搆得搆不得，未免喪身失命。若自伶俐漢聞與麼道，自然別有出身之句。有麼？有麼？擊拂子：不是龍門客，切忌遭點額。上堂：釋迦掩室於摩竭提國，淨名杜口於毗耶離城。是皆靈龜曳尾，拂跡跡生。太陽溢目，萬里不掛片雲。爭奈覆盆之下，漆黑黑地。四來禪侶，同此坐夏。既無兩錯商量，亦無正因可說。蒲團靜倚無餘事，永日寥寥謝太平。上堂：心心不昧，法法無差。金剛與泥人揩背即不問，且道鴟吻咬却佛殿脊，還有勘驗處也無？昨夜三更失却牛，天明起來捉得賊。賊！賊！便下座。上堂。布袋頭解開了，十方世界蕩蕩無邊。衲僧家緊峭草鞋，橫擔拄杖，東西南北，去住自由，不妨慶快。忽若撞著杜撰巡官，問道：上座！如何是行脚事？也須好好祗對他始得。驀拈拄杖卓一下，云：不向藍田射石虎，何人知是李將軍？璣藏主火。辯傾河漢，文綴珠璣，生死岸頭，總用不著。一大藏教是箇之字，祖師西來是箇右字。提起火云：勝熱門頭參得透，丙丁童子念摩訶。上堂。八月秋，何處熱？岩桂吹香滿寥泬。風景凄清，泉聲幽咽，祖意明明誰辨別？大藏小藏，橫說竪說，不出如今箇時節。同不同？別不別？堪悲堪咲老寒山，剛道吾心似秋月。拍禪床，下座。上堂。我宗無語句，亦無一法與人。達磨大師
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1418.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dai’an Puzhuang. Dai'an Puzhuang retells a case in which Xuansha draws a circle, Gushan says no one can get out of it, and the two dispute who can say so. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 作恁麼會，蘇盧悉唎；不作恁麼會，悉唎蘇盧。恁麼、不恁麼，總拈却悉唎蘇盧、蘇盧悉唎，截斷三路葛藤，放下舊年曆日，管取百城草偃、四海浪平。還委悉麼？如王寶劍繇王意，揮斥縱橫得自繇。復舉：藏叟老祖除夜小參，舉：僧問古德：年窮歲盡時如何？云：依舊孟春猶寒。叟云：古德恁麼答話，只怕諸人忘却。今日忽有人問：年窮歲盡時如何？拈棒便打。待他道：因甚打某甲？即向他云：更要我道孟春猶寒。那古德曾為浪子偏憐客，藏叟老祖愛向人前恣拍盲。有問北山，即向他道：但得雪消去，自然春到來。元日，上堂。元正啟祚，萬物咸新。年新月新，日新時新。大地山河，纖洪動植，一一俱新。且道衲僧分上事還有新舊也無？喝一喝，下座。請藏主、維那、侍者，上堂。一大藏教，是箇切脚，直指單傳，秦時𨍏轢。國師喚侍者，淨地何必拋泥沙？興化打克賓，瘥病豈假驢䭾藥？你有拄杖子，我與你拄杖子；你無拄杖子，我奪却你拄杖子。佛涅槃，上堂。一切無涅槃，無有涅槃佛，無有佛涅槃，遠離覺所覺。以拄杖畫一畫，云：一把柳絲收不得，和烟搭在玉闌干。上堂：望州亭相見了也，烏石嶺相見了也，發明空劫已前事。燈籠與露柱交參，庫廳對僧堂發笑，顯示現行三昧。嘉州牛喫禾，益州馬腹脹，天下覔醫人，灸猪左膊上。三世諸佛搆不著，歷代祖師搆不著。上堂：直下便會，尚涉廉纖。擬議不來，白雲萬里。北山別有通天活路，要與諸人共行。便下座。熈怡先師忌拈香。碁盤石斫破腦門，黑竹篦掀翻途轍。殃及天下師僧，何止楚淮閩浙。恁麼傳持臨濟宗，炎炎六月飄霜雪。琴川陳從道設齋求嗣，上堂。饑來喫飯，困來打眠，踏著尋常一路。恁麼衲僧也甚希有，更要萬仞峰頭濶步、荊棘林裏翻身底，萬中無一。馬祖一喝，百丈直得三日耳聾，黃蘗聞之不覺吐舌。且道是尋常一路？是萬仞峰頭濶步？旃檀圍繞旃檀樹，獅子還生獅子兒。佛生日，上堂：黃面老子初出母胎，幸自可憐生，無端道箇天上天下唯我獨尊。玉本無瑕，雕文喪德。只如雲門道：我當時若見，一棒打殺。又作麼生？相識滿天下，知心能幾人？結制，小參。明日結制，今夜小參。摩霄俊鶻，便合乘時；止濼困魚，徒勞激浪。高亭隔江望見剎竿橫趨而去，脚跟下好與三十玄沙築破脚指。遂云：達磨不來東土，二祖不往西天，頂門上猶欠一槌，自餘央央庠庠、莽莽鹵鹵，堪作什麼？北山今夜且放一線道：學道猶如守禁城，晝防六賊夜惺惺，中軍主將能行
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1422.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu. At a hall address for the Buddha's nirvana, Nanshi Wenxiu says there is no nirvana Buddha to grasp and no separate Buddha nirvana. He draws a line with his staff and immediately gives the willow strands trailing with mist across the jade railing. The couplet is Nanshi's own closing response to the nirvana theme, grounded in the recorded staff action; the Buddha is the subject of the occasion, not its speaker.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 云：『汝不是患盲。』復喚近前來，僧纔近前，門云：『汝不是患聾。』門云：『還會麼？』僧云：『不會。』門云：『汝不是患啞。』其僧有省。」師拈云：「玄沙夜半潑墨，地藏日午挑燈，雲門好肉上剜瘡，三人各自擔板。山僧今日露箇消息，也要諸人檢責。」遂豎起拂子，云：「若向這裏薦得，即瞎卻你眼。」復擊禪床，云：「若向這裏薦得，即聾卻你耳。若道總不恁麼，即啞卻你口。到這裏，也須眼裏有筋、皮下有血始得。還會麼？鶯囀上林花滿地，客遊三月艸侵天。」下座。晚參。舉：「座主問白馬曇禪師：『祖意、教意，是同？是別？』曇云：『如車二輪，如鳥兩翼。』主云：『將謂禪門有奇特，元來不出教乘。』遂回。後聞夾山盛化，遣小師馳問前語，夾山曰：『鏤冰無琢玉之談，結艸乖道人之意。』小師回，舉似主，主乃讚嘆，遙禮曰：『將謂禪門與教意不殊，元來有奇特事。』」師召大眾，云：「二老恁麼荅話，且道是同？是別？若同，鏤冰無琢玉之談；若別，結艸乖道人之意。畢竟如何？」乃豎拂子，云：「還會麼？一把柳絲收不得，和煙搭在玉欄杆。」化城菴見堂怨禪德病，請上堂。問：「如何是奪人不奪境？」師云：「你似一頭驢。」進云：「如何是奪境不奪人？」師云：「騎佛殿出山門。」進云：「如何是人境俱不奪？」師云：「薰風自南來，殿閣生微涼。」進云：「如何是人境兩不奪？」師云：「片雲橫谷口，歸鳥悉迷巢。」進云：「有意氣時添意氣，不風流處也風流。」師云：「且緩緩著。」僧便喝，師便打。僧禮拜，師驀拈拄杖，云：「提起金剛寶劍，直下不徇人情。」遂卓一卓，云：「劈破三玄三要，放出無位真人，便乃手之舞之、足之蹈之，欣欣然而說偈曰：『不思議，解脫力，妙用恒沙也無極，四事供養敢辭勞，萬兩黃金亦消得，粉骨碎身未足酬，一句了然超百億。』」遂召大眾，云：「且道是那一句？還會麼？庭前之古柏微微濕露，嶺上之白雲澹澹拖風。若向這裏薦得，不妨蹋破化城，親登實所；脫或未然，當堂無影跡，遍界不曾藏。」以拄杖卓一卓，喝一喝。復舉：「僧問曹山：『學人通身是病，請師醫。』山云：『不醫。』僧云：『為甚麼不醫？』山云：『教汝求生不得，求死不得。』」師云：「這僧正患入髓之沉痾，若不遇曹山老漢，殆乎危矣，何足救哉？雖然如是，曹山只具診候之手，而無瘥病之方。即今忽有問山僧：『學人通身有病，請師醫。』山僧劈脊便棒。何謂如此？
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB203.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yune Xi. Yun'e Xi recounts an older exchange in which a visiting doctrinal teacher first takes Chan and scriptural teaching to be the same, then changes his view after hearing another elder's reply. Yun'e asks the present assembly whether the two old answers are the same or different, lifts his whisk, and gives the willow strands across the railing. The couplet is Yun'e's current response to his comparison; the older disputants speak only within the story he has raised.
