ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB185.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Fushi. Fushi Tongxian raises the old tea-picking exchange between Guishan and Yangshan: shaking the tree, remaining silent, and the final allowance of twenty blows all turn on function and substance. Fushi comments that without those final blows the exchange would not have been settled, and then gives the willow strands that refuse gathering and drape the jade railing. The couplet is Fushi's present appraisal after the cited case; neither Guishan nor Yangshan speaks it in that earlier exchange.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB220.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Faxiyin. At the end of a retreat, Faxi Yin says the ninety days have been held and are now released. He points to bright sun, spring wind, green pines and young willows, asks what the listeners actually see and hear, strikes his staff, then asks who knows the point of his action. After a pause he gives the willow strands on the misty railing, throws down the whisk and leaves the seat. Faxi voices the couplet as his present closing challenge, not as a botanical observation detached from the question.

ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 一把柳絲收不得，和煙搭在玉欄杆

Senses.Explanation: Willow strands cannot be gathered and drift with mist over a jade railing: fourteen teachers use this complete couplet to answer a case, close a sermon or challenge an attempt to catch the matter in words. At a hall address Feiyin Tongrong compares the Buddha's robe kept at Mount Jizu with his own teacher Miyun's robe housed in a pagoda and asks whether they are the same or different. He says their historical circumstances differ while the underlying matter is one, then asks for a phrase suited to this very occasion. His answer is the willow strands trailing with mist over a jade railing. Feiyin voices the couplet as the seasonal close to his present comparison; the Buddha and Miyun are subjects of the question, not its current speakers. In a four-line hall verse, Shaweng Huihai first says neither the Tathagata store nor the patriarchs' devices can be adequately told. He then gives the willow strands that cannot be gathered and the mist over the jade railing. The couplet is Shaweng's own poetic close to the problem of putting this matter into words; there is no recorded monk's question or staff gesture in this short source window. Xiangya Xingting recites Su Dongpo's verse identifying stream sound with a teaching voice and mountain color with a pure body, then faults the verse for burying the Buddhas in sights and sounds. He asks whether anyone will defend Dongpo, strikes his staff and answers with the willow strands drifting across the railing. Xiangya voices the couplet as his own answer after criticizing an earlier poet; Dongpo did not speak this willow line in the present record. Hengxiulin Falin first quotes Yexian's old teaching on direct pointing and seeing one's nature. He says the older teacher is openhanded but that a thorn remains in the mud, then asks whether the assembly understands. Hengxiulin responds with the willow strands on the misty railing and drags his staff as he leaves the seat. The couplet is his present appraisal of the quoted teaching; Yexian is the earlier speaker of the passage under discussion. Lianfeng Su recalls two verses of the lay teacher Fu Dashi, one about sleeping beside the Buddha and another about carrying a hoe with empty hands. Lianfeng criticizes those verses as trapping readers in appearances, asks whether his listeners recognize Fu, and offers a new poetic gloss that ends with the willow strands spread over the railing. Lianfeng voices the willow couplet as his own closing gloss; Fu Dashi is the object of his critique, not the current utterer of that line. Yuejiang Zhengyin says that last night's drum-led gathering was called a small talk and today's drum-led gathering is called an address, though the teaching itself does not divide into two. He asks whether night and day could really make two meanings, strikes the Chan couch, and gives the willow strands trailing over the misty railing before a shout. Yuejiang voices the couplet to conclude his present comparison; it does not come from a second participant. In a hall address, Liaotang Weiyi speaks of raising a teaching banner and establishing a lineage claim, then marks the air with his whisk and gives the willow strands over the railing. The image follows his own visible gesture and closes the address without a separate recorded question. Liaotang is the current speaker; older teachers named in the preceding doctrinal phrases are examples, not the couplet's speakers. Dai'an Puzhuang retells a case in which Xuansha draws a circle, Gushan says no one can get out of it, and the two dispute who can say so. Dai'an judges both old teachers still lacking insight, then cites Xuedou's warning that fascination with the waves can lose the oar. He suddenly draws with his staff and answers with the willow strands crossing the railing. Dai'an voices the final couplet as his appraisal of this earlier case; Xuansha, Gushan and Xuedou are quoted or discussed figures. At a hall address for the Buddha's nirvana, Nanshi Wenxiu says there is no nirvana Buddha to grasp and no separate Buddha nirvana. He draws a line with his staff and immediately gives the willow strands trailing with mist across the jade railing. The couplet is Nanshi's own closing response to the nirvana theme, grounded in the recorded staff action; the Buddha is the subject of the occasion, not its speaker. Yun'e Xi recounts an older exchange in which a visiting doctrinal teacher first takes Chan and scriptural teaching to be the same, then changes his view after hearing another elder's reply. Yun'e asks the present assembly whether the two old answers are the same or different, lifts his whisk, and gives the willow strands across the railing. The couplet is Yun'e's current response to his comparison; the older disputants speak only within the story he has raised. Fushi Tongxian raises the old tea-picking exchange between Guishan and Yangshan: shaking the tree, remaining silent, and the final allowance of twenty blows all turn on function and substance. Fushi comments that without those final blows the exchange would not have been settled, and then gives the willow strands that refuse gathering and drape the jade railing. The couplet is Fushi's present appraisal after the cited case; neither Guishan nor Yangshan speaks it in that earlier exchange. At the end of a retreat, Faxi Yin says the ninety days have been held and are now released. He points to bright sun, spring wind, green pines and young willows, asks what the listeners actually see and hear, strikes his staff, then asks who knows the point of his action. After a pause he gives the willow strands on the misty railing, throws down the whisk and leaves the seat. Faxi voices the couplet as his present closing challenge, not as a botanical observation detached from the question. Buhui Fatong raises the story of Nezha returning flesh to his mother and bones to his father before appearing in another body to teach them. Buhui grants the old story a point yet says it still cannot fully settle the matter, then gives the willow strands across the railing and continues with his own freer verse. The couplet is Buhui's current comment on the cited Nezha story; Nezha does not speak it in the narrative. Hanyu Hongxian says the ancestral matter is exposed amid busy streets and sights and sounds. After a monk's earlier exchange and a blow, Hanyu asks why the true body could disappear if it is plainly present, pauses and gives the willow strands over the railing. The headword is Hanyu's present answer to his own question; the monk's earlier poetic replies belong to the preceding exchange, not this couplet.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n2000.xml). Recorded Sayings of Xutang, a mid-autumn hall address when the moon is absent: an unnamed monk raises Mazu's moon-viewing encounter with Xitang, Baizhang and Nanquan. Xutang Zhiyu dismisses Xitang's offering and Baizhang's cultivation. Asked what Nanquan's walking away means, he answers that once the bundle of bones has been carried away, he does not know whose house the bright moon falls upon. The bodily departure becomes a question of where the moon belongs, answering the monk's attempt to place Nanquan's response among the others.

Senses.Explanation: Xutang Zhiyu uses the couplet to answer what Nanquan's walking away contributes to the Mazu moon-viewing case: once the bodily person is carried off, the moon cannot be assigned to a known household. The answer shifts the questioner's ranking of the three disciples into an unsettled question of possession. In a mid-autumn hall exchange, Xutang dismisses Xitang's 'offering' and Baizhang's 'cultivation,' then answers the question about Nanquan's departure with this couplet. This single exact occurrence belongs to Xutang's appraisal of the moon-viewing case and remains provisional.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB281.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zizhouchuan of Tanxi. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J38/J38nB427.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhulangsheng of Qingcheng. Senses.Explanation: Juzhi's ‘one-finger Chan’ names Juzhi's recorded use of a raised finger in public interviews. A later record states the visible rule directly: "Whenever someone came, Master Juzhi only extended one finger; he called it one-finger Chan" (俱胝和尚逢人但伸一指頭，喚做一指頭禪). In the transmitted case, Tianlong raises one finger to Juzhi; afterward, whenever students ask, Juzhi raises one finger, and before dying he says, "I obtained Tianlong's one-finger Chan; through my whole life I could not use it up" (吾得天龍一指頭禪，一生用不盡). The record also preserves criticism rather than making the label an unquestioned formula: Xuansha says he would have broken the finger, Caoshan faults Juzhi's taking it up, and Sanshan asks, "What connection does one-finger Chan have? It cheated that monk and buried him alive his whole life" (一指頭禪有甚交涉？賺殺阿僧終身活埋). Its Chan-specific bend is thus a named, publicly repeated response inherited from Tianlong and continually examined by later masters.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1296.xml). Compilation of the School Gate's Raising Old Cases: the case reports Shakyamuni banishing Manjusri for forming views of buddha and teaching. After other masters' reactions, Baohua—Chaozong Tongren—says he would instead give half his monastery to anyone forming those views. He explains this with one palm not sounding idly and two palms making a clapping sound. The single palm is part of his own paired-palm saying, not the compiler's narration or a description of a slap.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp, Baizhang's fox case: after the fox's funeral, Huangbo asks Baizhang what someone who never gives a wrong answer would become. Baizhang invites him closer to hear the reply. Huangbo approaches and gives Baizhang a slap; Baizhang claps and laughs, praising the encounter with his red-bearded foreigner saying. One palm counts the narrated blow by Huangbo, rather than words spoken by either participant.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1310.xml). Picking Up Jewels from the Eight Directions: Pang Yun takes Danxia Tianran's prayer beads and the two trade challenges about fear, blows and receiving people. Danxia throws down the beads, turns back laughing at Pang's accusation, and seizes him; Pang gives him a slap. Yuanwu's following appraisal compares the exchange to opposing battle formations whose winner is unsettled. One palm counts Pang's narrated blow at the turn of this encounter, not Yuanwu's later description.

Senses.Explanation: One palm counts a single palm or a blow delivered with it. In the Baizhang fox encounter the narrator says Huangbo gives Baizhang one slap; in the exchange over Danxia’s prayer beads, Pang Yun delivers another. The same counted palm enters Chaozong Tongren’s saying that one palm does not sound idly while two clap together. The surrounding verb determines whether the palm is being counted as a striking action or set beside another palm in a saying. The expression counts one action or span made with the palm. Gesture, blow, and bodily measure must be separated by the governing verb.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB493.xml). At a Buddha-enlightenment small talk, the head monk questions Pufuzhuo about the Buddha seeing the morning star, then asks whether Pufuzhuo previous answer is his intimate point. Pufuzhuo gives the slap-and-staff pair; the monk says it needs no further note, and Pufuzhuo calls him deaf before taking up the staff later. The couplet is Pufuzhuo direct reply, while the later staff gesture is separate.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一擊忘所知，更不假修持

Senses.PreferredTarget: At one strike, what I knew fell away; no further cultivation was needed
SearchAliases: at one strike, what i knew fell away; no further cultivation was needed
Senses.Note: After failing to answer his teacher and leaving to tend a grave, Xiangyan hears a stone strike bamboo and speaks this verse. Shiyu asks whether the line proves he understood. Juelang asks why that encounter succeeded after so much study. Baichi gives the name One Strike to a student and explains the verse without making every sound an awakening. Guantao voices it and asks what it means now; Yuan’an relates it to the hard break with Xiangyan’s earlier learning. The line points to a decisive event, not a shortcut for repeating its words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不作者般不材不淨底事。黃金自有黃金價，何事和沙賣與人？香嚴知是從前錯路，遂將平昔所有底文字燒卻，道：『此生不學佛法了也，且作箇長行粥飯僧，免役心神。』豈不是以有所得心學無所得法，如何學得來？然則香嚴此時卻也平帖帖地了，乃泣辭溈山，溈山更不留，可謂白玉琢成西子骨，黃金鑄就伍員心，不妨千古師資、風雲際會盡在此處。當時者兩箇老古錐，若非等是純鋼打就底脊項，莫道香嚴後來聞擊竹聲悟道，便是聞無限微玅梵音聲、迦陵頻伽聲，也則是箇隨聲逐色底人，安有『一擊忘所知，更不假修持』之慶快平生也？此六祖所謂『若能一念自知非，自己靈光嘗顯現』，便是者箇道理。所以古人寧使一生不悟，不肯半青半黃，依俙相似，得少為足。然古來亦有一箇樣子，喚作南扁頭。者箇扁頭道人，胸羅三藏、學貫五車，其實有些子風彩，只是打頭不遇得箇咬豬狗底手腳，幾乎一生錯過。虧殺他結得箇好道友，喚作雲峰悅。一日，同遊西山，知其不實，悅歎云：『南有道之器也，惜其未遇本分鉗鎚耳。』也是為他閒事長無明。然如今人結道友，人情意況或有之，求其如此相為者，直是萬中無
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB386.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuan’an Feng. Yuan'an Liao retells Xiangyan's earlier failure to answer Guishan's question and his burning of his old writings, then asks why the later sound of bamboo striking could bring an awakening. He quotes Xiangyan's claim that at one strike knowledge fell away, but argues that without Xiangyan and Guishan's earlier hard encounter even fine sounds would have left him following appearances. Yuan'an narrates and comments on the recalled story; Xiangyan is the original voice of the quoted headword within it.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 不作者般不材不淨底事。黃金自有黃金價，何事和沙賣與人？香嚴知是從前錯路，遂將平昔所有底文字燒卻，道：『此生不學佛法了也，且作箇長行粥飯僧，免役心神。』豈不是以有所得心學無所得法，如何學得來？然則香嚴此時卻也平帖帖地了，乃泣辭溈山，溈山更不留，可謂白玉琢成西子骨，黃金鑄就伍員心，不妨千古師資、風雲際會盡在此處。當時者兩箇老古錐，若非等是純鋼打就底脊項，莫道香嚴後來聞擊竹聲悟道，便是聞無限微玅梵音聲、迦陵頻伽聲，也則是箇隨聲逐色底人，安有『一擊忘所知，更不假修持』之慶快平生也？此六祖所謂『若能一念自知非，自己靈光嘗顯現』，便是者箇道理。所以古人寧使一生不悟，不肯半青半黃，依俙相似，得少為足。然古來亦有一箇樣子，喚作南扁頭。者箇扁頭道人，胸羅三藏、學貫五車，其實有些子風彩，只是打頭不遇得箇咬豬狗底手腳，幾乎一生錯過。虧殺他結得箇好道友，喚作雲峰悅。一日，同遊西山，知其不實，悅歎云：『南有道之器也，惜其未遇本分鉗鎚耳。』也是為他閒事長無明。然如今人結道友，人情意況或有之，求其如此相為者，直是萬中無

Senses.Explanation: Xiangyan's old bamboo-strike verse is quoted in five distinct later teachings; each present master uses its claim to test a listener, explain an awakening or address a student. At a hall address requested by layman Rixin to commend his parents and seek blessings for his mother, Shiyu Mingfang asks the assembly for a word before one's parents were born. He recalls Xiangyan's older difficulty with that question and cites the verse Xiangyan composed after hearing bamboo struck: at one strike knowledge fell away and no further cultivation was needed. Shiyu then asks whether Xiangyan really understood and warns the audience not to be fooled. Shiyu quotes and examines the poem, but the text explicitly assigns its original spoken lines to Xiangyan, who remains the headword actor. Juelang Daosheng argues that students need both an entrance and a way out rather than merely repeating an inherited answer. He asks why Xiangyan's bamboo strike, Lingyun's peach blossom and Xuansha's injured foot each became a decisive occasion for an older practitioner. In that question Juelang quotes Xiangyan's line about one strike undoing what was known, then points to the meeting of teacher and student as the condition of such a turn. Juelang presently questions the old event, while the quoted lines are explicitly Xiangyan's original voice and remain attributed to him. In a preface for a monk formerly named Shoujing who asks to be renamed One Strike, Baichi Xingyuan recalls Xiangyan hearing bamboo struck and quotes Xiangyan's verse about knowledge falling away at one strike. Baichi tells the monk to take the name personally rather than treat it as a label: a word, finger, raised object, blow, shout, wind or bird call could become such a strike only when met directly. Baichi cites the poem for this student's new name; the quoted lines are explicitly Xiangyan's original voice and remain attributed to him. At a hall address requested by disciples honoring their old teacher Zhiyu, Guantao Daqi plants his staff and recites Xiangyan's well-known verse: at one strike knowledge falls away and no further cultivation is needed. Guantao then points to the busy hall and asks how to say that line now, lifting the staff again and bringing the current assembly and commemorated teacher into his answer. Guantao is the present reciter and questioner; Xiangyan is the inherited author of the verse he applies. Yuan'an Liao retells Xiangyan's earlier failure to answer Guishan's question and his burning of his old writings, then asks why the later sound of bamboo striking could bring an awakening. He quotes Xiangyan's claim that at one strike knowledge fell away, but argues that without Xiangyan and Guishan's earlier hard encounter even fine sounds would have left him following appearances. Yuan'an narrates and comments on the recalled story; Xiangyan is the original voice of the quoted headword within it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 過峰西。滿山筍蕨滿園茶，一樹紅花間白花。大抵四時春最好，就中猶好是山家。有人問我何年住，坐久纔方省得來。門外碧桃親手種，春光二十度花開。厭煩勞役愛安閒，箇樣如何居得山？百丈已前巖穴士，生涯全在钁頭邊。年老菴居養病身，日高猶自未開門。怕寒起坐燒松火，一曲樵歌隔塢聞。童子未曾歸動火，水雲早已到投齋。山菴喜免征徭慮，賸種青松只賣柴。玉堂銀燭笙歌夜，金谷羅幃富貴家。爭似道人茅屋下，一天晴月曬梅花。相逢盡說世途難，自向菴中討不安。除却淵明賦歸去，更無一箇肯休官。山厨寂寂斷炊煙，凍鎖泉聲欲雪天。面壁老僧無定力，又思乞食到人間。種了冬瓜便種茄，勞形苦骨做生涯。眾人若要厨堂好，須是園頭常在家。粥去飯來何日了，日生月落幾時休。都來與我無干涉，空起許多閒念頭。屋後青松八九樹，門前紫芋兩三疄。山居道者機關少，家火從頭說向人。此事誰人敢強為，除非知有莫能知。分明月在梅花上，看到梅花早已遲。過去事已過去了，未來不必預思量。只今便道即今句，梅子熟時梔子香。一日打眠三五度，也消不得許多閒。循環數遍琅玕竹，又出青松望遠山。攀緣起倒易消停，卒急難除是愛憎。我笑青山高突兀，青山嫌我廋陵層。真空湛寂惟常在，不覺良田妄所󳬿。真性何曾離妄有，花開花落自春風。天湖水湛琉璃碧，霞霧山圍錦幛紅。觸目本來成現事，何須叉手問禪翁。年老氣衰真箇懶，晨朝更不見和南。客來無語相抵對，辛苦空勞到草菴。老去一身都是懶，閑來百念盡成灰。與兄相見略彈指，無柰人情強接陪。田地無塵長不掃，柴門有客扣方開。雪晴斜月侵簷冷，梅影一枝窓上來。茅屋低低三兩間，團團環遶盡青山。竹牀不許閒雲宿，日未斜時便掩關。禪兄何事到煙蘿，老我生涯苦不多。巖下木樨香滿樹，園中菜甲綠成窠。一片無塵新雨地，半邊有蘚古時松。目前景物人皆見，取用誰知各不同。萬境萬機俱寢息，一知一見盡消融。閒閒兩耳全無用，坐到晨雞與暮鐘。巖房終日寂寥寥，世念何曾有一毫？雖著衣裳喫粥飯，恰如死了未曾燒。新縫紙被烘來煖，一覺安眠到五更。聞得上方鐘皷動，又添一日在浮生。門前枯木似人立，屋後好山如浪堆。老我為人無可說，高高雲路賺兄來。山形凹凸路高低，石占雲頭屋占蹊。地窄栽來蔬菜少，又營小圃在橋西。百千日月閒中度，八萬塵勞靜處消。綠水光中山影轉，紅爐焰上雪花飄。西方有路不肯去，地獄無門鬬要過。金閣銀臺仙子小
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1399.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiwu Qinggong. In Shiwu Qinggong's mountain-dwelling verses, he first describes the work and interruptions of an apparently quiet hermitage: cooking has stopped in winter, he thinks of begging for food, and a garden steward must keep tending the crops. Later, in a short first-person verse, he says that even napping three or five times in one day cannot use up all his spare time, then circles the bamboo and looks toward the pines and distant hills. The line is a deliberately ample image of unhurried mountain life within a sequence that also acknowledges ordinary work; it does not claim that the speaker literally sleeps through every day.

While Faxi Yin is closing the retreat of secretary Lingyue, Lingyue asks how a person acts after cutting through the many distinctions. Faxi answers with the line about napping three or five times in a day and still having leisure left. Lingyue shouts, and Faxi tells him to step back three paces and look. The pair is Faxi's immediate answer about unforced conduct; his follow-up prevents the hearer from treating a picturesque answer as a settled position.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB303.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xieyunji at the Fearless Hall, Guoqing. In a long present discourse, Xieyun Jiji moves through questions about travel, home, alms and everyday living. He imagines begging at a crossroads, eating, and then lying behind the closed door of an old temple; even several naps cannot exhaust the available leisure. He immediately turns that quiet image into vigorous talk of sounding a drum on the living body and making the whole earth small as a grain. The line marks freedom from a fixed place or task in his rhetoric, rather than a simple instruction to idle in a temple.

In an evening address, Wenmu Nian first cites Tian Ning Xibian's old question: if seeing form and seeking by sound are delusive, which one is the Tathagata? Wenmu answers with the napping-and-leisure pair, then says that while it is acceptable, it is much like digging a pit on level ground for someone. The line functions as Wenmu's deliberately risky reply to that old question; the warning is part of his present teaching, not an endorsement of the phrase as a final answer.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. At a small birthday address requested for attendant Zidai, Yushan Shangsi describes his own spare manner at the temple: he has not picked up the mallet or raised the whisk, and even three or five naps a day cannot spend the leisure. Because people still ask him for a word for long life, he turns to Confucius on the wise loving water and the humane loving mountains, asks what the humane person's lifespan means here, and raises his whisk. The pair opens Yushan's self-deprecating account of quiet daily life before the birthday question redirects the talk; it is his own present voice, not Confucius's quotation.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X70/X70n1399.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shiwu Qinggong. In Shiwu Qinggong's mountain-dwelling verses, he first describes the work and interruptions of an apparently quiet hermitage: cooking has stopped in winter, he thinks of begging for food, and a garden steward must keep tending the crops. Later, in a short first-person verse, he says that even napping three or five times in one day cannot use up all his spare time, then circles the bamboo and looks toward the pines and distant hills. The line is a deliberately ample image of unhurried mountain life within a sequence that also acknowledges ordinary work; it does not claim that the speaker literally sleeps through every day.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB220.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Faxiyin. While Faxi Yin is closing the retreat of secretary Lingyue, Lingyue asks how a person acts after cutting through the many distinctions. Faxi answers with the line about napping three or five times in a day and still having leisure left. Lingyue shouts, and Faxi tells him to step back three paces and look. The pair is Faxi's immediate answer about unforced conduct; his follow-up prevents the hearer from treating a picturesque answer as a settled position.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB303.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Xieyunji at the Fearless Hall, Guoqing. In a long present discourse, Xieyun Jiji moves through questions about travel, home, alms and everyday living. He imagines begging at a crossroads, eating, and then lying behind the closed door of an old temple; even several naps cannot exhaust the available leisure. He immediately turns that quiet image into vigorous talk of sounding a drum on the living body and making the whole earth small as a grain. The line marks freedom from a fixed place or task in his rhetoric, rather than a simple instruction to idle in a temple.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J36/J36nB363.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wenmunian. In an evening address, Wenmu Nian first cites Tian Ning Xibian's old question: if seeing form and seeking by sound are delusive, which one is the Tathagata? Wenmu answers with the napping-and-leisure pair, then says that while it is acceptable, it is much like digging a pit on level ground for someone. The line functions as Wenmu's deliberately risky reply to that old question; the warning is part of his present teaching, not an endorsement of the phrase as a final answer.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 年前生也本不曾生，二十年後滅也本不曾滅，既無生又無滅，則盡十方剎土若淨若穢，一任隨緣放曠、任性逍遙，慶雲拂子不妨為你證據。且道證據箇甚麼？更聽一偈：有相身中無相身，纖塵不染絕疏親，當人若解回頭看，剎剎無非是要津。」師到七里菴，大霖主規率眾檀越請小參。「者一片田地，自有祖以來便結契與諸人了也。若是箇善承紹底，一切時中不惟家歌樂業，亦且戶慶安居，縱饒僭竊公行，亦復不敢睥睨。諸人要識這箇來歷麼？」驀以拂子打圓相，云：「此是從上佛祖相傳的契券，任是智如鶖子，智不能知；辯似滿慈，辯不能悉。唯許上無攀仰、下絕己躬底衲僧一肩擔荷，始堪克振嘉聲，為當家種草。且道目前誰是其人？」乃豎拂子，云：「面目現在。」雨山和尚語錄卷第三雨山和尚語錄卷第四嗣法門人記住龍舒白雲禪院語住龍舒白雲禪院語子待上座四十誕辰，請小參。「冷落門戶，獨推風穴；破落門戶，還遜楊岐。東鼓門戶，冷則夜燃松脂，破則床盈雪霰，蓋真有二老風味也。所以，山僧自踏足此間，有椎不拈、有拂不豎，一日打眠三五度，也消不得許多閒。奈有箇無事尋事做底，朝和南、暮不審，欲求一言以永壽命，山僧推托不過，只得扯箇古話以塞其白。記得魯國老孔有云：『知者樂水，仁者樂山；知者動，仁者靜。』拋卻城隍古寺，來空閒寂寞之濱，不可不謂之靜。者既靜矣，且道：仁者壽量又何如演說？」驀豎起拂子，云：「看，看！秪者箇歷千劫而不古，任他白鼠推遷，要且銀臺不變。山僧恁麼舉揚，還稱諸上座意也無？」良久，云：「遇明眼人，一任舉似。」端午，師誕日祈雨，羽公蔣居士請小參。「山僧自到龍舒口邊，實情掃得白醭出，提著佛法兩字，如生冤家相似，非故不近人情，蓋從上風規應如是也。記得長沙岑和尚有云：『我若一向舉揚宗教，法堂前須草深一丈。』爾等既稱祖師門下客，何不略自回眸，看看先宗是何標格？真實向你道：若心地未明、智眼未開，切忌求佛、求祖、求心性、求玄妙，以當平生。設使求而得之，皆屬所依，譬如水母以蝦為目，無有自由分。試看天地未分、未有生佛名字以前一著，你還馳求得麼？你還依傍得麼？既馳求、依傍他不得，到這裏直饒智如鶖子、辯似滿慈，尚未彷彿其趨向，何況今時望道未見者妄自承當，一味露布葛藤以稱得旨？何殊平人妄稱帝王，自取誅戮？奉勸兄弟：既在此箇門中，參須徹、悟須透，莫秪向門頭戶口掠些光影，便為得本。如此見解
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. At a small birthday address requested for attendant Zidai, Yushan Shangsi describes his own spare manner at the temple: he has not picked up the mallet or raised the whisk, and even three or five naps a day cannot spend the leisure. Because people still ask him for a word for long life, he turns to Confucius on the wise loving water and the humane loving mountains, asks what the humane person's lifespan means here, and raises his whisk. The pair opens Yushan's self-deprecating account of quiet daily life before the birthday question redirects the talk; it is his own present voice, not Confucius's quotation.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 一日打眠三五度，也消不得許多閒

Senses.Explanation: Even several naps in a day do not spend the ample leisure of this saying. Shiwu's mountain verse places that leisure among cooking, alms and garden work; Faxi uses the pair to answer Lingyue's question about acting after distinctions fall away, then tells him to step back and look. Xieyun turns an imagined day of begging and resting in an old temple into a discourse about unconfined activity. Wenmu replies to Tian Ning Xibian's old question with the pair but warns that it can trap a hearer; Yushan uses it to describe his own quiet routine before answering a birthday request with Confucius and a raised whisk.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一旦生死到來，將何抵敵

Senses.PreferredTarget: When birth and death arrive, how will you face them?
AlternateTargets: When life and death come upon you, what can you use to withstand them?
SearchAliases: when birth and death arrive, how will you face them?
when life and death come upon you, what can you use to withstand them?
Senses.Note: Hansong Zhicao rebukes a robe-wearer who harms the teaching and asks how he will meet death; the question presses conduct against an unavoidable test. Nanshi Wenxiu warns monks against neglecting discipline and harming the community; his challenge about meeting death asks what can withstand the consequence. Huiguang asks Qianshan Shengren what will meet death after a day of restless activity; Qianshan answers by asking what Huiguang calls birth and death. Three independent recorded teaching contexts survive; this reading is provisional.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此則非魔，即魔所使。蓋假我衣裳，陰以破壞我法者，非但為名教之罪人，亦法門之罪人矣。一旦生死到來，將何抵敵。捨此報身，難逃淪墜。古人謂牢獄未是苦，袈娑下失卻人身，是為苦也。藥石之言，可不銘佩。

Occurrences.Kwic: 出家人棄捨父母，不顧奉養，已為不孝，是名教之罪人矣。期在悟明心地，續佛慧命，廣度眾生。如是，則非但報答今生父母養育以成大孝，直使累世父母冤親俱獲解脫，豈小可哉？若只區區碌碌，今日二、明日四，戒律不能持、禪定不能習，甚至傷風化、玷宗社，非但為名教罪人，亦是法門之罪人矣。一旦生死到來，將何抵敵？捨此報身，難逃淪墜。古人謂：牢獄未是苦，地獄未是苦，袈裟下失却人身是為苦也。藥石之言，可不銘佩？

Entries.SourceTerm: 一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深

Senses.PreferredTarget: One song, then another, understood by no one; after rain, the night pond is deep with spring water.
AlternateTargets: No one understands the songs; rain has deepened the spring pond at night
SearchAliases: songs no one understands, night pond after rain
Senses.Note: The couplet closes Feiyin's hall sermon, turns Minshu's Lantern Festival address and serves Nengren Jian's alternative case comment. An unnamed monk also raises it as a question to a teacher who responds sharply. These are four distinct present uses, not five independent source families.

Occurrences.Kwic: 日上堂，僧問：「三通鼓罷，四眾臨筵，學人上來，請師說法。」師云：「無耳人能聞。」進云：「恁麼則棒頭迸出獅子眼，香象奔騰失卻威。」師云：「怪你不得。」乃云：「誰知四月八，當人降誕時，休云黃面老，成佛獨是伊。所以不可高推聖境、甘處下分，個個具固有風光，人人有向上一路，只要透脫悟機，便能超方無礙，攝大千界於微塵，縱微塵為一大千，隨流得妙，動合淵源，如一滴水含大海性，似一金毛見全獅子，奮迅時天上天下唯我獨尊，哮吼也狐狼野干消聲絕跡，有如是氣概，具莫大威力，還信得及麼？」以手撫掌云：「一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深。」下座。請上堂，僧問：「達磨西來直指人心見性成佛，如何是直指？」師云：「鷓鴣啼處百花新。」進云：「如何是見性？」師云：「狼籍枝頭多少春？」遂以拂子左右擊一擊云：「從上諸佛從此出，一切祖師從此出，天下老古錐從此出，今日齋主王氏亦從此出，故曰：『一切諸佛及諸佛阿耨多羅三藐三菩提法，皆從此經出。』若識得此經，則壽筭彌衍、福德難窮，自古至今，山高水重，仙母獻桃無盡樂，還他受用主人公。」復舉：「當時六祖大師，聞《金剛經》『應無所住而生其心』忽然得悟，且道意旨如何？海闊從魚躍，天高任鳥
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. Feiyin Tongrong speaks in a hall sermon about breaking through and responding freely in all circumstances. He asks whether the assembly can trust this, claps his hands and voices the line about songs no one understands and deep spring water after rain, then leaves the seat. The selected couplet is his own closing challenge.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問近對，無非妄情卜度；舉東明西，猶涉意識廉纖。到者裏，不可以智知、不可以意識。何以故？有時拈起也，一人高拱無為，十方坐斷；有時放下也，萬民欣歌有道，四海無虞。不惟封疆萬里、眼蓋乾坤，且超凡入聖一句作麼生道？過現未來同種智，萬象森羅笑點頭。」擲拄杖，下座。上堂。揮拂子，云：「大眾！認作拂子正是逐色隨聲，到者裏若也會得，見色聞聲不妨百花叢裏繡鴛鴦，自從識得金針後，一任風吹滿袖香。」以拂子擊案，云：「到者裏方見今日上元佳節一段風光，火樹銀花、星橋夜月，戶戶歌聲、家家絃管；其或未然，一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深。」下座。上堂。舉杖召眾，云：「見麼？若以眼見，文殊於此現身。」以拄杖卓一卓，云：「聞麼？若以耳聞，觀音於此應跡。何故？蜀魄連霄叫，鵽鳩長夜啼，圓通門大啟，何事隔雲霓？不以色相見，不以音聲求，還有透出聲色者麼？若也透出，白玉池中蛙擊鼓，青山雲裏鳥吹簫；苟或未然，蝴蝶夢中家萬里，杜鵑枝上月三更。」卓拄杖，下座。解制，上堂。「諸仁者！休去，歇去，一念萬年去，寒灰枯木去，古廟香爐去，一條白練去。若向這裏會得，頭頭道合，法法歸真，以大圓覺伽藍為我身心，安居平等性智，一事圓，千事萬事齊
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB450.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Minshu. At the Lantern Festival, Minshu Ruxiang sweeps his whisk through an address on seeing and hearing without getting caught by appearances. He strikes the table and presents the festival's lights and music; for anyone who still misses that occasion he voices the full song-and-night-pond couplet before leaving. The selected words are his current final turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無奈船何，打破戽斗。保寧茂云：松源摟出心肝，要且未見，先保寧在。山僧今日重為拈出，會盡萬法一如，拈却金圈栗棘，也是泗洲人見大聖。保寧，上堂。風鳴條，雨破塊，曉來枕上鶯聲碎。蝦蟇蚯蚓一時鳴，妙德空生都不會。都不會，三個成羣，四個作隊。窈窈窕窕，飄飄颻颻。向前村後村，折得梨花李花，一佩兩佩。南堂欲云：保寧大似二八少年、風流才子，一向賣俏，於唱教門中足可觀光，在我衲僧門下正好喫棒。何故？禾黍不陽豔，競栽桃李春，翻令力耕者，半作賣花人。能仁鑑拈拄杖云：者裏則不然，白雲為葢，流水作琴，一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深。福州長慶惠暹文慧禪師福州長慶惠暹文慧禪師僧問：離上生之寶剎，登延聖之道場。如何是不動尊？慶曰：孤舟載明月。曰：忽遇艣掉俱停，又作麼生？慶曰：漁人偏愛宿蘆花。灜山誾別云：我不與麼道。或有問：如何是不動尊？祇向道：燒香禮拜著。且道與長慶是同是別？青十二△青十二鄧州丹霞子淳禪師鄧州丹霞子淳禪師上堂：乾坤之內，宇宙之間，中有一寶，秘在形山。肇法師恁麼道，祇解指蹤話跡，且不能拈示於人。丹霞今日劈開宇宙，打破形山，為諸人拈出，具眼者辨取。以拄杖卓一下，曰：還見麼？鷺鷥立雪非同色，明月蘆

Occurrences.Kwic: 取一頌：昨夜三更轉向西，昏昏宇宙幾人迷？澄潭影轉風初息，孤狖微聞嶺外啼。舉：黃檗和尚云：自達磨大師到于中國，唯說一性，惟傳一法。以佛傳佛，不說餘佛；以法傳法，不說餘法。法即不可說之法，佛即不可取之佛，乃是清淨本源心也。師云：法既不可說，佛既不可取，又指何物作本源清淨心耶？喝一喝，云：欲得不招無間業，莫謗如來正法輪。僧問：談玄說妙，舉古論今，盡屬非時語，不涉玄微一句作麼生？師云：百花香處鷓鴣啼。進云：便與麼去時如何？師云：眼中著屑。進云：不與麼去時如何？師云：重疊關山路。進云：一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深。師云：蝦䗫衣下客。師乃云：在凡全凡，在聖全聖，各各據本位，通達事理竟。譬如鐘中無鼓響，鼓中無鐘聲，鐘鼓不相參，句句無前後。若能於此徹根源，一任金毛喚作狗，忙忙途路未歸人，切忌面南看北斗。舉：同安問僧：近離甚處？僧云：東川。安云：雙洞孤松，煙青月白，阿那箇是你主人公？僧云：始屆。同安便領此問，安云：記劍刻舟，破珠求影，豈不是闍梨境界？且坐喫茶。僧云：如何是同安正主？安云：途中駒子不勝驊騮。僧便禮拜，安云：胡人打令，舞拍全無。師云：作家宗師手段，直如巨靈逞擘太華之威，蒼龍展奪驪

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 問近對，無非妄情卜度；舉東明西，猶涉意識廉纖。到者裏，不可以智知、不可以意識。何以故？有時拈起也，一人高拱無為，十方坐斷；有時放下也，萬民欣歌有道，四海無虞。不惟封疆萬里、眼蓋乾坤，且超凡入聖一句作麼生道？過現未來同種智，萬象森羅笑點頭。」擲拄杖，下座。上堂。揮拂子，云：「大眾！認作拂子正是逐色隨聲，到者裏若也會得，見色聞聲不妨百花叢裏繡鴛鴦，自從識得金針後，一任風吹滿袖香。」以拂子擊案，云：「到者裏方見今日上元佳節一段風光，火樹銀花、星橋夜月，戶戶歌聲、家家絃管；其或未然，一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深。」下座。上堂。舉杖召眾，云：「見麼？若以眼見，文殊於此現身。」以拄杖卓一卓，云：「聞麼？若以耳聞，觀音於此應跡。何故？蜀魄連霄叫，鵽鳩長夜啼，圓通門大啟，何事隔雲霓？不以色相見，不以音聲求，還有透出聲色者麼？若也透出，白玉池中蛙擊鼓，青山雲裏鳥吹簫；苟或未然，蝴蝶夢中家萬里，杜鵑枝上月三更。」卓拄杖，下座。解制，上堂。「諸仁者！休去，歇去，一念萬年去，寒灰枯木去，古廟香爐去，一條白練去。若向這裏會得，頭頭道合，法法歸真，以大圓覺伽藍為我身心，安居平等性智，一事圓，千事萬事齊

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 取一頌：昨夜三更轉向西，昏昏宇宙幾人迷？澄潭影轉風初息，孤狖微聞嶺外啼。舉：黃檗和尚云：自達磨大師到于中國，唯說一性，惟傳一法。以佛傳佛，不說餘佛；以法傳法，不說餘法。法即不可說之法，佛即不可取之佛，乃是清淨本源心也。師云：法既不可說，佛既不可取，又指何物作本源清淨心耶？喝一喝，云：欲得不招無間業，莫謗如來正法輪。僧問：談玄說妙，舉古論今，盡屬非時語，不涉玄微一句作麼生？師云：百花香處鷓鴣啼。進云：便與麼去時如何？師云：眼中著屑。進云：不與麼去時如何？師云：重疊關山路。進云：一曲兩曲無人會，雨過夜塘春水深。師云：蝦䗫衣下客。師乃云：在凡全凡，在聖全聖，各各據本位，通達事理竟。譬如鐘中無鼓響，鼓中無鐘聲，鐘鼓不相參，句句無前後。若能於此徹根源，一任金毛喚作狗，忙忙途路未歸人，切忌面南看北斗。舉：同安問僧：近離甚處？僧云：東川。安云：雙洞孤松，煙青月白，阿那箇是你主人公？僧云：始屆。同安便領此問，安云：記劍刻舟，破珠求影，豈不是闍梨境界？且坐喫茶。僧云：如何是同安正主？安云：途中駒子不勝驊騮。僧便禮拜，安云：胡人打令，舞拍全無。師云：作家宗師手段，直如巨靈逞擘太華之威，蒼龍展奪驪

Senses.Explanation: The same moon-image does different work in four current settings: a teacher portrait, two distinct Mid-Autumn questions, and a perception contrast on Buddha-awakening day. Wuzu Fayan praises an image of his teacher Baiyun. He opens with one moon in the sky casting reflections into many waters, then says that the teacher's true likeness is neither the moon nor the water and playfully describes the painted face. The selected line is Wuzu's own portrait-verse image, framing the relation between a single original and many appearances before refusing to identify the teacher with either side of the simile. At a Mid-Autumn hall address attended by visitors, Huanxi Weiyi says one moon is in the sky and its image enters many waters. He asks whether the moon at Double Sword Peak and the one in Furong Stream and Letan Pool are the same. If one says they are the same, the places remain apart; if different, there is no second moon in the sky. He presses the assembly for a response and cites another moon-and-shadow saying. This is Huanxi's present question about sameness and difference, not merely a decorative festival image. In a separate Mid-Autumn hall sermon at Tiantong, Huanxi Weiyi again says that one moon shines above and its image enters many waters. This time he asks whether there is a form to leave or no form to leave: if there is a form, what form does the moon have; if none, how does one account for the many water images? He repeats the line inside the same sermon and closes with an image of repeatedly searching a clear pool for the moon. This is a distinct present challenge about form, though its two exact hits belong to one occasion. At a Buddha-awakening day hall sermon, Gulin Qingmao places one moon in the sky and images in many waters beside one defect in the eye making illusory flowers seem to fall through space. He says Shakyamuni has entered the group of water buffalo, then contrasts what is gained or lost in the mind before striking the Chan seat and recalling Nanquan. Gulin voices the paired moon image in his own present teaching about perception; the source does not specify a literal astronomical event. Liao'an and Yu'an give separate current Guanyin verse applications of the one-moon image.

Senses.PreferredTarget: one moon appears in all waters; all water-moons are gathered in one moon
AlternateTargets: one moon is reflected in every water, and every reflected moon belongs to one moon
Senses.Note: A reflection image for the relation of one source to many appearances. In Chan instruction the image is often turned into a direct question about moon, water, and seeing.

Senses.Explanation: One moon appears in many waters without dividing into separate moons; the reflections are gathered by that one moon. Fangrong lifts a mooncake and points from the sky to the water before denying that reasoning alone reaches the image. Hansong sets many viewers under one autumn moon. Xueyan explains the image through one mind and many phenomena, then asks after the moon when clouds intervene. Chushi asks which is moon and which is water when the whole earth is each. Baiyun raises a staff and tests whether listeners can use the image in practice.

Senses.PreferredTarget: many kinds within one and no division within two
AlternateTargets: one is manifold while two remain undivided

Occurrences.Kwic: 興眼無筋，錯中南方蠱毒深，一掬肝膓俱裂破，年年此日痛傷心。謝新舊兩班，上堂。欲建大廈，須假眾材；欲駕巨舟，必資眾手。眾材既辨，大廈可成；眾手能為，巨舟必濟。山野濫尸祖席，曲荷諸人相成，老慧超法令如存，南禪師愿力猶在。到這裏，其進也，獰龍得水；其退也，猛虎靠山。何親？何踈？無新？無舊？萬事頭頭合轍，一門和氣藹然，前三後三，日面月面。然雖如是，且道：不動干戈，坐致太平一句又作麼生？一朝權在手，看取令行時。因事，上堂。是非長短耳邊風，切莫於中覔異同。要得八風吹不動，放教心地等虗空。慈受老人只解順水張帆，不能逆風把柂。黃龍又且不然，是非都去了，是非裏薦取。何故聻？幾度黑風翻大浪，未曾聞道釣舟傾。上堂，舉：雲門示眾云：十五日已前即不問，十五日已後道將一句來。自代云：日日是好日。師云：這跛脚阿師，始者與麼告報將謂將謂，及乎末後露出尾巴元來元來。黃龍即不然，十五日已前即不問，十五日已後

Senses.PreferredTarget: Once you embody it and become poor in the Way, your use of the Way still resembles a poor person’s.
AlternateTargets: When you come to embody poverty in the Way, you use the Way like someone with nothing.
SearchAliases: once you embody it and become poor in the way, your use of the way still resembles a poor person’s.
when you come to embody poverty in the way, you use the way like someone with nothing.
Senses.Note: An anthology preserves Longya Judun’s verse on learning poverty before approaching the Way. Longya says that even after embodying this poverty, using the Way looks like the life of a poor person. This is the original verse, not a new anthology voice. In his separate case commentary, Linquan Conglun explicitly quotes Longya’s verse, calls its poverty “still poorer,” and redirects readers to ordinary clothing and meals according to their means. The verse supports Linquan’s current appraisal. One original verse and one distinct later commentary survive; validation is provisional.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB189.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu. Sanyi Mingyu speaks to lay supporters in his home region. He describes the cooperation of learned officials and Chan elders, invokes ordinary acts such as planting fields, and calls the region an ancestral field whose title and boundaries are clear. Local mountains, waters, birds and buildings then fill his address. Near the end he mentions Fayan's long remaining with a view of scenery and Xuefeng's whole earth as the eye. Raising his whisk, he asks what sort of eye this is, and answers with one plum branch breaking the year's last cold month and all things returning to spring. The single branch and complete renewal cap that local scene and question about seeing; the line is not merely a seasonal greeting detached from the address. The headword is rendered: One plum branch breaks the last month of winter; all things return to spring.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J40/J40nB494.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Yushan. The second speaker is an unnamed monk at Yushan Shangsi's twelfth-month eighth-day assembly. The monk describes bitter wind and cold rain and asks for a timely phrase. Yushan answers that midnight is bright and dawn does not disclose it. When the monk declares that all beings open the right eye, Yushan asks for the monk's own eye; the monk replies with the plum-and-spring pair. Yushan asks what connection that has. The monk tells him that he too must use his eye, and Yushan strikes. The borrowed spring image is the monk's offered answer under examination, not Yushan's certificate that the eye has opened. The headword is rendered: One plum branch breaks the last month of winter; all things return to spring.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一根既返源，六根成解脫

Senses.PreferredTarget: When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are liberated.
AlternateTargets: Return one sense faculty to its source, and all six gain release.
SearchAliases: one faculty returns to source six faculties liberated
Senses.Note: The local challenge and the current teacher's response govern the reading; quoted evaluations are not universal factual claims.

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂舉起拂子云：「者便是觀音妙智之力，若喚作拂子，即不能證妙智；不喚作拂子，亦不能證妙智；若不見拂子、亦不不見拂子，即見性空。見性既空，眼不緣色；聞性亦空，耳不緣聲；乃至分別亦空，意不緣法。所謂一根既返源，六根成解脫，然後即見一切眾生皆隨境顛倒、隨情造業、隨業受報，三界昇沉無有休息。如是，發同體之悲、興無緣之慈。所以道：聞性空時妙無比，思修頓入三摩地，無緣慈力赴群機，明月影臨千澗水。」擲拂子，下座。

ActorAttribution.ActorLabel: Manjushri Bodhisattva as earlier verse speaker
ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: T19n0945 0130a14–16 says Manjushri speaks the verse; 0131a20–21 contains the exact line.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun. The six faculties are sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch and thought; the pair describes their release through one faculty's return to its source. Miyun Yuanwu raises his whisk and tests both calling it a whisk and not calling it one, then describes the empty nature of seeing, hearing and discrimination. He invokes Manjushri's scriptural verse and turns from this release to compassion for beings driven by circumstances, emotion, action and its results. Casting down the whisk, he caps the address with moonlight reflected in many streams. The quoted formula leads toward responsive care rather than a promise of sensory shutdown.

Occurrences.Kwic: 《首楞嚴經》云：「一根既返源，六根成解脫。」一根歸源，六根尚爾解脫，此以三處伏斷，諸根豈不清淨？肯向此三處做手腳，是為切要。

ActorAttribution.ActorLabel: Manjushri Bodhisattva as earlier verse speaker

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB219.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Zhuanyuheng of Purple Bamboo Grove. Zhuanyu Guanheng explicitly quotes the Surangama Scripture while counseling the layman Ruone. Although the highest matter has no fixed delusion or awakening, he says, one must work to wear down habitual self-love. He identifies body, speech and mind as its most active routes and asks that they be guarded through respectful conduct, gentle speech and even-minded attention. If one faculty's return releases all six, how much more relevant is attention to these three? The verse is applied to concrete conduct, not merely recited to declare that effort is unnecessary.

Occurrences.Kwic: 惟吾真宗，不於盤面上橫蕩而行，遇一卦，遇一爻，只是一針透底，則彼吉者不能吉、凶者不能凶，陰者不能陰、陽者不能陽，處處逢歸路、頭頭達故鄉，一根既返源，六根成解脫，又何根根塵塵非常住真心哉？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB311.xml). Complete Record of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie. Juelang Daosheng voices the pair in a discussion that takes images from divination. Instead of wandering across a diagram's surface, his account of the true teaching pierces a hexagram or line straight through, so favorable and unfavorable, yin and yang no longer command their usual effects. Everywhere becomes a way home. The pair supports that return, after which he asks how any faculty or its object is outside enduring mind. This is Juelang's present religious argument, not a verification that a fortune-telling chart predicts liberation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。僧問：「如何是透法身向上事？」師云：「腳跟下左纏右縛。」乃云：「雲濤日夜吼如雷，驚醒時人夢眼開，從此耳根都透徹，觀音老子為誰來？莫不是一根既返源，六根成解脫，見聞如幻翳，三界若空花，聞復翳根除，塵消覺圓淨？若也未悟，未免背覺合塵，與一切眾生從無始以來生死相續，皆由不識常住真心、性淨明體，被諸妄想執著，故有輪轉。爾諸人到這裏作麼生轉身？若也轉得身來，箇箇常光現前，人人壁立萬仞，舟通大海、月朗長空，不疑雁過瀟湘、影落寒潭；苟或未然，岸上行人聲有韻，船中漁父和來齊。」下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB450.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Minshu. Minshu Ruxiang answers a monk asking about what goes beyond the embodiment of the teaching with feet tangled left and right. He then describes roaring waves waking dream-filled eyes and asks whether this is the return of one faculty, release of six and purification of seeing and hearing. If the assembly has not awakened, however, he says they remain caught in attachment and must turn around now. The headword occurs within that interrogative testing. It does not establish that hearing a dramatic sound has automatically released every faculty in every hearer.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有為俗之事，如是僧、俗雖殊，其道一也。然而「道」之一字卒難體認，在俗有俗之體認、在僧有僧之體認，各各體認分曉，看是箇甚麼道理？若僧、若俗不二，一句作麼生委悉？糞多茄子大，地壯菜根麤。示玄白禪人示玄白禪人行腳住山，其用心是一，欲究其一則無不一也。然法法頭頭固是多種，則方便亦多門也。總之，一有多種，二無兩般。試問爾輩：如何是一？示紫芝禪者示紫芝禪者出家一段氣岸，天子不臣、諸侯不友，是一尊貴，法須要尊貴人，如獅子乳玻璃盞盛者是也。雖然如是，要且不是祖師西來意，且道如何是祖師西來意？一棒一條痕，一掌一握血。示陳善人示陳善人人生大夢中，大夢誰先覺？夢覺亦是幻，誰縛欲誰脫？但於二六時諦審誰一著，忽地覷破，渠渠誰無兩箇？若要執取一，依然當面錯錯錯。咄！破山禪師語錄卷第九破山禪師語錄卷第十當陽玉泉嗣法門人印正等編法語三法語三示秋水西堂示秋水西堂老僧過忠南相值之後，經今數年又來高梁，雙桂相從，共守寂寥。一日呈卷，欲老僧法語，老僧只得向義虎弄爪牙，話墻壁邊影響耳。試問：「十方無壁落，四面亦無門」，且道何為墻壁？何為影響？若向者裏道得，早在堂奧中打坐打眠，橫行直撞了。呵呵。示惺月禪者示惺月

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB178.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Feiyin. Feiyin Tongrong deploys the complete saying in a present recorded teaching turn.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB200.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Erzhan Zun of Shishuang. Shitian Faxun deploys the complete saying in a present recorded teaching turn.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Cast from one mold
Senses.Note: “Cast from one mold” means the products have a common shape. Luyan says it when three students offer different words that all miss the moon; Sanyi says it of repeated explanations that leave the old case untouched. Baichi gives the same image a positive force for lineage continuity, and Guxue does likewise for a transmitted seal. Yunwai uses it after striking the table, while Jiqi writes of the nose born with one’s face. The surrounding turn decides whether sameness is a virtue or a defect.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB452.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lüyan He. Lüyan He first asks the assembled students what the moon is after warning against staring at a pointing finger. Chaoang says it is pitch dark, Xi calls it spread across heaven and earth, and Xu replies with a mountain-and-river image. Lüyan says all three replies have come out of one mold: they recognize only the moon's reflected image, not the real moon. He then asks Xu again and covers his mouth as Xu starts to answer. The phrase criticizes interchangeable clever replies in this live examination, not the physical production of a seal.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB189.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu. Sanyi Mingyu retells Tianping's encounter with Xiyuan, who repeatedly calls him wrong and offers to discuss the errors over a summer; Tianping declines and later says that he had already gone wrong when he set out south. Sanyi says students have spent years recycling Tianping's later explanation or an easy line about being struck before boarding a boat, all cast from one mold. He urges them to investigate Xiyuan's point rather than consume another teacher's leftovers. Here the phrase rejects copied case interpretations that differ in wording but repeat the same evasion.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. In instruction addressed to West Hall monk Pu, Baichi Xingyuan traces transmission from Nanyue under the Sixth Patriarch down to his own Jingshan elder. He says successive generations have no gap in the central aim because each awakens and uses it for themselves, although their ways of helping people vary. The line about coming out of one mold is paired with one mirror reflecting another and one expanse of space meeting another. Baichi uses the image positively for unbroken realization and transmission, then adds a verse urging the present heir to put that inheritance into action.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB208.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guxue Zhe. Guxue Zhenzhe places the line in a verse titled 'Keeping the Seal' within a series of poems on monastery duties. He says words carry the teaching and the printer's carved wood speaks in their place; a skilled hand must raise the subtle seal fully, so that one impression comes out of the mold and is handed down across past and present. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB280.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunwaize of Shending. At the close of a seven-day retreat, Yunwai Xingze warns the assembly against treating Zhaozhou's case with stock shouts, blows or slogans. He picks up his ritual scepter and strikes the incense table, telling the students to break through the skull right here; then the four directions, above and below, ordinary and holy, being and nonbeing will emerge together from one mold for them. He follows by saying he does not slight them and that all will become Buddhas. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB452.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lüyan He. ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 月累益見其悟矣。然而此等境緣雖屬定分，以智眼觀之，總於吾道無所礙也。且作麼生是智眼？居士試向動靜閒忙中真實體究，自然寶藏豁開，獲大受用。政當恁時，忽若有人持東平鏡、趙州衫來，不作貴、不作賤，汝又如何還價？山僧立契券已定，待居士討箇分曉證據始得耳。示溥西堂示溥西堂六祖下南嶽，讓至我徑山老人為三十五世，源源有準，代代無差，究其旨歸，無非廓揚正眼，展演全機，徹底為人直截痛快，并及驚蛇打草、鬼出神偷、布網張羅、據款結案，總從自得自悟中來。所以，一模脫出如鏡照鏡、似空合空，無半點淆訛、無絲毫滲漏，脈遠流長，歷年而愈光大也。聖墨公受囑已久，茲破關入鹽省覲余，迺書其從上相承，大概若此。復拈一偈以盡之云：正脈流傳光且大，祖孫相繼振家聲，箇中機用天然別，要在當人勉力行。示道眉侍者示道眉侍者鶯吟燕語，麥秀花香，頭頭是道，更不囊藏。咄！與麼說話賺殺人。何故？為伊大煞成現，日見日聞，無有能知是道者。或云：「道在日用，日用不知，只此不知處便是真知處。」咄！與麼說話，秦山土地未肯點首在。初學後生不向這裏

Senses.Explanation: Coming out of one mold describes things or responses that take the same shape; the value of that sameness depends on the teaching moment. Lüyan rejects three moon answers that share a clever pattern, and Sanyi warns that repeated explanations of Tianping's case are likewise copied instead of investigated. Baichi praises continuity of awakening and transmission with the same image. Guxue draws on a printer's seal to picture a faithful imprint across time. Yunwai uses the mold after striking the table to challenge fixed divisions, while Jiqi turns the inborn nose into a verse after retelling Mazu's wild-duck case.

Senses.PreferredTarget: a single pivotal move
AlternateTargets: one responsive device
one turn of the mechanism
Senses.Note: One move is understood through its surrounding action or question; the records do not supply one fixed gesture that every speaker must perform.

Senses.Explanation: A single pivotal move is one responsive opening or act through which a larger range of handling becomes available. Mi’an Xianjie says that raising one move brings innumerable moves at once, and Yuanwu Keqin pairs one move clearly understood with countless moves turning freely. Yunju Zongzhen claims one move in his answering verse, while Xisou Shaotan illustrates his with eating and dressing. A monk’s question about the first move and Yuanjie Ying’s question about handing one over show that the wording can also be put forward for testing, rather than describing a performed gesture. One move is understood through its surrounding action or question; the records do not supply one fixed gesture that every speaker must perform.

Senses.PreferredTarget: where does the one return?
AlternateTargets: where does the one go back to?

SearchAliases: where does the one go back
ten thousand things return to one
Senses.Explanation: This is the stock second half of the question 'the ten thousand things return to one; where does the one return?' The first half supplies the otherwise missing antecedent of 'the one.' An unnamed monk puts the complete question to Zhaozhou Congshen, who answers that in Qingzhou he made a cloth shirt weighing seven catties. The question is not confined to that exchange: Hongzhi Zhengjue places beside it a version answered by Wenshu Yingzhen with 'the Yellow River's nine bends,' and Baizhang Mingzhao An answers that not one person has failed to ask. Gaofeng Yuanmiao makes the question his entire address before looking left and right and leaving the seat; Lanan Dingxu uses it as a chamber test; Zhuquan Liaohuan Falin supplies another answer. Zen bends an ordinary destination question into a portable public-interview challenge whose divergent answers are the history of one stable question, not different meanings of the headword.
Senses.Note: Across the collected corpus the exact question occurs 838 times in 216 texts; the full two-part question is also extensively attested with and without punctuation. No equation-style self-definition was found. Multiple respondents, answers, later comments, an entire hall address, a chamber test, and continuous use as an assigned saying all preserve one question rather than an individual-specific meaning.

Senses.Explanation: The mind's inborn luminity counted as one whole stretch, shining before birth and waiting to be reclaimed from ink and clamor. Zhufeng Zhenxu, on the ghost festival, sets autumn-pool moon-shadow and still-night bell-sound around one stretch of light that never dulls, and warns that whoever only half-grasps it is a dead man whose soul has not scattered; Hongzhi Zhengjue hangs the bright moon of a frost sky over the central peak and lets one stretch of light wash the dull darkness; Yezhu Fuhui, tonsuring the layman Chen Qin, takes up the upward hammer to spark the stretch of light behind that newly shaven head; and Qibai Defu, in xiaocan, declares the stretch shone on heaven before leaving the womb and lights the earth after, endowed in everyone, undimmed in the fool, unincreased in the sage. Ruibai Mingxue, writing to the layman Zhang Wofu, rules that with no second person or second thought to be found it is only one's own one stretch of light — set your eyes there and stop seeking outward; Shanhui Huan, recounting his own years in the lecture halls, groans that the stretch of light of the buddhas and ancestors was buried under ink and letters; Baiyu Jingsi, at the news of Yongjue's death, watches the old man's final stretch of light shoot three thousand miles into Yusi peak; and Lingji Xingguan, answering the scholar Zhu, orders him to squeeze out at full speed the sky-covering, earth-bearing stretch of light until it streams from his chest.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (B/B25/B25n0144.xml). Zutang Ji (Anthology from the Patriarchs’ Hall). An unnamed monk asks Luopu: if a single hair has swallowed the vast sea, what more could be said within it? Luopu answers that a household possessing a diagram of White Marsh has no such strange apparition. The monk voices the exact pair and Luopu responds; the metaphorical hair is not an action performed by either participant. The question presents an extreme image of inclusion together with a demand about what speech could remain, while the reply treats something in that presentation as a strange apparition to be checked. This retained historical witness supplies the old encounter for the later responses. Its parallel lamp copies do not supply more monks or separate exchanges, and the text gives no personal name for the questioner.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1425.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Danxia Zichun. Danxia Zichun includes the same monk’s question and Luopu’s diagram reply among his verses on old encounters. His own four-line response describes a thousand expanses of cloud before the cliff but no lamp indoors at midnight, then an enduring high ridge and layers of green in the slanting evening light. The exact hair-and-sea pair remains the anonymous monk’s quoted question, not a statement that Danxia himself witnessed such an event. Danxia supplies a new poetic response after Luopu’s words. The changing outside scene and the unlit interior do not simply restate the claim that all speech is finished; they give another scene in which to consider that claim. The record does not spell out a one-to-one doctrinal meaning for each landscape detail, so the verse should not be decoded into one with certainty.

Occurrences.Kwic: 姮娥呈巧妙，眼睛直上綉鴛鴦。師云：棋逢敵手難藏倖，詩到重吟始見功，世智辯聰難比況，枉將有限趂無窮。此之所謂非尋常也。譬如蟾桂遠布清香，普請諸人牢收鼻孔。據二老宿問答交馳，機辯冠眾，非唯空飛閃電，盤走明珠，有若姮娥特伸巧妙，拈芒長玉線，穿沒鼻金針，向眼睛直上綉出鴛鴦，豈非好手者歟？雖然如是，只知有功之功，寧曉無用之用？還相委悉麼？何如玉女夜拋梭，特來織錦於西舍。第二十五則洛浦一毫(飛走)第二十五則洛浦一毫示眾云：把斷要津，不通凡聖；放開一線，聊許商量。未審誰能祗對？舉僧問洛浦：一毫吞盡巨海，於中更復何言？浦云：家有白澤之圖，必無如是妖恠。師云：言言見諦言非有，句句超宗句本無。所以道：毛吞大海，芥納須彌。斯皆稱性之談，非同事相有局量者也。這僧向窮理盡性、杜絕辭源處引惹詞訟，是他洛浦終是老手舊肐膊，向伊做精揑恠、廝謾廝謼之時，輕輕點化。道家有白澤之圖，必無如是妖恠。白澤者，乃俚俗鎮宅師子之異號也。保福別云：家無白澤之圖，亦無如是妖恠。林泉道：詩爭一字新。若遇承言滯句杜撰，衲僧合作麼生禁治？但云：急急如律令攝。是他丹霞優遊平易，為伊指示。頌曰：巖前雖有雲千頃，戶內殊無半夜燈。極目
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1304.xml). Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Chan Master Danxia Zichun’s Verses on Ancient Cases: Xutang Collection. Linquan Conglun raises the old Luopu question in his commentary on Danxia’s verse. He says that talk of a hair swallowing the sea and a mustard seed holding the world mountain speaks according to nature rather than the ordinary limits of material things. He criticizes the monk for provoking a verbal lawsuit precisely where he claims reasoning and speech have ended. Luopu, he says, recognizes and checks that making of strange apparitions. Linquan explains White Marsh as a household-protecting lion figure, notes Baofu’s different answer denying that the household has its diagram, and asks how one should deal with monks who cling to received words and improvise explanations. His own proposed cap is the urgent command to obey the ordinance and be seized. Thus the exact pair is the old anonymous monk’s question; Luopu answers it, Danxia composes the verse, and Linquan now diagnoses and counters the verbal maneuver. Baofu’s alternative is a comparison inside that discussion, not a further selected occurrence.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一氣不言含有象，萬靈何處謝無私
Entries.CreatedBy: Codex Iriya construction lane C evidence-first

Senses.PreferredTarget: one breath speaks no words yet contains all forms, while the myriad beings have nowhere outside its impartiality from which to give thanks
AlternateTargets: without speaking, one breath contains every form; no being stands outside its impartial reach
one vital breath is wordless but form-bearing, impartial to every being
SearchAliases: where can all beings give thanks
Senses.Note: Four distinct answer and comment uses span four distinct works.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且正令當行，如何理論？乃擊拂子曰：一氣不言含有象，萬靈何處謝無私。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120). Jinshan Zhong strikes the whisk and gives the couplet after asking how the active command is to be stated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 且功不浪施一句作麼生道？一氣不言含有象，萬靈何處謝無私？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J37/J37nB388.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yikui of Shending. Yikui Yuankui gives the couplet as his answer to the request for a sentence in which effort is not spent in vain.

Occurrences.Kwic: 法林音云：東禪恁麼道，還扶得起國師麼？南堂欲云：國師不得雲門，洎合勞而無功；總似雪竇，未免白日見鬼。如今或有人問，但向道：一氣不言含有象，萬靈何處謝無私？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X66/X66n1297.xml). Grove of the Mirror of the School. Jialing Xingyin reviews earlier comments on the national teacher and supplies the couplet as the answer he would give a questioner.

Occurrences.Kwic: 正與麼時，且知恩報恩一句作麼生道？一氣不言含有象，萬靈何處謝無私。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu. Liao'an Qingyu gives the couplet as the answer to his own request for a sentence that knows and repays beneficence.

Senses.Explanation: One breath says nothing yet contains visible forms; the myriad beings have nowhere outside its impartial reach from which to offer thanks. Chan masters preserve the two lines as one answer about an active command, effective work, and repaying beneficence. Jinshan strikes the whisk before giving it; Yikui gives it for a sentence in which effort is not wasted; Jialing offers it after reviewing earlier case comments; and Liao'an gives it for knowing and repaying beneficence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一氣轉一大藏教，水流濕兮火就燥。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chushi Fanqi (楚石梵琦禪師語錄): Chushi Fanqi authors the send-off verse; the canon custodian named in its heading is the recipient.

Senses.Explanation: To turn the whole great canon in a single breath is Chushi Fanqi’s hyperbolic image for delivering its entirety in one continuous burst. The line occurs in his send-off verse for a canon custodian traveling to Tiantai and Yandang, between ancestral transmission imagery and the paired line that water runs toward wetness and fire toward dryness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明總別。廣辯異同。研一法之根元。搜諸緣之本末
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2016.xml). Zongjing Record, Yanshou's own preface: Yongming Yanshou compares essence and activity to water and waves, then says he will clarify the general and particular and investigate the root of a single teaching or phenomenon and the sources of its conditions. This introduces the organizing purpose of the hundred-roll compilation. The preface's author line names Yanshou; the headword belongs to that first-person program, not anonymous compiler narration.

Occurrences.Kwic: 七歲時，於村校書處得一法門，超情離見，絕妙絕
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps, Zhihai Benyi section: in a hall address Zhengjue Yi recalls obtaining one teaching at village school when he was seven, more than sixty years earlier. He asks the assembly to listen and recites a verse about returning from farming with a calf and firewood, a hearth fire, and clothing for the household. One teaching is his own retrospective description of what he presents now, not the compiler's report outside his speech.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門來？文殊曰：我不見一法在門外，何以教我入門
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X83/X83n1578.xml). Record Pointing at the Moon: Shakyamuni asks Manjusri why he remains outside the gate rather than entering. Manjusri replies that he sees not a single thing outside, so how can he be told to come in? The headword is the object of Manjusri's denial within his explicit reply. Later masters test whether this is speech from inside or outside the gate.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The explicit Manjusri speech marker introduces the first-person denial of seeing a single thing outside the gate. The surrounding invitation belongs to Shakyamuni, not the compiler.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門來。文殊曰。我不見一法在門外。何以教我入門
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X80/X80n1565.xml). Five Lamps Compendium: Shakyamuni calls Manjusri to enter the gate. Manjusri answers that he sees no single thing outside it and asks how he can be ordered in. One thing is what his reply denies seeing outside. This is a recension of the same exchange preserved in the other lamp witnesses; its voice is Manjusri, not the compiler.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The explicit Manjusri speech marker introduces the first-person denial of seeing a single thing outside the gate. The surrounding invitation belongs to Shakyamuni, not the compiler.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三塗乃有獨立分假使有一法過於涅槃者亦無少許生
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (C/C077/C077n1710.xml). Recorded Sayings of Ancient Masters, Baizhang Huaihai's second discourse record: Baizhang warns that even freedom from possessiveness can become attachment to a teaching. He says that even if there were a single teaching beyond nirvana, one should not form the slightest thought of treasuring it. One teaching marks the hypothetical superior object his warning refuses to privilege; this is Baizhang's continuing discourse.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本來法無法無非法何於一法中有法有不法說偈已。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T51/T51n2076.xml). Jingde Transmission of the Lamp, Mahakasyapa's transmission to Ananda: Mahakasyapa tells Ananda he will not remain long, entrusts the teaching to him, and bids him hear a verse. Within that verse he asks how one teaching can contain both teaching and non-teaching. The headword belongs to Mahakasyapa's quoted transmission verse; the compiler resumes after the verse with his departure to Cock's Foot Mountain.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The Mahakasyapa section explicitly introduces his instruction to Ananda to hear the verse; the headword is inside that verse, before the compiler resumes with his departure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 門來？文殊云：我不見一法在門外，何以教我入門
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp: when Shakyamuni asks why Manjusri does not enter the gate, Manjusri replies that he sees not one thing outside it. The phrase denies an outside object on which the invitation could depend. Xuanjue's following question about inside and outside and Dawei's reply are later voices; the exact headword is Manjusri's own quoted reply.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: The explicit Manjusri speech marker introduces the first-person denial of seeing a single thing outside the gate. The surrounding invitation belongs to Shakyamuni, not the compiler.

Senses.Explanation: A single thing, phenomenon or teaching: the counted unit takes its force from what the speaker singles out. Manjusri denies seeing even one thing outside the gate; Baizhang refuses to treasure even a hypothetical teaching beyond nirvana. Yanshou speaks of investigating a single teaching’s root, while Zhengjue Yi recalls one teaching encountered in childhood. Mahakasyapa’s transmission verse turns the relation between one teaching and teaching or non-teaching into a question. These settings keep the phrase concrete to its sentence rather than making every instance one technical object. The governing sentence determines whether the counted unit is a thing, phenomenon or teaching.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一法若有，毘盧墮在凡夫；萬法若無，普賢失其境界

Senses.PreferredTarget: If even one thing is fixed, Vairocana falls among ordinary people; if all things are absent, Samantabhadra loses his field
SearchAliases: if even one thing is fixed, vairocana falls among ordinary people; if all things are absent, samantabhadra loses his field
Senses.Note: The saying says that holding to one fixed thing lowers Vairocana, while declaring all things absent leaves Samantabhadra without a field. Poshan gives the pair after questions from his assembly; Zhangxue adds a hand gesture to test what is meant by one. Hanyu tells listeners to cut off the two sides, and Minshu follows the pair through a sermon on forms of present activity. The two halves work together as a refusal to settle in either position.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB177.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Poshan. At his opening address after taking the seat, Poshan Haiming strikes a monk who asks whether today's abbot and the Buddha of old are the same or different, and strikes again when the monk asks for the one-to-one transmitted intent. After the monk retires, Poshan tells the gathering that if even one thing is held to exist, Vairocana falls among ordinary people, while if all things are held absent, Samantabhadra loses the field for his activity. Senses.Explanation: The paired line rejects treating either a single thing as fixed or the whole field of things as absent. Poshan speaks it after twice striking a questioning monk and moves into large and small interpenetrating. Zhangxue turns his palm sideways after speaking it and challenges the assembly to recognize Vairocana without calculation. Hanyu uses it after a monk asks how to get past busy and idle, warning against both sides. Minshu places it in a sermon on robes, bowl and the entire field of activity, before separately citing older teachers.

Entries.SourceTerm: 一法雖無異，三人乃見差

Senses.PreferredTarget: Though the teaching does not differ, the three people see it differently.
SearchAliases: one teaching three people see differently
Senses.Note: The people and comparisons are supplied by each passage. The line does not always identify the same three figures, and Heyi does not let it settle a question by choosing one or two.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。雲巖傍參道吾。雪峯傍參巖頭。君子不恥下問。今雲巖雪峯之道大行。亦退己讓人之餘慶也。而巖頭天資英邁。抑揚德山之道。天下橫行。無敢當鋒者。蓋見處洞達蘊養成就。故得如是。看他二僧。雪峯門下。箭鋒相直。也是箇行脚漢。為甚直至夏末。尚疑末後句。只為眼鈍頭迷當面蹉過。巖頭與他說出許多道理。雪峯與我同條生。不與我同條死。一法雖無異。三人乃見差。這僧與雪峯。一時道是甚麼。及至論末後句。說與也不知。豈非差之毫釐失之千里也。且道。這僧實不會。要放這話行。溈山哲云。大小雪峯巖頭。却被這僧勘破。萬松道。冷眼不防。巖頭雪峯。猶可恕也。後來又點德山亦不會末後句。直是難甘。是故天童兩次頌出。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2004.xml). Wansong’s Commentary and Chanting on Tiantong Jue’s Verse-Comments on the Ancients: Record of the Congrong Hermitage. Wansong Xingxiu uses the line while discussing a monk's exchanges with Xuefeng and Yantou about the last word. He praises the elders' training and capacity, but asks why the monk could still doubt at the end of summer. Yantou's explanation that Xuefeng shares his line of birth but not his line of death leads into the one-teaching, three-people contrast. Wansong says the monk and Xuefeng both say, 'What is it?', yet the monk still does not understand when told about the last word: a hair's difference becomes a thousand miles. He also reports another teacher's claim that the monk exposed both elders and does not simply accept every verdict. The phrase locates a difference in understanding within this disputed exchange, not three equally authorized opinions. The headword is rendered: Though the teaching does not differ, the three people see it differently.

Occurrences.Kwic: 林泉道：父聞子徤，恨不殺身。想來肐膊豈肯外屈？只如仰山聲色與踈山聲色是同是別？一法雖無異，三人乃見差。溈仰酬酢廝殺，無過父子兵；踈山這僧一言道斷處，千古意分明。為人手段，盡在於斯。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X67/X67n1304.xml). Elder Linquan’s Commentary and Chanted Remarks on Chan Master Danxia Zichun’s Verses on Ancient Cases: Xutang Collection. Linquan Conglun first asks whether Yangshan's sound and form and Shushan's sound and form are the same or different. He then gives the one-teaching, three-people line, and compares Guishan and Yangshan's exchange to father and son fighting together. Shushan and the monk, he adds, end the matter in a word. The phrase connects these differing exchanges while preserving their particular handling. This occurrence does not fix one permanent list of three people for every use of the saying. Senses.Explanation: Though the teaching does not differ, the three people see it differently. Wansong Xingxiu uses the line while discussing a monk's exchanges with Xuefeng and Yantou about the last word. He praises the elders' training and capacity, but asks why the monk could still doubt at the end of summer. Yantou's explanation that Xuefeng shares his line of birth but not his line of death leads into the one-teaching, three-people contrast. Wansong says the monk and Xuefeng both say, 'What is it?', yet the monk still does not understand when told about the last word: a hair's difference becomes a thousand miles. He also reports another teacher's claim that the monk exposed both elders and does not simply accept every verdict. The phrase locates a difference in understanding within this disputed exchange, not three equally authorized opinions. Linquan Conglun first asks whether Yangshan's sound and form and Shushan's sound and form are the same or different. He then gives the one-teaching, three-people line, and compares Guishan and Yangshan's exchange to father and son fighting together. Shushan and the monk, he adds, end the matter in a word. The phrase connects these differing exchanges while preserving their particular handling. This occurrence does not fix one permanent list of three people for every use of the saying. Senses.Explanation: One stick of incense is a counted offering used in formal dedications, blessings, memorials, and, in some records, as the duration of an act. A later Linji-line master dedicates one stick to his teacher Linji, while Yulin’s ceremony offers separate sticks for the Three Treasures, the empress dowager, and the emperor. Huanyou Chuan names a wider field of recipients, and later memorial scenes burn one stick before the named predecessor’s stupa. These are corpus-wide ceremonial uses, not a Linji-only expression. Where a source uses the burning of one stick as elapsed time, the counted object remains the same but its grammatical role is temporal.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB193.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yinyuan. At the first full-moon festival, Yinyuan Longqi compares a lamp lighting countless lamps and one moon appearing as many reflections. The one is immeasurable and the immeasurable one; large appears within small and small within large. Yet even a Buddha-land on a hair-tip remains a means of guiding and teaching, with no claim on the monk's further turn. After warning against chasing shadows, he returns to the festival's prayer for blessing by raising the mind-lamp over every household. The headword joins plurality and unity, but Yinyuan expressly refuses to make this expansive formula the final accomplishment.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB218.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lanshi Ling. Lanshi Ling raises his whisk and gives the one-and-immeasurable pair. Sky, earth, sun, moon, beings and objects are all threaded through the impossible turtle-hair whisk and bound into one bundle. He casts it down and asks the assembly to look at its layered, gathered appearance. Then he raises Yunmen's eastern mountain walking on water and proposes his own black-lacquered lantern as an answer to where Buddhas emerge. The assembly shouts, he shouts and strikes the staff. The formula is enacted through gathering and casting down; the text does not report that a physical whisk literally contains astronomical bodies.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J29/J29nB234.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yichuyuan. In an address before the memorial tablet of Lady Jihua, Yichu Wuyuan says events of immeasurable ages are present today and today's face appears throughout countless worlds. The one-and-immeasurable pair leads immediately to green bamboo, yellow flowers and clear daylight. If understood, where is birth and death to be sought? He then asks whether the deceased has actually realized this; if not, his final staff strike offers instruction again. The conditional question matters: the cosmic statement does not by itself certify her private realization or make the ceremony's help automatic.

Chulin Shangrui begins with Avalokiteshvara discerning the emptiness of the five aggregates, then says that even the end of birth and death can become a wedge in the eye. Neither living among worldly troubles nor dwelling in remote mountains should abandon care for beings. He gives the one-and-immeasurable pair and joins the Buddhas' compassion with beings' longing for help. Even so, he says, this is not yet the Chan monk's actual path. Asked for that path, he shoulders his staff and heads directly into the peaks. The formula's compassionate reach is affirmed and then placed under a further enacted test.

Senses.Explanation: At the first full-moon festival, Yinyuan Longqi compares a lamp lighting countless lamps and one moon appearing as many reflections. The one is immeasurable and the immeasurable one; large appears within small and small within large. Yet even a Buddha-land on a hair-tip remains a means of guiding and teaching, with no claim on the monk's further turn. After warning against chasing shadows, he returns to the festival's prayer for blessing by raising the mind-lamp over every household. The headword joins plurality and unity, but Yinyuan expressly refuses to make this expansive formula the final accomplishment. Lanshi Ling raises his whisk and gives the one-and-immeasurable pair. Sky, earth, sun, moon, beings and objects are all threaded through the impossible turtle-hair whisk and bound into one bundle. He casts it down and asks the assembly to look at its layered, gathered appearance. Then he raises Yunmen's eastern mountain walking on water and proposes his own black-lacquered lantern as an answer to where Buddhas emerge. The assembly shouts, he shouts and strikes the staff. The formula is enacted through gathering and casting down; the text does not report that a physical whisk literally contains astronomical bodies. In an address before the memorial tablet of Lady Jihua, Yichu Wuyuan says events of immeasurable ages are present today and today's face appears throughout countless worlds. The one-and-immeasurable pair leads immediately to green bamboo, yellow flowers and clear daylight. If understood, where is birth and death to be sought? He then asks whether the deceased has actually realized this; if not, his final staff strike offers instruction again. The conditional question matters: the cosmic statement does not by itself certify her private realization or make the ceremony's help automatic. Senses.Explanation: A measured metaphor unit naming the inherited endowment as one whole field, handed over long ago and left open for all to till. Xuefeng Yicun, recorded in his disciple's extensive log, declares the matter like one whole stretch of field left for everyone to till, with none who fail to owe it strength; Xuansha Shibei, preserved in Dahui's old-case verses, deeds away the field's four borders to all while keeping only the center tree for the old monk; and Huitang Zuxin laments heirs who let the handed-down field run to brambles while chasing daily grain, telling them to claim the original deed with its borders plain. Yuanwu Keqin runs his hall address through false takes at the staff's head and the shout below before landing on the field handed over long ago and plain deceit; Dahui Zonggao holds that one who knows where this whole field lands cannot be moved a hair by birth and death; Buhui Fatong answers the elders' chain by refusing any re-deed, since the field needs no handing over and the four directions are nowhere else; Juelang Daosheng judges the Xuefeng and Xuansha pair as leaving the field mutually abandoned and answers the asking with a staff; and Zhe'an Jingfan tells the assembly everyone has this field, which no season has ever dared damage, so why redraw its bounds.

SearchAliases: this field was entrusted to you long ago
Senses.Note: An old teacher says the field has been entrusted for a long time and waits for the listener to reach it. Later masters question that waiting. Baichi calls three elders overly solicitous; Liao’an says standing, sitting, and ceremonial repentance all miss the time. Tian’an offers thirty blows whether the listener reaches it or not. Tianyin asks why an already entrusted field must still be reached; Buhui says it needs no transfer. Yezhu strikes the table and says the field has long been given. The image presses the gap between possession and recognition.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB202.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baichi. Baichi Xingyuan first cites an unnamed old teacher saying the field was entrusted long ago while he waits standing for the student to reach it, then Fayan's seated version and Foguo's public repentance version. Baichi calls all three caring but ultimately burdensome. He explicitly revoices the same field clause in his own present response and asks why the listeners are still seeking anything here, then drives them away with his staff. The exact headword occurs in both the older quotations and Baichi's later revoicing; this occurrence attributes the active response to Baichi while keeping the earlier voices distinct.

In a winter-solstice hall address, Tian'an Sheng jokes that he will pay gold to anyone who finds where returning yang comes from or where departing yin goes. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J25/J25nB171.xml). Recorded Sayings of Monk Tianyin. Tianyin Yuanxiu cites the unnamed old teacher's standing invitation and Fayan's seated version. In his own comment he asks why, if the field was entrusted long ago, anyone must still reach it. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB276.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Buhui. In a small instruction, Buhui Fatong first quotes an unnamed old teacher promising to wait standing for the student to reach the long-entrusted field and Fayan's seated variant. Buhui then changes the wording rather than repeating the exact headword: this field needs no entrusting. Pointing with his staff, he says there is nowhere in the four directions or above and below where it is absent. The exact phrase here belongs to the older quoted voice, and Buhui's distinct reply rejects the need for a transfer.
